div.p: RELIGIOUS e-SOC/AL

Archdeacon Spooner's Visitation. The Welsh Church Bill. Archdeacon Spooner held a Court at the Werrington Parish Church on Wednesday morning, for the purpose of admitting the newly-elected churchwardens and sidesmen to office.

div.head: Confirmation at Emmanuel Church.
div.p: Confirmation at Emmanuel Church.

The Right Rev. Dr. Eldridge (presiding Bishop of the Reformed Episcopal Church) administered the rite of confirmation at Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, on Sunday evening, when twenty-five candidates (eight boys and 17 girls) were presented. The Bishop gave an impressive address on the words " J\luch hindered snd marvellously helped." He pointed out that it was the universal law that only by conquering difficulty after difficulty could real and lasting success he attained. That was the natural law of the spiritual life. There was always something to heat back the man who sought to run the Christian race, but all the hindrances could he successfully overcome, and they could he marvel- lously helped. In fact in Christian life they might always find more help than hindrances, and in this con- nection the Bishop urged the newly-confirmed to make use of the means of grace within their power in the church. They did not stand alone in spiritus.l strife pnd suffering, and they should remember that work for God not, only glorified Him and assisted others, but enriched themselves.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

In speaking of the region in which love ia not per- mitted to dwell, usually describea as the world and pronounced as alien to God, the Rev. W. Reid, at the above church on Sunday evening, sought to show how, while the term might not be supposed to cover the material world, there might not exist just xcuse for such an injunction in this committee. He proceeded to point out that the "world " indicated that sphere in which life is purely selfish, and which presented itself in the two-fold aspect of an invisible world hidden in man's heart, in which self seized upon ever/ craving vision and contribution of life and caused them to feed self, and an external world which was the creation and visible counterpart of the invisible, a world of lusts and lying in death, which is not of God, but of the corrupted will of man. The folly of allow- ing our love to dwell therein was shown in the fact that to do so invariably meant incapacity to love God, and further in the fact that the " world" was con- tinually passing away and that our capacity for enjoy- ment of it was also passing away. Immortality could only be found where there was obedience to the will of God.

div.head: Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.
div.p: Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.

The Sunday school anniversary services were held on Sunday, and proved a great success. The morning service, held in the chapel, Thewlis-street, was very well attended. The afternoon and evening services in Parr Hall drew large congregations, in fact all the ttiree services were better attended than at any previous anniversary. The special singing (assisted by an orchestra) reflected great credit upon the conductor, Mr. F. Atkinson, must have spent much time in training the large choir (over 250) to such a high state of efficiency. Mr. Tom Tanner presided et the organ. Mr. J. W. Deakin, of Northwicb, was the morning and evening preacher, from whom the congregations heard two very helpful and eloquent sermons.— In the evening he took as his text, "Who shall declare His generation ? " He showed how, during :30 years, ,Jesus bad spent His time in the ordinary humdrum duties of every-day life—He had written no hooks. He had made no lengthy speeches, and at last He had died the most awful of deaths on the Cross, yet the whole Christian world dated theirepochs from the year of His birth. History could not explain Him. Before His birth there was a break in the world's upward progress, and He was a leap forward—the start of a new line of development. Without His direct inspiration nine- tenths of the measures of social improvement passed by the world's Governments could not have been carried out

The Rev. T. T. Jamee, M.A. gave an address to th'e schola-s at the afternoon services, and exhorted all never to be ashamed of the Sunday School. Mr. Thomas Dale, senior superintendent presided. The total collections for the day amounted to .£36 10s.

div.head: Mr. Owen Toole and Catholic Organisation.
div.p: Mr. Owen Toole and Catholic Organisation.

Mr. Owen Took, President of the Warrington Catholic Association, proposing the toast of the Wallasey Catholic Association, at their annual banquet, said that it had been held that the Church, as a Church, was well able to look after its own interests, and that there was no need for these Catholic organisations. Their value, however, had been clearly shown. Cardinal Bourne said a few years ego that the time was not ripe for the formation in England of a political Catholic party, and with this opinion tbe members of Catholic societies agreed. They would all agree that politics should be kept outside the Catholic Associations, in which they banded themselves together in Catholic interests solely. (Hear, hear ) The members were left free to take their place in organisations in which their politics had expression. And if a Catholic led the life he was taught in the Church to lead, he would be a worthy citizen and a worthy member of any party With which he was associated. (Hear, hear.) For , Catholic Associations there was not to-day the need ' thatexisted in 1323 when the first such organisation was formed by Dan O'Connell and Lalor Shiel, with different objects than thosewhich they had at present. The first Association was formed to remove the disabilities under which Catholics then laboured, and the results of the work of that Association were expressed in the liberties they now enjoyed. (Hear. hear).
Responding to the toast, Mr. F. A. Pane welcomed Mn. Toole as a new and distinguished recruit to the Association.

div.head: IHE WONDERS OF NATURE.
div.p: IHE WONDERS OF NATURE.
C rl7lZlci if T .1
AI3MOTSIZ-PLAI'I7.I) ANIMALS.

Man caLnot 1 ightly claim to be the first Inventor of coats cf mail and the armour-plated. coating ,tsed for defensive purposes by our early knights. At least two types of defensive armour are common in nature. The first type almost exactly resembles the jointed plate-armour of n)edieval knights: as shown in the armadilla and the lobster and closely followed by the tortoise, the beetle, and many hard-shelled insects. The second type is both offensive and defensive at one and the same time; as exhibited in the porcupine, the hedgehog, the bramble, the thistle, and a host of other plants and animals. With the second group the armour consists, not of plates, but of prickly tipines and thorns, which repel assailant,, by wounding the tender flesh of the mouth or lips. Such prickliness of surface is the commonest among all the protective devices invented by living creatures.

div.head: DOIIN COMEDIAN.
div.p: A DOIIN COMEDIAN.

The common English hedgehog is a good ex- ample of the prickly-a rmoured class. Ills tamiliar squat, square. inquisitive appearance, with very short legs and no tail to speak of, in fact one of nature's low comedians, covered on the back and upper surface with dirty white spines, and there you have him. Comic to us he is serious to him- self. He i not built for hasty movements. but slowly and sedately he strolls calmly along on his bandy legs, showing little sense of fear, knowing that even when caught out in the open, he has only to roll himself into a ball and his coat of spines is a fitting armour when he helps it to be an effective passive resistance. Though he belongs to a very ancient and honourable family —that of the insect eaters—long since superseded in most place,,, of the earth by more advanced types, still he manages to hold his own in the struggle for life against al comers, mainly by virtue of his excellent suit of spiny armour.

div.head: USING UP THE ODDS AND ENDS,
div.p: USING UP THE ODDS AND ENDS,

Nature is a great utiliser of odds and ends; she always finds some unexpected use for dis: carded organs. Thus we have some of the cactuses, turning themsei,•es into vegetable hedgehogs, by turning what slauld really be the 'cares of the plant into spines in order to protect the precious store of internal water laid in by the spongy pith for the plant's own pur- poses. Even lizards have adopted some such protection from their enemies in hot countries where food is scarce and hunger drives the few animals which can exist in a dry region to attack every living thing they come across, be it animal or v.getable. The Moloch is a good example. It frequents the driest and sandiest soils of Australia, and it is thus specially adapted for holding its own against the local lizard-eaters of its neighbourhood. Science knows it by the scriptural title of Moloch—and, indeed, it is ugly enough to be called any bad names: but the Western Australians describe it familiarly as the " thorny devil."

div.head: WELSH BILL.
div.p: THE WELSH BILL.

In the courue of his charge he dealt with the Welib Church question. He said the theory that this continual agitation against the Bill must necessarily prove futile was a pure assumption, and it was the plain duty of Churchmen to foster by all legitimate means that public opinion adverse to the Bill which was steadily growing not only among Churchmen and Churchwomen, but among fair-minded and really religious Nonconformists as well. With regard to the financial aspect, when a Corporation, sole or otherwise, was dissolved, the whole of the property passed to the Crown for want of an owner, so that all property belonging to bishops and clergy by right of their respective offices would become alienated from the Church. In that way £250,000 per annum given for religions purposes by the devotion of their ancestors was to be withdrawn and assigned to the erection of libraries, district halls, dispensaries and other public institutions, excellent in themselves hut quite foreign to the intention of the original donors. Among the effects of the withdrawal of property, there would be the leaving of 193 parishes at once and ultimately of 511 parishes (more than one half of the total number in Wales) with no endowment and of 53 parishes with ss. per week, while if what was to be lilt so generously to the Church of her own possession were equally distributed among the beneficed clergy ot Wales, each recipient would be in the enjoy- ment of the magnificent sum of Bs. per week. Besides that the stipends of 560 curates (more than one-third of the total number of the clergy in Wales) would cease at once. It might be argued by some that the fete of the Church in Wales was no concern of theirs—a most indefensible, harmful and short-sighted position to t,ke up. They were all interested, or claimed to be by profession or ought to be interested in the cause of religion, its strengthening, quickening and diffusion. It was religion which would inevitably suffer, at least. for a time, if the Church in Wale 3 was despoiled. The Welsh dioceses were an integral part of the English Church of the Province of Canterbury. Disestablish- ment and Disendowment in the Principality were sure precursors of the seine in England. Therefore let them take warning betimes and be up and doing.

div.head: LATE CHANCELLOR ESPIN.
div.p: THE LATE CHANCELLOR ESPIN.

The Archdeacon paid a tribute to the late Chancellor Espin, whose intimate knowledge of matters eccle4i- astical, staunch yet broad-minded Churchmanship, com- bined with a courteous and sympathetic nature, eminently fitted him for the high office which he so long and efficiently held in that and the diocese of Chester, as well as for the dignified and important post of Prolocutor to the Lower House of the Convocation of York. To his successor—Mr. Cballoner Dowdall— the diocese had accorded a hearty welcome, and his general culture, training as a barrister, his interest in ecclesiastical affairs, and his demeanour as a gentleman and a Churchman, had already manifested themselves in the transactions of the first Courts over which he had presided. They heartily wished him a long and successful tenure of office. "GRAVE SCANDAL AND _DISQUIETUDE.

Grave scandal and disquietude had at various times been created by the introduction, through want of due precaution, into the celebration of Church offices of unauthorised, irregular, and even criminous clerks, and indeed of persons not in Holy Orders at all. The Bishops therefore desired that the following regulations should be strictly carried out :—(1) In every church there should be kept and duly exhibited to the Rural Dean and Archdeacon, when so requiring it, a book containing the names, addresses, and indication as to licence of all strange preachers ; (2) No stranger unlicensed by the diocesan, and personally unknown to the incumbent wishing to employ him' should officiate at all in the particular parish without the exhibition of his letters of Orders and testimonials as required by law ' • (3) No clergyman, unlicensed or unpertuitted by the Bishop, should be engaged for more than one Sunday to officiate in any Church, without his name and references being signified to his Lordship.

div.head: PENSIONS FOR THE CLERGY.
div.p: PENSIONS FOR THE CLERGY.

The BISHOP wished special attention to be directed to the scheme for providing clergy pensions, thereby enabling incumbents who, through advancing years or other infirmities, were incapable of efficiently discharg- ing the duties of their cure, to retire with a fair prospect of a comfortable provision in old-age, and without reducing the income of their successors by claiming and appropriating some portion of the emolu- ments of the vacated benefice—a procedure which had frequently greatly impro.verished the incoming incum- bent, and serionsly handicapped the effective working of the parish.

div.head: INSURANCE
div.p: INSURANCE

The ARCHDEACON emphasised the importance of adequately insuring all churches and parochial buildings and spoke strongly of the criminal folly of exposing parishes, by under-insurance or no insurance at all, to the risk of having to find large sums of money for rebuilding. In that archdeaconry, and indeed throughout the diocese, considerable advance had been made in regard to insur- ance during the last few sears.

div.head: EASTER OFFERINGS.
div.p: EASTER OFFERINGS.

Allusion was made to the fact that in five parishes included in the visitation the laudable and rubrical practice of presenting Easter offerings te the incumbent was still unobserved. Not only were Easter offerings due of common rigbt, but they afforded members of any congregation a special opportunity for expressing appreciation of the services rendered to them by those who ministered in holy thing, and often proved the means whereby an overworked incumbent or curate was enabled to obtlin that much-needed holiday which would not otherwise come within his reach.

div.head: LAND AND SEA ARMOUR.
div.p: LAND AND SEA ARMOUR.

The 'highest point armour attained to was a Sp] end i dly fitting jointed case of iron plates, all :exquisitely polished. The joints of the plates were arranged in a most ingenious in so as to move freely over and under one another, with- out exposing any part of the body for a moment to the deadly chance of a sword-lunge or a lance thrust. Yet if one looks at, a lobster's tail we see at a glance that all these • clever devices of mall's imagining had been invented and patented king before by Mother Nature. The elaborate workmanship of the Plantagenet craftsmen, wlm cased knight and horse for the battlefield or the tournament in movable plaqi-gs of glistening metal, Was but a poor imitati jof the great skill with which the unheeded crustaceans of the time protected every vulnerable portion of their bodies from the assaults and attacks of their aubmarine enemies. Shielded by his impenetrable corslet of stony armour, provided with huge pinching claws which can crush a sea-shell like so much paper, he is a soldier and member of a dominant type, capable of attacking almost any t9.P Ile meets in his own element. TWO COATS OF MAIL.

Perhaps the most marvellous, however, of all the mail-coated animals are our good old friends, the common tortoise and turtles. We have been so long familiar with their shape, and their coating of bone and horn, that we have long ago ceased even to wonder at them. There are usually two shells, one covering the -upper part of the body and one the lower; and in many species of tortoise, the head and legs can be entirely withdrawn within shelter of the shelly covering. In such eases, just as in that of the armadillo, the gaps in the armour are neatly filled up, for the exposed parts are covered on purpose with horny masks or aprons, which thus complete and round off the entire defensive Diechanism. Crocodiles have their backs, tails, and the under side of their bodies amply de- fended by square horny shields, which move freely against one another at the edges. In Hifi more vulnerable parts. such as the back, how. ever, the wily crocodile does not trust to ths strength of these horny plates alone; he 'has developed beneath them a similar series of stout hotly plaques, each of which is neatly and deftly jointed at the edge with the ones beside it. Sportsmen will tell you that the only sure way to kill a cm ocotillo is to hit him in the eve. 1-:,4rywherc, else a bullet glides off him harm. lessly. He lolls in the water unconcerned and Avinlz.

div.head: SUFFRAGETTES ASSAULTED BY WOMEN.
div.p: SUFFRAGETTES ASSAULTED BY WOMEN.

Women carrying sandwich boards advertising a local militant suffrage meeting were set upon by a number of women at Holloway, North London. Their boards were seized, placards announcing the meeting were destroyed and the suffragettes were harrassed until the police arrived and escorted them away.

div.head: "GOLDEN SANDS" OF BLACKPOOL.
div.p: THE "GOLDEN SANDS" OF BLACKPOOL.
At Blrckpool, the annral sale of licences for stands en the toreshore realised the record sure of £1,770. As much as £lOO was paid for one stmi for the sale of ioe-cream.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"A BUTTERFLY ON THE WHEEL."

" A Butterfly on the Wheel," by E. G. Hemmerde N.C., M.P., and Francis Neilson, M.P., will be the attraction at the Court Theatre next week. Mr. Arthur Hardy is sending his London Company with the play. We notice in the cast Miss Francis Titheredge. who plays the trying part of Peggy Admaston, Miss Violet Greville as Pauline and Miss Daisy Cordell as Lady Attwell, Mr. Douglas Greet as Lord Ellerdene, Mr. Herbert Greville as S. W. Robert F 5 ffe, N.C., and Mr. T. A. Shannon as Coßingwood. In Act 3, there is one of the most realistic Divorce Court scenes ever wit- nessed. All the London scenery and t fleets are carried. The Company are playing this week at the Theatre Royal Portsmouth to record business.
MISS VIOLET GREVILLE, as Pauline, in "A Butterfly on the Wheel."

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

A capital programme was well received by two large " houses " on Monday evening. One of the weirdest spectacular productions vse have seen ( n the variety stage is the comedy drama "Change," pre- sented by James A. and Herbert B. Jewel's Company. Some lightning scenic transformations are executed, for in an incredibly short time we are transferred from a bar in Whitby to the miser's castle, where the audience is treated to many gruesome surprises. Six persons are involved in the cast, Mr. James A. Jewel calling for hearty applause for the very clever manner in which he plays the part of the miser. Mr. Herbert B. Jewel is also successful as Joe Dunn, the bibulous , sailor. Mr. Fred Marsh as Peter Sparkles is respon- sible for the major portion of the comedy, ?especially so with his adventures in the haunted castle. Mr. Leslie Bishop is well placed as Jack Pedlar, and Miss Queenie Harvey and Miss Helen Elmer contribute their quota to a novel production. The Bros. Jenkins work very hard and score a distinct success in their really funny acrobatic eccentricities. They are smart tumblers and burlesque comediens. James Dixon calls for a cordial reception as a baritone of a good quality, who is heard to advantage in his two songs. " Mrs. Edwards and her cat" is the title of a farcical act presented by Johnny Fuller and Miss Ada King. From beginning to end there is not a dull moment, the audience rolling with laughter all the tune. Karr and Kooney create much merriment with their funny gags and cross-talking. Their string- ing together of a number of snatches from pantomime , songs is exceedingly smart. Spry and Mot ti make a welcome return visit and, as usual, are favourities with the audience. ,Their turn is indeed a happy mixture of amusement Mabel Costello, described as "The Magnet," has excellent drawing powers for she is a dashing and captivating c.,mmedienne with catchy songs. "The bachelors bride" is a humorous picture shown on the cinema. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

A highly attractive bill for-next week includes : Newhouse and Ward trio, comedy cycliats ; The Gascoignes, cnmedy jugglers, with their wonderful dog Bertha ; Victor and Louis, comedians ; linnie Paget, the concertina queen ; The Three Owens; "Dollies deforming themselves" ; The Firnans,original comedy scene "The Fire Station" ; Lorrie Elliston, inimitable vocalist ; Kathleen O'Hanlon and Kiri Rivkin, musicians, vocalists and dancers.

div.head: PICTUREDROME.
div.p: THE PICTUREDROME.

The star picture for Monday, Tuesday, and Wednes- day is "The Vengeance of Durand."' This is one of the Vitagraph great dramas and is in two parts. "Dora Thorne "will be shown on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. It is a pathetic story of the marriage of a lodgekeeper's daughter to the Earl's son, and what came of it.

div.head: "FROM MANGER TO GROSS" AT PARK HALL.
div.p: "FROM MANGER TO GROSS" AT PARK HALL.

Messrs. Andrews Pictures Ltd. announce the presentation of the remarkable film "From Manger to Cross: Or Jesus of Nazareth" at the Parr Hall twice daily—at 2.30 and 7.30 p.m.—next week. The pictures were actually taken in the Holy Land, which has changed so little in appearance, in the manners, customs, and costumes of the inhabitants, that one might almost say it is to-day as it was in the time of Christ. 'l'he utmost pains have been taken to ensure the historical accuracy of the scenes, every possible authority being consulted, notably the remarkable series of religious pictures by the French artist Tissot, who spent twelve years in the country in order to get his general setting and details correct. Music has been carefully chosen to aid in creat- ing that atmosphere of reverence which the manage- ment desire shall predominate. Among the notable people who have seen the film is the Dean of St. Paul's (Dr. Wm. Inge) who states : " I thought the exhibition reverent and beautiful. I shall certainly recommend others to see it."

div.head: THEATRE ROYAL.
div.p: THEATRE ROYAL.

Mr. Manville Morton achieved a notable artistic success on Monday at the above tbeatre, when tbe Repertory Company presented "Send him victorious," which wss received with enthusiasm by crowded houses The scenery, which since Mr. Morton's arrival has been a feature of the productions, was painted by the resident Lscenic artist, Mr. Walter Barlow, the last scene—Ravonia—deserving special merit. The Royal has been for a long time in the hands of the elec- tricians, and when the lighting effects on the stage are- complete it will undoubtedly be one of the finest install- ations in a theatre of its kind in the kingdom. The work is being carried out by the Central Theatres chief electrician (Mr Foster), and on Monday the lighting was a commendable feature. The theatre is now to undergo re-decoration, and under Mr. Morton's guidance, it is taking a worthy place among repertory theatres.—The play deals with the adventures of a young English officer in Ravonia. The King was well portrayed by Mr Sidney Ellis. Col. Heinsich Kaufman, the scheming traitor, was played by Mr Clavering Craig, who in a short

time has become extremely popular. Mr Chas) E Warne made a commendable Karl Strausfh Captain Frank Allison was in the capable, hands of Mr. Charles Vivian Charles. Mr. Edwin Mackenzie appeared in his original role, Sergeant Max. The popular comedian, Mr. Jack Carroll, played Geordie Walker and was ably supported by Miss Vera Olga as Gretchen Holtz. Countess Cara Von Michlenberg was impersonated in telling style by Miss Hazel Head and Aliss Phyllis Morton, back after a week's indisposition, gave a charming study of Ethel Harding and was warmly welcomed. Next week the Company will present the charming; Anglo-French play 'Under Two Flags" front Ouida's famous novel.

MR. P. M. OLIVER'S CHALLENGE Ta
INSURANCE ACT DETRACTORS.
The Courage of the Government.

Mr. P. M. Oliver, prospective Liberal condidate for the Knutsford Division, had an enthusiastic welcome from the members of the Stockton Heath Women 'R Liberal Association on Thursday evening when he attended their annual social gathering in the Provi- dence schoolroom and gave an interesting speech on current politics. There was a large attendance at tea, which was followed by a concert. Mrs. Henry Robert 4 (president of the essociation) was in the chair, and among others present were —Mrs. Grounds (hon secretary), Mrs. Longland (hon. treasurer), the Rev. G. Curtis, Councillor Henry Roberts, Messrs. J. Longland, W. H. Sherburn, E. Lloyd Jones, and S. Albinson. Mrs. Roberts commented with satisfaction upon the increasing interest displayed in the work of the association, which was entering upon its fourth year. Mr. P. M. Oliver said he looked to the Women's Liberal Association to he of great assistance when the battle came. There were six branches in the division and everyone of them was doing well. The old ones were not becoming decr?pit and the young ones were bouncing children. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Oliver next quoted the lines of Burns :- 0' wad some power the giftie gie us To see airselves as ithers see us. He often wished that politicans could be given that gift and particularly that the Opposition might have it at the present time. If they could only see themselves. as the Liberals saw them, they might think a little better of their ways. (Laughter.) They were con- stantly calling theras4v es a united party. Lora Derby and Mr. Boner Law hardly ever addressed a meeting without making a declaration to that effect. Liberals were not ceaselessly speaking about their unity—they took it for granted and went on their way rejoicing. SF.RIOUS AND AMUSING. The Conservatives looked upon the Liberals with views that were altogether distorted by party passion- They invented all sorts of calumnies against them, some of which were amusing, while some were very serious. An example of the amusing kind was given a short time ago when Mr. Touche, a Conservative member of Parliament who was also chairman of a company whicb provided penny in the slot machines for the railway stations, solemnly told a meeting of shareholders that, the bad coin placed in automatic machines had more than doubled since the Liberal Government came !;10 power. (Laughter.) That was one form of abuse,which they could stand very well, but there were more vicious kinds—insinuations, for which there wee - not the slightest justification. The Liberal party would, however, live through them, as it had done before, without suffering any harm. DOMINATING(AppIause).- FOREIGN POLITICS. The other day he was reading a remarkable article which appeared in one of the chief German newspapers. It dealt chiefly with foreign politics and it began ito follows :-- Sir Edward Grey assembled in London two peace conferences, directed the eyes of the world, and especially of the East, on London, and presided over the Ambassadors' conference in the capaeitY of an arbitrator. The German therefore saw England, under ibis; supposedly incapable and degenerate Government-- (Laughter)—and, looking perhaps with envious eyeg, he saw that London once again was becoming the centre of the universe. He saw Sir Ede ard GreY assembling two conferences and dominating inter- national politics. For a long time the clouds of War had been hanging over ?Abe East and the Britiali Government—and all Governments—had been passing through a more anxious period than many people realized. Happily the fire which originated in th,e Balkan States had not, as was at one time feared,. spread over Europe, but we owed the maintenance 01' peace to a large extent to Sir Edward Grey and this despised Liberal government. A COURAGEOUS GOVERNMENT. The German writer from whom he had quoted wenV -on to say : It is necessary to bear in mind that Sir Edward Grel9 belongs to a Government whose very existence a based upon initiative, lifa, courage, progress, Sfl that this Government is not afraid o cool col° in every democratic draught, but is, on th-, control, leading the nation against everything that tis become obsolete." That, remarked Mr. Oliver, was high praise from 0, oreigner. He had seen what many Liberals had Nile,' o realize—that there were two sides to this Governi. ment. It bad not only again attained for England that great position in international politics which she 10.9., at the time of the Boer war, but bad also turned lt'" attention to domestic politics. It bad led the count' against an obsolete House of Lords ; it was now lead- ing it against an obsolete land system. Some peoPl? might object that such work was destructive. After al: they were not only Liberals but Radicals, and a Radies, meant a man who went to the roots of things : If thei destroyed something that was outworn and obsolete, they in reality left things better than they found them" If they destroyed the veto of the House of Lords tba loft a more powerful House of Commons, and if thef destroyed the present, union with Ireland, they estab. lished a better, sounder and more generous one. A CHALLENGE. As to the Government not being afraid of democrat draughts, they caught a very bad cold last year nver the Insurance Act. They were gradually losing weight every way, and wise physicians werelstanding round fie°' anYing they would soon be dead and buried. However'" they had now recovered and he believed they were- stronger than ever they had been since 1909. Everl speech which he made last year about the Insurance,. Act, he would not mind repeating this year. Applaune'i He did not think be could say that of most of the Con: servative orators in that division. Mayor Allan SYk,e; himself did not criticise the Act unfairly, but he (the speaker) challenged many of those who spoke in tbe' Conservative interest to deliver the same speeches ca the Act which they made twelve months ago. They se; the Government were going to destroy the friendle societies and that the approved societies would 01(1_ their doors. As a matter of fact over 13,000,000 pe01),% were insured through those societies. (Applawe';., Many speakers stated that they did not know vvbethe the benefits of the Act would ever come into operatio?" They were saying that in public houses in Cheshire iv December, and that money was being taken from tbr, people which would never be given back. Kvery wervi there had been paid in sickness benefits £142,000 and !ci maternity benefits £30,000. Opponents of the Act Effild it would destroy the freedom of the people, but it 104 actually made the people freer, as the returns pauperism were declining and would continue to do Ss' as the benefits of the Act were realized. (Applause-)

PENSIONS AND PAUPERISM. Now that they had gotvtheir pensia p they seemed to live longer. (Applause.) The effect !: the pensions on out-door pauperism in Cheshire more marked, the number of recipknts of relief Wit') declined from 3,157 in 1906 to 286 in 1912. Otho-t... had been bo intent upon social reform that their l look had become purely national. The present Libe,4o Government had not only caused London to dorniorhe Europe and become, in a real sense the centre of rug universe, but had not forgotten to feed the str4r° children in the schools. div.head: LANCASHIRE INSURANCE COMMITTEE
div.p: LANCASHIRE INSURANCE COMMITTEE
CLERK.
A £5OO APPOINTMENT.

At a meeting of the Lancashire Insurance Committee on Monday a spirited discussion arose over a recom- mendation of the Finance Committee to appoint Mr. Harcourt Clare, clerk, at a silary of £5OO per year. Mr. Walker concluded that the Insurance Act hid not been pasied for the benefit of insured people but for the benefit of the County Council staff. It was coming a bit thick, be said, to pay £5OO per year for. a part- time man.

Mr. Ormerod said Mr. Clare was a man of outstand- ing ability, eminently fitted to deal with the intricacies ot the Act. The County Council, the Pubic Health Committee, and the Insurefloe Committee were really and truly partne s, and Mr. Clare could competently serve each partner in the true interests of all. Mr. Forshaw opposed the recommendation,and moved that the committee advertise for e permanent clerk. lie asked the other members to join with him to bring about the time when public bodies would not think of employing a spare-time man at a salary of £lO per week, hut ould engage a -full-time man who would serve the best interests of tho committee.

Mr. Wit Men said it would be a public scandal if they gave a man who had already £2,000 or £3,000 per sear another position amounting t.,1 £5OO, while outside they had plenty of men williog and able to take up the duties.

Aldarman Scott Barrett (chairman of the County Council) said Mr Clare had managed tho committee's affairs in a manner in which scarcely anyone else in the country could have done. J. was impossible to go out- side and get a clerk for £5OO to do work as capably es Mr Clare.

Sir Henry lidabert, M.P., said that even if Mr Clare had fifty appointments each worth £l,OOO per year, he would be dirt cheap to the committee at .C 50014 advis- ing them how to surmount the difficulty of the Insur- ance Act. _ _ _
Only uevfn voted for the amendment. which was defeated, and the committee's recommendations were carried.

div.head: WALLFLOWER EARLY PARIS,
div.p: WALLFLOWER EARLY PARIS,

This useful plant is undoubtedly ore of the most valuable of Wallflowers, owing to the long period it m y be bad in bloom. By sowing seeds now, flowers may be Lad from the end of the summer on through the autumn and vtinter—providing they are planted in a warm, sheltered spot and the weather mild—till the spring, when they are followed by the :Wallflowers that are usually grown, giving us this favourite flower most of the you, The early Paris type can be had in yellow and bruwn shades, and seed is 9.be3p.--" The Varden.'

div.head: MOSES AS SANITARIAN.
div.p: MOSES AS SANITARIAN.
Religious Authority for the Promotion of Bodily Health.
STRIKING LECTURE BY DR. MANSON.
Dr. Manson, before a good attendance of the members of the Bewsey Adu:t Schoil, 1 ist Sunday morning, spoke on the questim of democracy and health.

The speaker referred to what D. ILbhert and Mr. Flood had told them about the causation of disease and of the methods of promoting health, and said that he would treat the subj( ct rather frcm the standpoint of the responsible citizen than from that of the individual man or woman. This involved the con- sideration of wider notions than were usually associated with health problems. Health meant wholeness or soundness, and the term should include the mind as well as the body We were apt to concentrate our thoughts on problems of bodily health, and forget about the equally important. problems of mental health. The largo army of the mentally disordered—about a quarter of a million in this country should bo in itself a fact striking en' ugh to prevent us forgetting the question of the hygiene of the mind. The great religions of the world -always tried to deal with both sides of the health question, aud according to their various standards and traditions the h&y mind was the healthy mind. They also had laws and rites laid down by the full force of religious authority for the promotion of bodily health. Sir John Cockburn, the other day at the Royal Sanitary Institute, saiu that Moses was the first medical officer of health, and there can be no doubt that the principles of the Mosaic rules of health— if not the rules themselves—are still followed in our public health legislation of to-day. THE FIRST CENSUS.

In Leviticus there are rules of dietary, rules for cleansing domestic utensils, for the isolation of contagious disease —leprosy—and for the cleansing of infected houses. Moses also took the first census. There was an absolute necessity of a census in order to attain anything like accuracy in public health work. Hinduism and Mohammedanism had also strict rules of dietary and among the Hindus religious sects are divided by peculiarities of diet. All are agreed that prk should be prohibited, very probably because it was found that the pig was very liable to be infested with tape worm and other noxious parasites and s'..) spread disease amongst the faithful. There is a tradition that Buddha himself died from eating dried boar's flesh the oriental lotm of smoked ham. The vice of those old religions was that these laws for bodily health were taken as an end in them- selves and a man was inclined to think hirnself a saint if he abstained from pork or ate a certain kind of bean.
The speaker thought this vice still existed among those who thought long and seriously over physical health and who did not deem themselves at all religious.

div.head: BODY AND THE MIND.
div.p: THE BODY AND THE MIND.

It was characteristic of Christianity that it threw the Mosaic code to the winds and concentrated on mental health cr holiness In the course of time its devotees and heroes neglected the body altogether in order to attain perfection of mind. They rejeiced in dirt, disorder and vermin, and the consequences followed in the r_c.-eat plagues which swept Europe in the middle ages. The great plague of the 14th century nearly depopulated Europe, broke the lily Empire and led to the renaissances and the revival of learning in the 15th century. Since then the pro- gress of the sciences has placed public health in the keeping of secular authority, and epidemic diseases are kept in check and many diseases abolished. But secular authority is not all powerful. It deals with masses, not with individuals, and there is plenty of scope for the individual to violate nearly all the rules LI health without coming into conflict with the health authority. At the most it can educate the individual. How far such teachieg is to have practical result depends on the co-operation of the taught, and here it seemed to the speaker that a taro Christian Science could be evolved by giving the full force of religious authority to the practice of the truths garnered by modern science. All sides of the health question
would then have full weight, and they as Citizens sh:;uld consider this as one of the chief responsibili- ties of democracy.

div.head: WAGES AND HEALTH.
div.p: WAGES AND HEALTH.
WARRINGTON COUNCILLOR AND ECONOMIC DIFFICULTY.

" Warrington stands amongst the healthiest of Lincashire towns' was the gratifying declaration of Councillor J Hawthorn in a 11,:.alth Week address at a meeting cf Wycliffe P.S.A. Society on Sunday. He added that we had reason to congratulate ourselves that we had succeeded in recent years in materially reducing the death-rate. We were fortunate in not having such a large percentage of married women in mills as obtained in some of the cotton towns of Lancashire and which had such a seri,us effect on the infantile death-rate.

here was no need to take a pessimistic view of the he ilth of the community. There was an all-round improvement. One had only to look back at the con- dition of things in the nineteenth centuly to realise that, There was, however, still a great wastage of human life which was preventible. We must not overlook the fact that the health of the community restul largely with ourselves Improved sanitary conditions might do much, but those required the intelligent and responsible co-operation cf everyone. The essentials to Om preservation of health were pure air, wholesome dict, regular exercise, scrupulous eleanlinr ss, proper clothing aLd regular hours. The local Heath Corn- nittee was doing its duty in carrying out the powers entrusted to it and in this connection the speaker instanced the efforts which w ere being made to deal with consumption and also to ensure the purity of the food supply. It was, however, one thing for the Corporation to see that the food supplied was wholesome, and quite another for the workers to obtain the wherewithal to buy it. That brought us to the far deeper question of the wage level. We bad set the worker an impossible task when we asked him to feed, house and clothe himself, his wife and his family on £1 a week. Under modern conditions that could not be done, and that economic question would have to be faced if the stamina and vitality of the race were to be maintained. Parents and children were being pinched of their food and we were suffering for it in a toll of illness which was making the workers less fit for their daily toil.

Slums were a legacy from the past, but the Health Committee had pursued a policy of demolition of insanitary houses which had made a vast improvement of recent years. Despite the opposition of interested property owners, some of those plague spots were dis- appearing, and we might hope that the time was not far distant when we should have no slums to visit during Health Week. Even the slums presented contrasts of how people viewed their private responsi- bility to the commanity. Some of the houses were clean and neatly kept and the dwellers in them possessed a knowledge of the value of personal cleanli- ness, whilst others were dirty hovels with unwashed and unkempt occupiers, a source of danger to them- selves and to their neighbours. The abuse of alcohol was very prevalent in Wallington. Anyone who had walked ur streets on Saturday night was aware of that. The habit of drinking led to neglect of family, t) forgetfulness of all social duties, to distaste for work, to want, tLeft and crime. It led at the very least to a hospital, for alcoholism caused a great variety of diseases add rendered more serious every acute ill- ness Maintenance of health and the avoidance of the conditions which induced disease were a matter of public and social duty on the part of every member of the communi.y. Legislation could lay down regulations as to the provision of light and air in private dwellings, shops, schools and factories, and it might enforce precautions as to the contamination of milk, but it could riot effectively help those who would not help themselves. The meeting was presided over by Mr 13 Farrar and other members taking part were Mr W Beswick and Mr C Cotton. Miss Senior feelingly sang " A dream of Paradise," Mr W II Paybn presiding at the organ,

div.head: DEATH OF CEIAPLAIN TO TIIE BLIND.
div.p: DEATH OF CEIAPLAIN TO TIIE BLIND.

The Rev T W M Lund, for 29 years chaplain of the Church for the Blind, Liverpool, died ou Monday in his 71st year. For several years he was chaplain to the Ist Lancashire and Cheshire Royal Garrison Artillery. He was also a member of the Committee of the School for the Blind, Liverpool, and the Committee of the St Paul's Eye Hospital, Liverpool, and a vice- president of the National Home Reading Union. Ile graduated at Cambridge in 1866 and held various curacies for the following five years. Then for thirteen years, from 1871 to 1881, in which year he went to Liverpool, he was Rector of the Church of St John the Evangelist, at Cheetham, Manchester, He was the author ot two books on Como and the Italian Lakes.

div.head: MILITARY ABSENTEE.
div.p: MILITARY ABSENTEE.

In our last week's report of the Police Court we unfortunately gave the name of Richard J Burke as the sergeant of the King's Liverpool Regiment, who was charged with having absented himself from the annual training in 1912. The defendant's name was Thomas Wilson, and Sergeant Burke to whom we express our regret for the error, was the witness who bad charge of the case

div.head: GYMNASTIC DISPLAY.
div.p: GYMNASTIC DISPLAY.
THE MAYOR AND PHYSICAL CULTURE.

In these days, when the value of phyical culture is so generally recognized, the work cf an institution like the Borough Gymnasium commands an ever- increasing degree of interest. It was gt atifying to see the large audiecce which assembled on Monday evt fling when the pupils - foremost among whom are the champion right—gave their annual gymnastic display, together with Swedish and musical dtir.s. The neatness and prec:sion with which the various evolutions weie gone through spoke much for the exc( hence of the training given by Mr. A Mottram who directed the exercises. The champion eight worthily prcved their claim to that proud title by their smart work OD the parallel bars, including the forma- tipn of pyramids. They also executed some striking feats on the rings. Great excitement was aroused by the tug-of-war between big girls and boys. As in 1912, the " weaker " sex proved the stronger, winning the first two pulls, and thus achieving the victory. In a similar contest betwecn the little boys and girls, the girls were also triumphant, thus avenging their defeat of last year. The programme also included displays with the dumb-hells, Indian clubs and bar bells, rope climbing, marching and Swedish drills, girls and boys atike acquitting themselves most creditab!y, Miss W. Jones (winner of the United Kingdom championship) gave a " club FE.lo " in finished style. Miss A. Clayton provided the pianoforte music for the exercises. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided and was accompani«l by the Mayoress, who distributed the prizes. Members of the Gymnasium Committee in attendance were Councillors Cunningtoa, Broadhurst, and Shaw and Mr. T. Locker.

div.head: MUSCLES AND THE MIND.
div.p: THE MUSCLES AND THE MIND.

The MAYOR 'warmly commended the ircreased attention which had been given to gymnastics and physical exercises of late years. He could remember the time when comparitively little exercise of that kind was engaged in, and of all the improvements which had ta'ien place in the education of the young he did not know of any that could be so important and useful. He could also remember the time when the principal schools had hardly any spice attached to them for playground purposes. The first school he went to over 30 yea's ago, was a small one, containing 20 scholars. The schoolmaster took them out fcr a walk for an hour two or three times a week, and they were hardly allowed to look at anything or anybody. The master, like a shepherd, walked behind his flock, and that was about all the physical exercise they got. How much better off were the children of the present day ! (Hear, hear, and applause.) The muscles were exercised with the will, and the will bad a great power over the muscles, if n( t complete power. That being so it was important that muscular exercises should be conducted upol certain principles, mainly th it they should be congenial to the mind. The boys and girls who engaged in the, exercises they had seen that night should be fond of them ; otherwise they ought not to engage in them. They should not indulge in exercises when the mind or body was tired, and another pre- caution was to adapt boys and girls to certain forms of exercise. In conclusion his Worship said this was the third time the Mayoress and he had attended that annual event and he had no hesitation in saying that the performances that night had excellei all the previous ones. That fact spoke well for the progress of the gymnasium and the tact and skill of the director. (Applause).

div.head: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.
div.p: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

The Mayoress first distrit.uted the prizes to the champion eight. Nlr. T. Maio (the chamoion of the team) rectived a gold medal, Mr. S. Hied° (2nd) a silver medal with gold centre, and the remaining six a silver medal each, viz.: J. Sanders, J. BoEcow, A. Barry, A. Lloyd, A. Holmes and NV. Sitson. Other prizes wore awarded as follows —Boss': class: 1, J. Morris; 2, A. Boardman ; 3, C. Perks and T. J. Hill. Girls' class : 1, M. G.,lhourne ; 2, L. Lunt ; and 3, 11. Sergf ant. A v. to of thanks was passed to the Mayor and Mayoress on the motion of Councillor BROADHURST, seconded by Councillor CUNNINGToN.

div.head: BABY.
div.p: BABY.
AND THE FOOD PROBLEM.

No one doubts the immense advantage of breast milk over the very best of artificial foods, and in many instances the use of the bottle is prejudicial, not alone to baby's health, but to his very life. The latest information is of a Me where the child was born,weighing only Vb.,was naturally very weakly, and would not have lived if placed on the bottle. As a last desperate chance the mother decided to give a trial to lactagol, a preparation which almost every chemist has in stock, and which, taken by the nursing mother, results in an excellent supply of breast milk, containing its due proportion of fats and albumens. In the case mentioned, lactsgol was taken, and within 12 hours of the tint dose the full fl,w of milk returned and continued. _ _ _ . . .

Every mother, therefore, desiring thus to do her duty by her baby, should obtain a few ounces of la.ctagol, and take a teaspoonful three times a day. As a rule, the result is quickly apparent, though in a low cases it may be delayed. In the case mentioned, the mother,by taking lactagol and thereby increasing and enriching her breast milk, undoubtedly saved her baby's life, and many thousands of others have done the same. - .

_ Another great advantage in the use of lactagol,which, by the way, is quite pleasant to take, is that it prevents all nursing pains, and at the same time is quite an excellent tonic for those weakened by illness or overstrain.
Mothers may have every confidence in taking 'Wage], as it is a pure extract of cotton seed, and not a manufactured composition.

div.head: STAGE MORALS
div.p: STAGE MORALS
MR. HAROLD SMITH, M.P., ADVO- CATES ABOLITION OF CENSORSHIP.

Mr. Harold Smith, M.P , took part in the debate in the Hou,e of Commons on ‘Vednestlay evening, on Mr. Robert liarcJur t's resolution asking for the IMAM' lation of the licensing procedure of the theatre with that of the music hall, and for the removal of the cens,rship. He was precedid by Sir J. Spear (Tavistock, C), who believed the aoolition of the censorship would be a menace to the morality of many persons. He thought that on the whole it had acted very beneficially. Mr. Harold Smith said, speaking with some little practical experience of and considerable enthusiasm for the tgreat profession of the stage, he could not help thinking that his hon. friend was entirely ignorant of the force and effect of the opinion of the British public which had never in the long history of the comatry approved immoral or degrading plays on the public wage. (Hear, hear.) He attached enormous weight to that opinion, and still greater weight to the safeguard of a licence being refused renewal by the magistrates where a theatre was improi e.ly conducted. The Under Secretary spoke on very inadequate instructions and with very little knowledge of his case. He drew a wholly ridiculous picture of what would happen if the censorship ended. What nor.sense he talked about the police in every theatre ! And when ha was interrupted by a question about the music halls, he said they did not have the police there,therefore the stage plays pro- duced there had to pass the Censor. His only answer am that it was not true. A play could be produced upon a music hall stage without having been submitted to the Lord Chamberlain. Mr. H. Simuel : The hon. rrember is mistaken. MANAGERS IN CLOVER.

Mr. H. Smith said the right hoe, gentleman had inn- suited the officials, and that it might be a fact that in London plays on music-hall stages had to pass the Ceuscr, but be knew as a fact that plays were produced in music halls day after day which the Censor had never seen. The jurisdiction of the Lord Chamberlain might extend all over England as regards stage plays, but it did not exteni beyond London as regards the music ball. If that were so, then his argument was as logical as that of the Under Secretary was illogical. The position he had pointed out was an anachronism. The Under Secretary cover dealt with the fact that there was no censorship in Ireland. As to the attitude of the theitrical profession, the Under Secretary gave no proof except the opposition of an actor, who was also a manager. Every manager under the present systemwas in clover,and was determined to do everything he could to cling on the protection which the present system gave him, under which any gags or" business " could be subsequently introduced without any danger, however suggestive, and somaimes indecent, they might be. Under ,the present system the Under Secretary could not be caricatured on the theatre stage, but ho might be made to perform all sorts of antics which were perhaps quite foreign to him on the music hall stage. He really thought our present system was indefensible. He was not criticising the ability of the council of five. Ho declared that the whole principle was wrong.
"A RIDICULOUS OFFICE."

If we were to abolish this ridiculous cfrioe of Censor- ship of Stage Plays, ho believed we should be in an ivfinitely stronger position, and should be encouraging dramatists to work their very best without fear of blue pencil. In doing so, we should be placing the responsibility on the owner of the theatre, who had to apply for his licence every year, and he eai confident that that great safeguard, together with the still greater safeguard f public opinion, wculd suffice. The pro- posals of the amendment, if carried out, would give greater liberty and justice to all sides, and Aould tend to elevate the whole atmosphere of stage-phying, whether in the theatre or in the music hall. Our piatent system was an anachronism, and he was glad that this question had been raised and that the Govern- ment had advanced so far that they were prepared to leave the matter to the unfettered judgment of the House. The resolution was passed without a division.

div.head: HAS THE BOOM IN TRADE REACHED ITS HIGHEST POINT?
div.p: HAS THE BOOM IN TRADE REACHED ITS HIGHEST POINT?

Has the boom in trade reached its highest point, and is a decline now to be expected? This question is being seriously asked by business men. In the Board of Trade Returps h r March there was not the buoy• ancy that has distinguished the monthly returns for nearly two years. 'There has not been a decline, but the increase was, insignificant. The master boiler- makers assert that the boom in the ship-building trade has already begun to show Signs of decline. Invariably abnormal activity is followed by depression, and it is to be feared that those who have been gaining most will take least kindly to the change. Einployers in this same boiler-makers' business make a serious complaint in regard to their workmen. They say that although wages never have been higher and scores of workmen are earning as much as £3OO a year, they have got in the habit of wastin;; their time at foot- ball matches to such an extent that if they worked their proper hours, wages, by that fact alone, would be increased to the extent of eighteen per cent. The advance that has been made,it is asserted, has to a large extent been lost by the bad timekeeping of the men. —" Country Life."

div.head: Compromise effected after dispute lasting eight days.
div.p: Compromise effected after dispute lasting eight days.
THE, MAYOR'S SUCCESS AS PEACEMAKER.

The Warrington carters' strike, which had lasted eight days and directly involved 300 men, was settled on Tuesday evening. Although the carters have accepted considerably lees than they originally demanded, they have obtained a eubitantial advance in wages and have also gained the important principle of the recognition of their trade unions. Briefly, the terms of settlement are :

Official recognition of both unions, namely the United Carters and Motormen's Association, and Tramway and Vehicle Workers' Union. A minimum wage of 24e. per week for one-horse drivers and 27. per week for two-horse drivers. Hours of labour: 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on Saturday when work concludes at 2 p.m. Over-time to be paid at the rate of 6d. per hour. Sunday duty to be paid for at the rate of 9d. per hour, with a minimum of 3s.

General relief was felt on the termination of the dispute. The carter is an important link in the industrial chain and the fact that he was on strike made it impossible for manufacturers to maintain an adequate supply of fuel and raw materials. The con- sequence was that Messrs. Rylands Bros., Ltd., were compelled to close down the greater portion of their works last week-end and several of the mills and forges at the works of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and iron Co., Ltd., also ceased operations. The great majority of the carters who went on strike are members of the United Carters' and Motor- men's Association, but until Tuesday the teamowners had resolutely declined to recognize that body. They intimated that they were prepared to negotiate tixrough the Tramway and Vehicle Workers' Union, of which Mr. Edwin Plinston is the district secretary, but that ffer, of course, did not commend itself to the men who had thrown in their lot with the other Union. It was accordingly decided to combine in a demand 10 the recognition of both organizations.
At a subsequent meeting, called- at the instance of the Mayor, the masters agreed that the wiiges mentioned above should be the minimum without stipulation as to length of service.

div.head: MASTERS MEET MEN.
div.p: MASTERS MEET MEN.

On Tuesday the team-owners agreed to meet the representatives of bath unions at a conference at the Patten Arms Hotel. Ai the request of the disputants, the Mayor, whose diligent efforts in the cause of peace have earned the thanks the community, acted as mediator. The negotiations occupied three hours and at the close the Press repre- sentatives were informed that the masters had agreed to rec,gnize the unions and to pay a minimum wage of 2.15, a week for one-horse drivers and 275. a week for two-horse driven.. There would be immediate re instat ment .f all the stzikers and the representa- tives of the mtn had agreed to recommend the accept- ance of the terms.

Later in the evening there was a crowded meeting of carters in the Old Music Hall: Prior to the arrival of the delegates who had attended the Confirence, the indications appeared to be against a settlement on he lines stated, the general fooling, as far as could be ascertained, being that the minumnm wage should not be less than 25a. However, the conditions were fully explained hy Mr. A. Hilton, general secre- tary of the United Cartels' and Motormen's Associa- tion, Mr. E. Plinstm, di Arict secretary of the Tramway and Vehicle WI:It-ken' Union, Mr. H. Ball, the Manchester district delegate of the Carters' Union, and two other delegates. Shortly after eleven o'clock, it was announced that the following sesoktion had been carded by a large majority : That this mass nseetitig of Warrington carters endorses the recommendations of the General Secretary of the United Carters' and Motormen's Association and Mr. Plinston, district secretary of the Tramway and Vehicle Workets, and accepts the conditions offered by the employers, and guarantees to organize all available carters with the object of winning further concessions at a more epportnne date."

div.head: WHAT THE CARTERS GAIN.
div.p: WHAT THE CARTERS GAIN.

Mr. Hilton, in an interview- with an " Examiner ' reporter said the terms would. involve an advance of 2s. per week to 150 men and as much as 4s. to another 100 men. When they took into account the question of over-time, it meant a ss. advance all round. Before the strike, overtime wam practically left to the generosity of the employer„ but now it was placed on a definite basis.

The employers, added N 1... Bilton, were willing to give further consideratiointo the original application at an early date, and mummer, they were prepared to see that all their emplo3us were members of a trade union. They had definitely expressed their indebted- ness to him (Ur. Hilton))for placing the men's position before them in such a syaapathetic manner. Thoy recognised that the in bad a good case, but unfortu- nately the rates under wl ich the teamowners had accepted some large contracts, were so low that it was impossible for them to pay the full amount which the men asked for. They prom ised to make application for improved terms, so as to enable them to meet the carters' rightful demands. Asked for his opinion on the settlement, Mr. Hilton. said: "I consider that we have won a good victory and I feel certain that a better feeling will exi,t between employers and employes tbrough the coo- cession. of recognition." "A SATISFACTORY SETTLEMENT."

Mr. Piinston also expressed the opinion that a satisfactory settlement had b min arrived at. He believed , the men were wzli advisee. in accepting the terms. Recognition, which was the principle at stake, was fully granted. He thought & there was general satis- faction, and the resolution sanctioning the settlement was carried almost unarimously. Mr. Ball said the set &lei:Gent was, in his opinion, very satisfactory, consi(lering that five weeks ago they bad only eleven men in the Carters' Association. Now they had about 300 re embers. The agreement embodying the above terms, has been signed by the president and secretary of the Team Owners' Aswociation, the chief offici ils of the two unions, and cruntersigned by the Mayor.
WHIT THE MEN ASKED FOR. The men's original demands were : Official recognition.
Carters with—one horse, miv imum wage of 265. per week.

Carters with. two horses, minimum wages of 289. per week. All carters to start work at 6 a.m. and the day's work to finish at 6 p.m. in harness. After 6 pm. overtime to be paid at the rate of 6d per hour. Carters called upon to drive a third horse to be paid at the rate of 6d. per day or portion thereof. Extra pay for attending to the horses on Saturday afternoon and Sunday. Sunday work to be paid at the rate of is. per hour, with a minimum of 49. WHAT THE MASTERS OFFERED.

In reply the masters ported a notice on the stable doors of members of the Team Owners' Association stating what they were prepared to concede,namely :- 235. per week for one-home men who have been in the firm's employ constantly for 12 months or upwards. 265. per week tor two-horse men who have been in the firm's employ a similar period of time. New men for one-horse work are to start at 21s. per week for the first six months, 225. for the second six months, 235. when they have been employed constantly for over 12 months. New team men are to start at 21s. a week for the first six months, 255. for the seoond six months, and 265. when employed constantly for over 12 mouthe. Any man baking an additional horse to be paid at the rate of 6d. a day extra. Overtime will be paid after six p.m. on ordinary days and two p.m. on Saturdays. On the question of official recnnition, they said, "We, as masters, consider that we are capable to deal with our own affairs, knowing them, better than any officials or any individual carter.."

div.head: CORPORATION MEN INVOLVED. WORK OF NIGHTSWL DEPARTMENT AT A STANDSTILL.
div.p: CORPORATION MEN INVOLVED. WORK OF NIGHTSWL DEPARTMENT AT A STANDSTILL.

The strike took a more serious turn last week-end when .the carters employed in the sanitary department of the Corporation became involved. Although having no grievance of their own, with regaid to wages or conditions, the men were induced to cease work in sympathy with the carters on strike. Consequently, the nightsoil collection could not be completed in the Howley and Fairfield Wards on Friday night but the superintendent (Jr. Parfitt) endeavoured to arrange for the work to be done on Sunday. The carters,however did not turn out and there were numeroirs complaints from iesidents as to the Conditions of affairs. A special meeting of the Sanitary Committee was held on Monday night, and a small deputation was appointed to wait on tbe men at Howley forthwith. They did so and a conference lasting until one o'clock on Tuesday morning took place. The men expressed their willing ness to return to work although they feared disturb- ances would arise if they did so. Adequate protection was promised, whereupon the men decided to take out the horses and vans on Tuesday morning at seven o'clock. The i romise was carried out and the work was done satisfactorily.
.it.i'i:O..llilif, ~.,..N;l;;;.,zogii l'..._:iiirgi
IrrlP:

A correspondent writi s :—One of the most eerious aspects of the carters' at, ike, which has now been happily settled, was its effect on the sanitary condi- tions of the town, Some of the workmen employed by the Sanitary Works Department in the collection of nightsoil returned to Howley Depot shortly after mid- night on Friday last and complained that, although they were not concerned in the dispute, they had been subjected to intimidation and abuse by strikers and others, and they therefore declined to run the ri,k of going out again with their vane. Fortunately the work of nightsoil collecti n had been nearly completed for that week and the temporary stoppage was not regarded as serious. But when the wok should have been resumed on Sunday night,the carters and carriers with few exceptions, again refused to turn out and the work of the department practically came to a stand- still. The effect of the stoppaga on the sanitary con- ditions of the town was immediate. The Cleansing Superintendent (Mr. Parfitt) was inundated with com- plaints on Monday that the non-collection of the rails was causing a serious nuisance, and it was feared that an epidemic would break out unless prompt msasures were taken to resume the collection of pails which had been interrupted on Friday night. A meeting ef the Sanitary Works Committee was hastily summoned for Monday evening, when it was decided that the chairman )Mr. Wilson) and the Deputy Chairman (Mr. Hawthorn) along with the Cleansing Superintendent should interview the men. The committee was so impressed with the importance of having the work done that it empowered the deputation to apply Lr other men if the employes refused to resume the work. Fortunately this latter step was not necessary as the men expressed themselves willing to restart their rounds at midnight. This decision rapidly spread amongst the other carters and their friends, so that when the hour of midnight arrived a large crowd gathered in the vicinity of the Howley depot, evidently with the intention of showing their displeasure at the decision of the Corporation employes, and if possible, inducing them to continue their " sympathetic strike. Under the circumstances, it was deemed advisable by the authorities to postpone the resumption of work until seven o'clock on Tuesday morning. The men promised to turn out at the hour stated and promptly to time every man turned up and the work of collection has continued during the clay-time this week. Now that normal conditions have been restored, it is anticipat ed that the night-collection will be resumed as formerly.

div.head: CARTERS AND THEIR DEMANDS.
div.p: CARTERS AND THEIR DEMANDS.
CLAIM ENDORSED BY MASS MEETING

A crowd of abut 2,000 assembled near the old mill at Bridge Foot on Su,lday afternoon when a meeting in support of the men's demands was held. A resolution was adopted endorsing the claims of the carters and calling upon the Mayor to use his influence to bring about a conference with a view to a speedy settlement. Mr. II Ball (district delegate of the United Carters' and Motormen's Association) presided. He Ea'd they wished the public to know that the clrters of War- rington were not altogether responsible for the con- tinuance of the strike.

div.head: MR. PLINSTON AND THE MASTERS.
div.p: MR. PLINSTON AND THE MASTERS.

Mr E Plinston, local secretary of the Tramway and Vehicle Workers' Union, which the employers had offered to recognise, said that some few weeks ago both sections of carters in Warrington sent in two separate and distinct demands for an increase of wages, but one happened to be a little larger thin the ethers. The replies, which were posted on the doors of the stables, were to the effect that while the employers were quite prepared a nd williz g to allow the men to belong to trade unions, they mist reserve to themselves the absolute right to deal with their men, as between employer and employed. Referring to the subsequent Lifer of the employers to negotiate through him (Mr. Plinston) as a local man,the speaker said he valued the respect of the master carters of Warrington and would say nothing to lessen that estimation. At the same time he wished to point out the

div.head: VERY AWKWARD POSITIQN
div.p: VERY AWKWARD POSITIQN

in which be was placed. He representcd only a section of the carters, while Mr Hilton represented the organiz • ation which now hnd in its ranks the majority o f carters in the town. At a meeting of the men it was resolved that any negotiations for the settlement of the dispute must take 'place with the repre- sentatives of both sectiors. He was sorry to say that some remarks had been made daring the previous day against himself. He was not powerful enough to sway the feelings of the whole of the carters and say " You must do as I tell you." He was willing and anxious to do everything in his power to bring that terrible grievance to a settlement and while
The Examiner, Saturday, April 19, 1913.

he was agreeable that either Mr Hilton or he should meet the employers, the men, who held the key of the situation, said both of them must be present. The dis- pute was entering upon its second week and he Eaw no signs of wavering on the part of the men. At a meet- ing on Saturday the team-owners agreel to the pay- ment of a 23s Gd minimum to one-horse drivers—an advance of is 6d on the present wages—hut the men asked for a minimum of 25s Gi. He believed there were employers who were willing tl go further to meet their demands, but the chief and only stumbling block was the recognition of both Unions.

div.head: TIRED OF MARGARINE.
div.p: TIRED OF MARGARINE.

Mr. H. krancis, of Oldham, said the cartels had got absolutely tired of living on over- weight margarine and had decided that they were entitled to a little bread and butter. The caner was the connecting link of all the greatest indus- tries, and when hs decided to" down tools" there was general anxiety to persuade him to return to work. Some of th 3 employers in Warrington seemed to be under the impression that if they conceded recognit;on, the Unions would attempt to dictate to them every time they discharged a man for getting too much beer. He wished them tl understand that neither the United Cirtcrs' Association nor the Tramway and Vehicle Workers Union upheld any man getting drunk while on duty. Referring to the
" NASTY " STREET SCENES

which had occurred in connection with the strike, Mr. Francis said that, in his opinion, they had on mlny ozoasions been due, not to the fittikers alone, but to the the police not allowing them to approa h mn properly. They had a perfect right to approach any nail, whether an employer or anyone else who was out with a horse. He did Inot any that they were entitled to upset carts, but when they approached a driver it was not fair that eight policemen should rush him out of the way. The carters who we-e on strike c intributed to the maintenance of th 3 police force, but they did not get their share of police assistance in fighting their battles. Tne whole of the industries of Warringtoa were Buffering throng') the obstinacy of a mere handful of men. Every credit was due to the M.iyor for the ell )rts be had put forth to settle the dispu'e, but Ee hoped the Town Cou-:61 would eecide that, instead of basing " skilly-wag "..team3wners doing their work,,h3y would -buy horses of their own, do their o wing directly, and pay decent wages. A carter as entitled t 3 nothing less than 253. a is eek. (Applause). WHAT OF THE CHILDREN?

Mr. C. DUKES said he did not wish to say much against the police. The membns of the force were merely men of the strikers' own class, thotigh moment- arily divorced from them. Not one amongst them knew but what to-morrow he might be precipitAed back into his own class and compelled to earn his own livelihood just as workingmen were. Just as Tom Mann said to the soldiers "Don't shoot ! " he (Mr. Dukes) would hay to the police "Don't use your batons ! " Tha speaker also complained that the Act for the Feeding-of School Children was not being put into lorce, 9.3 regarded the children of the strikers, lie estimated that 900 children must be going to school insufficiently fed to take advantage of the education given them. Mr. WEBSTER, of Oldham. urged the worke-s to stick t the three weapons—the ballot box', the boycott and the strike.

div.head: STRIKERS ATTACK MEN IN CHARGE OF CARTS.
div.p: STRIKERS ATTACK MEN IN CHARGE OF CARTS.

The sequel to further strike scenes was heard at the Borough Police CGurt on Wednesday.—John Weaver carter, 3, Leigh's-yard, was summoned for assaulting Richard Hinton, carter,Shrewsbury-street, the previous day.

The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been on strike with the carters At eleven o'clock on Tuesday morning Hinton, who was a carter in the employ of the Corporation, was in charge of a dust cart, proceeding along Lythgoes-lane in the direction of Brick-street. The prisoner went up t ) him and asked him whether he was at a meeting the previous evening. Hinton made a reply, whereupon prisoner began to threaten him. Hinton got cff the vehicle, whereupon the prisoner struck him savagely, and Biton h d to defend hinist If. Chief Inspector Williamson and P.C. Green came upon th 3 scene and, fortunately for the prisoner, they were able to save him from receiving what he deserved.

Hinton s'ated that defendant c.ught hold of the horse's head. When 'witness tried to push him away, he received a violent blow on the nose. The horse was restive and witness was in danger of being run over Prisoner was under the influence of drink. Prisoner alleged that Hinton struck him when he asked him a question.

The Chief C:onstable stated that prisoner had been before the court three times previously. Behaviour of that kind, when a strike was in progress, might easily lead to serious trouble. Corporation emplosees had been threatened "up hill and down dale" and p-e- -vented from going out to their work, and this was one instauca where the police had caught a man doing it. Ile asked the Bench to make an example of him. Another strike had begun that morning and whatever the Bench might do, might have a I eneficial effect in helping the police to carry out their onerous duties. Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, with the alterna- tive of a month's imprisonment. Peter Hanlon, caster, CoAhedge-lane was charged with committing a breach of the peace by being disorderly in linutsford-road end also with assaulting Charles Ellison Chappell and Michael Foy. Mr. (happen, who is the proprietor of the Howley Mortar Company, stated that, owing to the carter's strike, he had been compelled to drive his own vehicle. On Tuesday afternoon he was taking a load of mortar along Knutsford-road and, in the vicinity of the Golden Lion Inn, prisoner cam 3 up and attempted to draw the " kecker " bar and upset the cart. He told witness that he had no right to take the horse out. Witness tried to push him away, R boreupon prisoner struck him slightly on the face, with his fist. lbey closed and Acting-Sergeant Armstrong Came end took prisoner into custody.

Michael 'Foy, carter, Predetick-street, said he was taking a load of sand along Mersey-street when the prisoner attempted to upset the cart. They struggled and prisoner struck him on the shoulder, pushed him across the street, and tore his j icket. Prisoner alleged that Mr Chappell tried to strike him witha

The Chief Constable stated that pris,ner, who h-d been before the Court ten times previously, had been taking a very prominent part in the strike. He had not only been using peaceful persuasion when the police were about, but he had done more when they were out of sight.
A fine of 30..4. and c-sts, with the option of a month' imprisonment, was inflicted.
