div.head: BREWERY STRIKE.
div.p: BREWERY STRIKE.
WARRINGTON LABOURERS DEMAND RECOGNITION.

On Monday the Gasworkers' and General Labourers' Union gave notice t 0 Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons Ltet., that, failing recognition of their Union, the un.killed workmen in the employ of the firm would go on strike io-day (Saturday). The case for the men is fully stated below. Briefly, it is that a demand for higher wages, put in by the Union, was ',Mewed by the disruissil of a number of workmen, most of whom are stated to have been old servants of the company. The Union endeavoured to open negotiations on the matter, but were told thatithe firm invariably treated their employees with every consideration and they thclinid to discuss the control of their men with any timid° source. They also refused to receive a depu- tation from the Union. Under these circumstances, the men, at a meeting on Sunday, decided to give notice of their intention to strike. An unexpected move was made on Wednesday morning when, during the breakfast half-hour,seventy labourers went on trike. The respion alleged for this precipitate action is that the firm were taking steps to fill the places of the men who had been dis- charged. As the week's notice had not expired, the strike has not the full authorization of the Union.

div.head: "WILL NO 2 REOOGNISE THE UNJON."
div.p: "WILL NO 2 REOOGNISE THE UNJON."

Interviewed early in the week by an " Examiner ' reporter, Mr. It. Hutton, head brewer to Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons; Ltd., declined to enter into a dis- cussion of the causes of the trouble. He, however, stated that the firm were quite capabje of managing their affairg without outside i!,tetference.

Yesterday Mr. Hutton, on being asked to state how the strike had affected the firm replied, : 'lt his not affected us at all. We have got plenty of non-mion" men to take the places of those who have gore on strike, and everything is going on as usual. There have bee-u no disturhaLces and everything is sati-factory, as far as I am con- cerned. You cin state this : "We will Lot recognize the Uhion."
Mr. Hutton added that the men whom the firm had ergaged to take the places of the strikers were glad to gPt jobs at 2s. per week .more than they had been receiving hum certain other fi ms.

div.head: CASE FOR THE MEN.
div.p: THE CASE FOR THE MEN.

The case for the n-en is thus E t .ted by Nfr. J. R. Olynts, MP, general secretary of the_ Gasworkers' aid Central Labourers' Union, who has conducted the overtures on their behalf : "On March 11th, the CasWorkers' end titneral Labourers' Union,-on behalf of various classes of workmen and labourers, made application for -advances in wages ranging, with few exceptions, from Is. to 34. per week. After the firm had btated that the application would be put before the managing director, a Lumber of the men, among whom were some of the oldest servants, were dismissed I wrote to the firm asking if they wou!d give the union some inforrnation as to why the men were stopped, and also asking what they proposed to do with refer- ence to the claim for an advance of wages The firm answered that they invariably treated their employs with every consideration, and declined to discuss their control of their men with any outside source. "I replied to the firm, saying that it would give their workmen some satisfaction if the firm showed a, willingness to discuss the claims the union had pre- senteet for them, and that so long as the men wished the union officials to act for them the union would not forfeit the right to do so. The men held a meeting and resolved unanimously to ask the union to press their claim and to demand the reir.stAtement of the dis- missed men. I again communicated with the firm stating that the situation was becoming serious, and that a rep' esentative of the union would call on the firm to obtain information to-day (Monday). The firm replied that it was no use calling, as they would decline to see the representative. The men on Sunday night held a mass meeting, and 88 a result of their decision I at once sent the following letter to the fi • m - -

_ . "Dear Sirs,—ln view of the terms of your reply to our letters, and your treatment of workmen, who have asked for tl eir cases to be considered, we regret that we are compelled to carry cut the definite instructions oA the men concerned... _ .

"'We herewith notify y m that the whole of the men covered by the terms of our letter of March 11th will, at the end of a week's notice, hereby conveyed for them, cease work on Saturday, April 19th, unless the claims submitted are satisfactorily met. In the hope of a settlement on peaceful lines we have arranged for a few of the men, with a representative of. their society, to attend for any discussicn of the point at issue which may be arranged.--Yours faithfully, J It aLYNES."

div.head: "NO BEER."
div.p: "NO BEER."

The strike was forecastel at a public meeting held on Sunday in support of the carters out on strike. Mr Fleming Eceles,a representative of the Gasvvorkers' and General Labourers' Union, prefaced his reference to the strike with the remark that it was because employers had known in the past that men were badly organised that they bad set one .against another, and they were thinking that in the future they could ride rough shod over the working people. After referring to the notices which were sea on Monday, the speaker said there was every indication that there was going to be trouble in Warrington. Messrs Walker did not recognise trade unionism from the " bottom dog " point of view. In the past they had recognised the skilled workman but as for the mere workman, the labourer, what did he count ? His jucctions were to clean the barrels, brew the beer and to mop out the " boss's" motor-car. He had nD pen work to do ; be was not a clerk of import- ance, so therefore he did not count at all. They were going to show the firm that unless the workmen's organisation were recognised, there would be no beer. (Laughter and applause.)

div.head: IRISH FARM LABOURERS
div.p: IRISH FARM LABOURERS
Strike for Shorter Hours and more Pay.
Sankey and Lymm Districts affected.

The strike fever has been prevalent in the country districts among the Irish farm labourers, who are employed en the land from the beginning of April until the end of September. Considerable inconveni- ence has been caused, not only in Cheshire but in some parts of Lancashire. In St. Helens, Burtonwood, Bold, and the surrounding districts nearly 300 labourers struck work on Saturday last. Their demand was for 2s. per week increase in wages; two pints of beer per day and work to cease at four o'cl( ck on Saturdays. On Tuesday information was received in Sankey to the effect t hat a body of the strikers were coming along the road from the direction of Bold, and it was surmised that their intention was to induce the Irishmen in Sankey to join them. An " Examiner " representa- tive journeyed along the road and met about twenty of the men at a point just beyond Sankey. He ascertained that it was not the strikers intention to interfere with the Irish labourers employed in Sankey. One of the men ventured to remark "They can please themselves, if the conditions of labour do not suit them, they can join us." After further assurance that they were nat going to caw e any disturbance they went off in an opposite direction to the village. Interviewed whilst setting potatoes, two Irish labourers on a Sankey farm expressed their satisfaction with the conditions prevailing and announced that they did not desire to join the strikers. A farmer also stated to our representative that the prospec s of a strike in Sankey were practically nil. He explained that for the most part the Irish labourers were only employed from April to September on English farms. He did not think that tLey would successfully sow the seed of discon- tent amongst the English labourers.

div.head: UNUSUAL SCENES AT LYMM.
div.p: UNUSUAL SCENES AT LYMM.

Demands similar to those stated above were made ont Saturday by about 100 Irish labourers in tbe quiek country districts of Lymm and Heatley. Ceasing so' on Saturday, the men announced their intention oi remaining out on strike until they got what thl termed " their just rights." On Monday about a doze farms were deprived of the services of the men and thief caused sei ions inconvenience in the impertant work Of potato setting. There has been tbe unusual sigh_, bands of Irishmen walking about the roads, while Is".; week-end some were observed to be taking personal Effects with them, no doubt bound for job, or Erin's isle. At one farm the men after haviVs left their work in the afternoon came back at night 1 hate up their residence in the" shanties" they Is, previously occupied, only to encounter the sogra farmer who, after ejecting the Irishmen se their possessions, had the buildings boarded ot, The men who are at present paid from 16 to 20 shilling° a week, in addition to free lodgings in the farm buildi it gs or" shanties," and aro in mmay instances suPPILe„, with potatoes, milk and coal—to say nothing of 14'- 4 bagging; " of bread, cheese and beer—demand a riee of 2s. a week for cowmen and horsemen, and Is. week)! for men employed on the land. On Monday eveuls: there seemed every likelihood of the trouble extendlOo to the surrounding distric te. Although the stall have no union to support them, their leaders shoW°. great activity in getting hands to join them. In soot instances they succeeded in bringing out a few &lOW men who are employed all the year round. On Monday the licensee of the Saracen's Head hosted' Warburton, closed his premises to the Irish labanrergt as a precautionary measure. No disturbances OLP place, although at times some of the wilder spin' became a trifle unruly. On Tuesday a settlement was arrived at, the cof being satisfied with the concessions the farmws oasri rhe quietude which invariably prevails in the distno was resumed, and although in the morning some of th,ei farms had not the full complement of men nearly s'," the hands were back by evening. The conditions varl on the different 'arms. On Wednesday the conditions were normal and tb°. police authorities stated that there had been very disorder.

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY AND PARR HALL ORGAN,
div.p: MUSICAL SOCIETY AND PARR HALL ORGAN,
REPLY TO RECENT CRITICISMS.
Recital Tickets for Poor People.

Replying to a suggestion made at the last meeting of the Warrington Town Council that the Musical Society was quite unconcerned about the poorer people, Mr. J. P. Re3nolds (hon. treasurer), suggested at the annual meeting of the society held in the Cairo- street schools on Wednesday evening, that if the new organ were erected in Parr Hall, recitals should be given and free tickets provided for those people who could not afford to pay for admission. There was a large attendance of members o%er which Sir Gilbert Greenall Bart. presided. He was supported by Mr. Lionel Fairclough (hon. secretary) and Mr. J. P. Reynolds (treasurer). An interesting resume of the past season was given in the secretary's report submitted by Mr. Fairclough. It statml " Our season last year opened as usual with the opera, and it speaks volumes for the interest members take in this particular branch of the society, when we find that although rehearsals are carried on practically all summer, there are always plenty of members ready and willing to take part. Dorothy' was the work given on this occasion, but whether it was modern enough for the critical public, or whether there were too many attractions in Warrington, it was certain that the financial result of a net profit of £.2(..) Os was not an adequate return for the time and trouble spent upon it. (Applause). The opera San Toy,' given the year before, produced a profit of £O4 Ss." Mr. FAIRCLOUGH quoted figures from which he said they would see that although by no means good, the average attendance at the rehearsals was better than during the previous season. They had an excellent set of bosses, but it was rather disappointing to report that, as compared with the previous season the society lacked the services of three tenors less. He urged the members to rack their brains "for schemes in bring- ing in some more tenors ; with another It) or 1.5 the society would possess, altogether, a really excellent chorus. He understood that the attendances of the band at rehearsals was remarkably good. In conclu- sion, Mr. Fairclough said three concerts were given last season, all of which did some good, but the audiences were small. He thanked Messrs. Crossley and Reynolds, and all the officers and members of the society, for their co-operation and assistance during the past season.

div.head: LOSS ON THE CONCERTS.
div.p: LOSS ON THE CONCERTS.

Mr. REYNons in presenting the financial statement compared the finances of the society for the last five years. An interesting comparison was between the figures for the past season and the one prior to it. In regard to subscriptions the society raised ;‘....111 17s. Gd., as against £lll ltls. Gd. in 1911-12; 5.,126 10s. in 1910-11; 3s. in 1909-10; and .3:75 10s. 4d. in 1908 9; so that this year they managed to hold their own, exceeding the previous year by a solitary shilling. (Laughter.) In members' subscrip- tions toe society received i',54 in 1912-13, as against .£53 58. in 191'1-12 ; 17s. 7d. in 1910-11 ; and .f-02 12s. Gd. in 1909-10. There was a loss in the sale of tickets and programmes, the past season realizing .1;50 7s. Bd. as compared with 16s. 2d. in 1911-12, A'.B2 Bs. 7d. in 1910-11, and -£129 Os. id. in 1909-10. Opera profits, too, were down nearly £2O as compared with the previous year, the amounts being 29 in 1912-13 and in 1911-12. The total receipts for 1912-13 amounted to 3.:250. In regard to expenditure the total for the past sewon was ;.i.',254 12s. 4d., the previous years' being £203 Bs. 4d. in 1911-12, .4:385 15s. 11d. in 1910-11, and £343 Os. 2d. in 1909-10. They had been success- ful in keeping down professional fees, the amount for the year being -9..154 10s., as against .:(.:151; IGs. tld. in 1911-12, A:209 192. in 1910-11, and :,.:219 14s. in 1909-10.

The loss on the three concerts during the past season amounted to .4:33 11s. 2d. as compared with .tl2 ss. 10d. 1911-12, £B4 us. Bd. in 1910-11, and 4s. 7d. in 1909-10, and the balance due to the bank now was ;£.25 Ds., as against £36 is. sd. in 1911-12, £92 9s. 11d. in 1910-11, and I'l9 Os. Bd. in 1909-10. Continuing Mr. 11EvNor.Ds said the first thing which. struck one in connection with the finances of the society was the continusl reduction in expenditure That was very gratifying and proved that the com- mittee had been endeavouring to keep the various items as low as possible. After referring to the sub- scriptions and the sale of tickets, the treasurer urged the members individually and collectively to do as much as they could to boom the society in the town and elicit the general public's sympathy. That was what they desired most of all, and when that was not lacking, the funds of the society would cease to cause them anxiety. Ile hoped that they would finish the forthcoming season with a balance in hand. (Applause) On the motion of Mrs. Asirrox, the reports were unanimously adopted.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

On the proposition of Mr. FAI RCLOUGH, Sir Gilbert Greenall was re-elect:3d president and promised to personally patronise the concerts next season. On the proposition of Mr. FIELDHOUSE the vice- I presidents were re-elected cii bloc and the other officials appointed were : Mr. L. Fairclough, secretary ; Mr. J. P. Reynolds, treasurer ; Mr. J. B. Huxtable, registrar ; Mr. P. Walb, librarian; Mr. F. Fieldhouse, auditor ; and Messrs. J. W. Bibby, 11. Bond, C. H. Hoult, A. Evans, J. B. Hannan, J. Scotson, J. Lee, U. H. Smith, and W. Hipkiss, committee. THE NEXT OPERA. Mr. F. W. CROSSLEY (conductor), invited suggestions from the member 3 of suitable works for the coming season. The trial of voices for the opera "Miss Hook of Holland " would take place the following Tuesday in that room. Hardly any of the parts had been definitely allotted and he hoped that one or two good principal parts would be given to new members. (Applause.) In a way the accounts were somewhat dis- appointing, but they must not take it too much to heart, as any artistic enterprise invariably failed as regards money-making. They had to contend, of course, with music-halls and picture palaces, although skating- rinks had gone out of date—(laughter)—and it would need a collective effort on the part of members to make up leeway. He was hopeful that times would change, that the apathy of the public would become a thing of the past, and finally that members would take a keener interest in the society'

div.head: PARR HALL ORGAN
div.p: PARR HALL ORGAN

Mr. REYNOLDS referred to the discussion at the Town Council meetings with regard to the proposed erection of an organ in Parr Hall. At the last meeting of the Council several members seemed to try their best to belittle the Musical Society. They said the society was selfish and that it did not cater for all classes of the community. in order that there should be no mis- apprehension as to what the society was, he would like to state emphatically that during the many years it had been in existence it had worked in the interests of the town and had striven to maintain public interest in good music. The indication of that good work was to be seen in the vast improvement whicu had taken place in the various church and chapel choirs and other musical organizations. Such improvements were indirectly the outcome of the Musical Society's work. Those people who said that. people did not get. any good by attending festivals and by practising and working in conection with musical training, were hopeleso. it was hoped that the organ, which would be the finest and best interest of its kind in the neighbourhood, would be erected by the end of the year. To repudiate the inference that the society did not care a a rap for the poorer people he would suggest that recitals be given in the Parr Hall. Those could be provided at a very small cost, and a small amount of trouble, and free tickets could be given to members of the poorer community of the town who could not afford to pay. This would be an influence for goodond would stimulate the musical interest of the whole town.
(Applause). SUGGESTED CURTAILMENT OF PROGRAMME THE CONDUCTOR'S SALARY.

Mr. Jack, a member said it was all light for Mr. I Reynolds to suggest those things but they had three deficits on concerts to consider before they attempted anything more. They should make the Society pay its way before they attempted anything further It \VHS a great mistake to take on anything more until they had got straight. Members of the operatic section were disappointed that the proceeds of their effort were given for the benefit of the society,while no efforts was being made directly by the music.l section. Ile asked what was the conductor's salary ? r. REYNOLDS : The conductor's salary is .£sf. 10s. Mr. JACK : I had a suspicion it was £5O but it is £2 10s. more than I thought. I think that amount too much for this Society ti pay. Mr. REYNOLDS : That is a question for the: Committee. Mr. JACK: I don't think so. It should be for the mernLers. Mr. Reynolds was about to reply when Mr. JACK stated that if he bad not got the sympathy of the meet- ing with him he would not discuss the matter further. Mr. JACK suggested that the society should only run two concerts instead of three, seeing that that would keep the deficiency down. At a later stage in the discussion Mr. REYNOLDS said if you have a suggestion to make write a letter to - Mr. JACK : I suggest it here at the annual meeting and this is, I contend, is the proper place.

A LADY. MEmitErt said that the Huddersfield Society had been greatly helped by its being a "social affair.' Mr. JACK: Ours could be made social, it is not social enough. After further discussion a recommendation to the letter that two concerts should be given insteai of three, moved by Mr. JAM- and seconded by Mr. MOULT, was defeated.

Mr. REYNOLDS remarked that they ought to think a great deal before they curtailed their programme. If they got the members interested in the financial affairs of the society they would have no trouble at all. A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman closed the meeting.

div.head: ATHLETICS,
div.p: ATHLETICS,

ENGLISH CHA.IIPIONSHIPS. The ten mile flat and seven mile walking champion— ships of the A.A.A. are set for decision on the ground of the Chelsea Football Club, Stamford Bridge, this afternoon. Of the 30 entries for the former, W. Scott (holder) will be a non-starter therefore Northeners will he looking forward to the doings of E. Glover (Northern and National Cross County Champion). G. C. L. Wallach (Bolton, East Lancashire C.C. and Scottish champion), and T. Fennah (Crewe), G. W. Hutson Surrey AC.) is looked on as a certainty by Southerners but Sergt. (Connaught Rangers) is said to have got hack to his best form and may prove the greatest trouble to the Northern division who have only to repeat their latest doings to hold the opposition at bay. Hutson and O'Neill, both soldier athletes, must, however, render a great account of themselves if they come anywhere near fulfilling the anticipations of their friends. R. Bridge, the Chorley postman, W. G. Yates and 'l'. H. Dumbill are the only entrants repre- senting the North iii ese walk and. if they are not unduly harassed by cautions or actually disqualified, they should account for the other 19.

div.head: LOCAL FIXTURE.
div.p: A LOCAL FIXTURE.

Warrington sportsmen will probably see the best or the runners competing on the Wilderspool football ground on May loth, when Warrington A.C. bold their sports, at which is to be decided the ten miles flat championship of the Northern Counties, and it is hoped that local sportsmen and athletes will make that occasion worthy of the best sporting traditions of thel. town.

div.head: crv.ious S.
div.p: crv.ious S.

The' African Baobab, or Llonkey-breed tree, may justly be called the elephant of the veget- able world. Near the village Gurney, in Fas- sokl, Hussegger saw a baobab thirty feet in dia- meter and ninety-five feet in circumference; tho horizontally. outstretched brancheA were so large that the negroe6 could comfortably sleep upon them. • The Venetian traveller Cada- ma-;to, found near the mouths of the Senegal-. baobabs measuring more than a hundred feet in circumference. As these vegetable giants arc_. generally hollow, they are frequently made USA of as dwellings or stables; and Dr. Livingstone mentions one in I‘hich 'twenty or thirty men. could lie down and sleep, as in a ,hut. 7ln the- village of Grand Galarques, in Senegambia, the rieigrocs have decorated the entrance into, the cavity of a monstrous baobab with rude siulp- tures cut into theliving wood, and makeuse of the interior as a kind of .assembly room, .where they meet to deliberate on the interests of their small. comMunity. .As it is of very rapid growth, it acquires a diameter of three or four feet, and lts full 'altitude in about thirty 3-ears, and then continues to grow in circumference. The oval fruits, which are of the size of large cucumbers, and :brownish yellow when ripe, hang from long twisted stalks. and contain a, ,white substance, agreeable to the taste,. They are the favourit,a food of the nionkeyo,.whettoe -the tree has de— rived one of its name.

NEWLY-PLANTED FRUIT TREES. In many districts, owing to the very wet and sticky condition of the soil, the planting of fruit trees could not be carried out in such a satisfactory manner as when the e:trth is more Triable. Now that it is becoming drier, cracks of various sizes will probably appear, which must be immediately filled, and it will be expedient to see that the soil is quite firm around the base of the trees. The wind has also been very rough in most parts of the country, and it behoves the grower to see that his trees are secure, especially where any staking has been done, for it sometimes happens that the tying material or stake is chafing against the rue, which will cause irreparable damage Unless given. I rtumpt attention.—" The Garden."

div.head: BOGUS TRAVELLERS.
div.p: BOGUS TRAVELLERS.
A Falsehood to Obtain Beer.

At the Warrington County Petty Sassions, on Wednesday, David Yates and Cnarles Mollow, colliers, of Collins Green, were summoned for falsely repre- senting themselves as trav?llers in order to obtain drink from the Limerick Inn, Burtonwood. On Sunday, April Gtb, the defendants called at the inn at 11.30 a.m. When the barman challenged them they said they had come from Newton-le-Willows. They signed the hook to that effect, and the landlord supplied them with beer. Constable Molding visited the house and recogni3ed the men as bailing from Burtonwood. A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed. COMPENSATION MONEY,

div.head: Alleged Theft at Haydock.
div.p: Alleged Theft at Haydock.

At Vat) Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day., Arthur Bannon, Church-road, Ilaydock, was com- mitted to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on a charge of stealing £l3, the money of Nary Ann Harrison, with whom he lodged. Presecutor received £lO from the South Lancashire Tramways Company as compensation for an accident_ The money, along with another sum of £3, was placed in a dressing table drawer. Whilst prose- cutrix and her husband were visiting some friends at St. Helens, it is alleged the accused took the money. On their return he complained that there had been a robbery and that his money amounting to £lO had been stolen. When the police made a search of the house accused was seen to take a purse containing £l4 10s. from underneath the paper at the bottom of a tin trunk. Daimon told the police that the money was his own savings. He reserved his defence and was allowed hail.

div.head: AFFER SIX MONTHS.
div.p: AFFER SIX MONTHS.
Bench Refuse to Grant Separation Order.

" It is a wretched state of things for a young couple like you to want a separation order and we are not going to lend ourselves to such a thing with.ut adequate c•use, which we don't think has been shown said Councillor H Roberts (chairman), at the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, when Herbert Lambert, C.L.C.lamplighter, 9, Park-place, was summoned by his wife Ethel, 25, Frederick-street, for neglecting to pro- vide proper maintenance. In outlining w hat he termed a " peculiar " case, Mr. A. Browne,who appeared for the wife, said the parties were married at a registry office in November last. They resided in Ilume-street. The defendant had always insisted on paying the money out himself and only gave his wife 4s. for the rent. His wages averaged is. Id. per week. When the wife asked for money, the defendant told her to go home to her mother, and he also sent her there to obtain food. On January 21st he abused her. She left him and had a very serious ill- ness. In a letter to Mr. Browne, defendant stated that his conduct had been such as was required by law. He had done his best to make his wife happy. Continuing Alr. Browne said the defendant had agreed to a mutual separation, with alimony at the rate of 6s. per week but he had not carried out the arrangement. Mrs Lambert said her husband used to get brown flour and bake bread himself. Defendant said his wages averaged £1 Os 7d per week. He had done everything he could to make his wife happy and provide sufficient food for her, as far as his wages would allow. His wife was disaereeat le and dis- satisfied with everything he did. He did not desire to have a separation order. The case was adjourned for a month, the Chairman expressing the hope that the parties would come together again.

div.head: Borough Police Court.
div.p: Borough Police Court.
SATURDAY. Before Mr A J Jolley (in the chair), Alderman Tinnion, Councillor Locker, Messrs T Pemberton and R T Fairclough.

" HARD IVORDS."—ThomaS Kearns, 4, Six Houses, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Dallam-lane, and further with assaulting P C Faulkner. —On Friday night prisoner was quarrelling with his mother and she complained that she had had to sleep in an out-house on three occasions on account of her son's conduct.—P C Faulkner said that the prisoner rushed at him and struck him on the side of the face with his fist. With the assistance of Detective-Sergeant Woollacott he brought the prisoner to the Police Station, On the way down, prisoner becarde very violent, used threaten- ing language, and kicked witness on the hip.—Prisoner admitted that he had had some drink.—The Chief Con- stable said prisoner acted like a brute towards his mother.—Prisoner: You would not say that if you were outside. Those are h.i.rd words for you to say.— The Chief : You are known to us. You are an abso- lute brute to your mother.—Priso- er : I always support her. No-one else will work for her.- The Chief: He has been here nine times previously and has had two months for assaulting the police. He is a violent man in drink.—Prisoner : If you send me to prison who is going to keep her? You people won't keep her.— Kearns was seut to prison for two months, with hard labour.

div.head: .NIOND.IY.
div.p: .NIOND.IY.

Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst Rm.! James Evans, Councillor Wilkinson, Mussrs S Wright, %V Robert, %V Furness, T Locker and G Pilling. BEEP STEAK INSTEAD Or BEER.—John Mulligan (35), 39, Tilley-street, was fined 5i and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street on Saturday.-- The Mayor : You don't look as though you ought to take drink.—Prisoner : No; Tam not right, sir,--The Mayor: A good beefsteak would do you more good.
TUESDAY.
Before Councillor H__Roberts (in the chair), Messrs C
Jackson Holmes and T Locker.

"No MONEY AND NO PROMESE."—Wa-Iter Brown, labourer, 124, Winwick-road, was charged with being .1:2 in arrears of wife maintenance.—The Clerk explained that the prisoner should contribute 6s per week to his wife, Ellen.—Prisoner said that the money would have been paid if it had not been for false statements made by his wife.--The Chairman asked what promise prisoner could make that morning.—Prisoner : 1 have no money and no promise to make to her.—The Chief Constable said the man had been impertinent to the officer who had charge of the case.—Brown was sent to prison for lone month.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

Before Mr. A. J. Jolley (in chair), Messrs. W. Richardson, .1. Upson and W. Roberts, and Dr. Naden. 1N A PLACE OF " SAFETY."—Louisa Hardman, 15, Oldham-street, was charged with stealing on April 14th 309. worth of clothing, the property of Mabel Newport. —Elizabeth Hardman, 17, Oldham-street, was charged with stealing April 9th, 10e. worth of clothing. also the property of Mabel Newport.—The Chief Constable said that, the prisoner Elizabeth was the daughter-in- law of the other prisoner. The prnsecutrix resided at 13, Oldham-street up to the sth April when she sold all her goods. She left several articles in two boxes in the empty house. After she had vacated the house the prisoner effected an entrance by breaking a window. She took some of the goods and pawned them. A day or two afterwards the husband of the other prisoner heard a noise in the empty house and he transferred the box to his own house for safety. During his absenie hie wife took some of the goods. She rawhed part of the stolen clothes and hid some of the other articles in various parts of the house. Detective-Sergeant Holland arrested the prisoners who. however, had not worked in concert. —A fine of 304. was imposed, with an alternative of a month's imprisonment.

div.head: Fell into a Lime Pit.
div.p: Fell into a Lime Pit.

Mr. F. A. Jones (deputy coroner), held an inquest at Warrington, on Monday, on Thomas Stokes (75), Viaduct-street, Earlestown, who died at the Warring- ton Union Hospital, on Saturday.—Deceased was employed as a watchwan at some new schools which are being erected on Newton Common. On March 29th he tripped over a plank and fell into a lime pit, sustaining burns from the hips to the knees. Ile managed to crawl out of the pit and make his way home. He was taken to the hospital and attended by Dr. Valentine.—Tho jury returned a verdict to the effect that death was due to shock following an accident.
THE CHURCH ASSOCIATION: AN APPEAL TO
THE KING.

The Secretary of the Church Association has forwarded for presentation to His Majesty the King, " A. grave remonstrance against the vresent lawless con- dition of the Church of England, and an appeal to His Majesty King George V., beseeching him to be pleased to issue directions to his Ministers that good and effec- tive laws may forthwith be enacted so as to cause the Bishops to do their duty by enforcing discipline, and that the Church of England may be delivered trona the dangers by which she is surrounded, and his Protestant people be relieved from intolerable grievances." The signatures to the petition reached close on 36,000.

The Examiner, Saturday, April 19, 1913.

Fortunately, it is unnecessary to labour this question, for Lancashire and Cheshire readers. Years ago, LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, shrewdest of Tory politicians, had become convinced that the heavy losses in the counties which the Tory Party had sustained in three General Elections he had specially .noted must be mainly attributed to the Protectionist doctrines preached by a section of his party. It was the unfortunate spread of the Protectionist doctrines to the general body of his party that nearly caused its annihilation in 1906. The best friends of the Opposition hope they may find a means of getting rid of the incubus—by giving it to the Colonies or by any other "new method" that may he devised. But Women Tariff Reformers, strong in their devotion to a fallen cause, proceed as though their League had still a mission to perform. They cannot but com- mand our admiration. We hope their trips will thrive and that their cinematograph shows will prosper, but that they will con- tinue to ignore the discussion of Tariff Reform. It is indeed an intricate question and the issues involved are really serious, as the working-class populations of the North of England are always prepared to prove at ' the polling booth.

STRIKES AND RUMOURS OF STRIKES.

Warrington and the immediate neighbour- hood have had their share of industrial unrest of late, strikes and rumours of strikes having, to a considerable extent, agitated local industrial and agricultural life. After a strike lasting eight days, the dispute between the teamowners and the carters ended on Tuesday in a compromise by which the men secured wages concessions falling considerably short of their originals demands. Next the unskilled workers employed by Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd., gave notice that, failing recognition of their trade union, they would go on strike to-day. Some of the more impetuous spirits, however, took the law into their own hands on Wed- nesday and, without the sanction of their union, left work in a body as a protest against the filling of vacancies created, they state,by the discharging of a number of men The unrest has now spread from the town to the country and, both in Lancashire and Cheshire,we hear of strikes of farm labourers who are bent on improving their economic position.

For the settlement of the carters' strike we are to some extent indebted to the Mayor whose never failing diligence and unquench- able optimism, in the role of mediator, have earned the gratitude of the community. In the interests of our great manufactories and of the thousands of workpeople dependent upon them, it was imperative that steps should be taken to relieve a situation which daily assumed deeper gravity and threatened to bring the principal works to a standstill. The men at first demanded a minimum wage of 265. per week for one-horse drivers, and 28s. per week for two-horse drivers, but they have resumed work for minima of 245: and '27s. respectively. The teamowners pointed out that the rates which they were receiving for certain large contracts precluded a higher advance to the men at this juncture, but a satisfactory feature of the case was that they promised to re-consider the carters' applica- tionwhen they had obtained more favourable terms for themselves. The establishment of a minimum wage and the placing of overtime on a definite basis are achievements upon which the men may fairly congratulate themselves. Above all, from the progressive and tradeunion standpoint,is thegaining of the principle of "recognition." Collective action is as justifiable on the part of the workmen— who, if left to their individual resources would almost inevitably fail to do justice to, their own cases—as it is in the case of the employers by whom it is now so generally adopted. To attempt to treat the workmen organizations as if they were non-existent, is in these enlightened days, almost as futile as Mrs. Partington's heroic but absurd effort to stem the incoming tide. EDUCATIONAL TOPICS.

There are several subjects on the agenda for Monday's Education Committee meeting that promise to raise the gathering some- what out of the ordinary groove. It will be reported that a Committee has been appointed to consider an application from the Warring- ton Teachers' Association asking for an increase in the scale of salaries for head mistresses and certificated class teachers. This is part of a national movement being made by the N.U.T. and all education authorities have received a similar applica- tion. It will be noted that only female teachers are affected by this request. The School Management Committee having considered the request of the Rector for an alteration in a time-table for religious instruction in the Seconday School will report that they cannot see their way to accede to the request. It will be remembered that the letter was referred to the sub-committee by the last meeting of the Education Corn mittee, after it had been read and commented upon, in strong terms, by the Chairman, Councillor, Henry Roberts. A much-needed reform is foreshadowed for the curriculum of the Secondary School. The opinion of the parents tof children attending that really splendid institution, has been taken, and, as a result, the Director has been requested to submit definite proposals for the introduction of a commercial side in the school. In a town of the size of Warrington, with its many-sided commercial aud trading interests, such an advance will be appreci- ated and, in course of time, will have its effect upon the business life of the place. There may be another discussion on new schools, architects, architects' fees and arrangements to be made in the event of the committee deciding not to go on with the building of any school for which plans have been prepared. This is a complicated affair in which Councillor Pemberton might be expected to revel.

The Board of Education have paid the local education authority a direct and practical compliment that ought not to be lost sight of, especially by those who make a point of asking whether we are getting value for what we pay in the shape of educa- tion rates. The Warrington Committee have so pleased the Board that the latter have granted £319 ss. sd. in respect of the expenses incurred by the Committee in following up and seeing that children are properly treated after they have been reported upon as suffer- ing from defects of the throat or eyes, or otherwise, in a manner that would interfere with their educational advancement. The point about this grant is that it is the maximum assessment that can be made under the Board's regulations. RECOLLECTIONS.
The article by our contributor " A.M.," which embodies some recollections of the late

Mr. Frederick Monks concerning old Bridge- street, is of a kind which many of our readers appreciate. Possibly there may be 3ther of our older readers who would like to voice their remembrances of old Warrington, and if this be so our con- tributor (knowing the difficulty most folks have in getting things down upon paper) would be glad to set forth such points of interest as their memories may carry. Not many people realize the interest that old memories have, and we are sure that some of our readers could give great pleasure to others by telling what they remember. After contributing another article or two Mr. Mounfield proposes to conduct for a time a new feature under the heading "I Remember "—to which he will invite letters,notes,and recollections of every kind. Among the subjects suggested for comment are old Warrington schools and schoolmasters, doctors, quaint folk whether of high or low degree, buildings, inns, and institutions. Those who would like to con- tribute are asked to address a post card to this office. GOLF ENTHUSIASTS.

Any mention of the progress that is being made in the world of local sport would be incomplete without a pointed reference to the advances that are being made by the Warrington Golf Club. The course, naturally situated,at Hill Cliffe, so as to make it one ot the most picturesque in the country, has been improved so greatly that the season now beginning inds it also one of the best appointed in the kingdom. A new feature will be the competition for the Henry Fairclough Memorial Prize which has been subscribed for by the members upon a scale indicating, by its generous nature, the respect in which Mr. Fairclough, who was their captain at the time of his death, was held. The prize consists of a silver cup, to be held for twelve months, a personal trophy for the winner and an oak panel to be fixed in the , club house, upon which the winners' names are to be recorded for the edification of ' posterity. A scheme for the competition , will be submitted to the annual general meeting of members to be held this month. It is proposed to have four qualifying rounds to be played in May, June, July and August, and the final will be played, 36 holes, in September.

MUSICAL SOCIETY DIFFICULTIES. The annual meeting of the Warrington Musical Society's members—usually a most uninteresting affair—was, this year, marked by one of those little surprises which are not infrequently sprung upon the deliberations of semi-public bodies when pursuing the even tenour of their way. From the hum-drum business of reading accounts, deadly dull in their chronicling of ever-recurrent losses,and of re-electing, apparently as a matter of course, the society's accustomed officers and committee, members suddenly emerged into a discussion touching the very roots of the society's policy and management. Mr. Jack's expression of dissatisfaction upon the question of expenditure, and his contention that the Musical Society should see to it that its present three concerts a season are made to pay before embarking upon additional enterprises, deserve serious consideration by the society's executive. Having regard to statements reflecting upon the Musical Society's constitution such as Mr. Reynolds referred to as having been made at recent meetings of the Town Council, the problem of how to keep the society's head above water must be tackled in all serious- ness. Unfortunately, the way of the War- rington Musical Society's 80 year's activity, is, like that of many another kindred society in the kingdom, strewn with annual losses, and paved with more or less earnest efforts to meet them, and there seems little likelihood that, in the present trend of public taste, any better results can be expected in the future. But the fact that undoubted educational benefits are, as we are bound to admit, conferred upon communities by the work of these societies, unquestionably lifts them , above considerations of a narrow corn- I mercialism. The means to enable such institutions to continue their useful work are, we think, to be sought in the direction of some judicious subsidy by municipal authorities under powers they already possess, rather than in a niggardly cheese-paring on the part of private individuals self-sacrificingly trying to carry them on. For this reason we are not in accord with Mr. Jack's idea of decreasing the number of concerts the society gives during a season in order proportionataly to curtail its losses, for obviously such an argument, carried to its logical conclusion by any society, must end in its self-effacement. The cheerily expressed preference of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., the society's genial president, for =l, line of action involv- ing a special effort on the part of each and every member of the society to popularise and arouse interest in its object and work during next season, is therefore one with which we specially desire to associate our- selves.

THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, APRIL 19, 1913.
THE WOMAN TARIFF REFORMER'S
DEVOTION.

The best of the many good qualities of a woman is, and always has been, her devotion to those around her in the day of adversity. As the great poet-novelist of the North emphasised in one of his most famous passages, woman when all is going well is afflicted with a disposition to be coy and hard to please and is so unstable as to be as variable as the shade cast by the aspen, but in the midst of difficulties may safely be regarded as a ministering angel. It will doubtless be in a guise of ministering angels that Mr. BONAR LAW will look upon the members of the Warring- ton Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform League, who, this week, have held their annual meeting for the election of their officers. To outside observers it had appeared to be more than probable that since Mr BONAR LAw had given the final death blow to Tariff Reform, women tariff reformers would have become weary in well doing . but, locally at all events, they are made oi sterner stuff. Belonging to the race of which, in the bulk, we are so proud to belong, we cannot but admire the fidelity of thq League to a lost cause, a fidelity that impels large bodies to cling to a flag that has lost its glamour and floats, when there is sufficient wind to stir it, at half-mast.

But perhaps the local Women Tariff Reformers have not yet heard of the disaster which has overtaken the policy for which they stand. Certain it is that one looks in vain for any reference to tariffs or food taxes, either in the "fourth annual report" or the speeches by which that illuminating docu- ment was supported. Huge processions, a huge Union Jack, great tea parties, birthday celebrations, service medals, and trips to New Brighton are, quite properly, discoursed for the delectation of the members of the most successful organisation of its kind in the country; but the nearest approach to I food taxes appears in one forelorn and lonely sentence which speaks vaguely of the "inaccuracies of the present Radical Govern- ment, and the disastrous effects of Free Trade in our country." We confess to not being able to understand. It is one of the easiest things in the world to charge opponents with being guilty of "inaccuracies"—a graceful way of expressing another word very becoming to the occasion— ane. the report wisely leaves the charge in the safe keeping of a generality. As to the "disastrous effects of Free Trade," we have only to look around us for proof of the justice or otherwise of the assertion, more hinted than made. We have not to go further than the works of Messrs. Rylands Bros. and see how surely they are spreading themselves over a large district in the midst of which they were, not so very long ago, a compara- tively small works employing less than half the men they now employ, to show the kind of " disaster " that Free Trade has brought to Warrington. If we were disposed to go further afield, we might quote the deserved success of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company—to say nothing of the huge extension that is about to come into exist- ence at Partington.

div.head: HEART'S MORNING.
div.p: HEART'S MORNING.

My heart is full of the morning, My soul is full of the spring, I am all on fire with gladness, And I cannot choose but sing. • A million flowers are breaking From every dewy lawn, And to merely live is rapture In the light of such a dawn.

What though the world be weary, There burns within its breast The gleam of the summer's glory, The dream of the autumn's rest; What though men's brows are aching, And women's eyes be wet, God moves in the budding daisies, And he will not forget.

My heart is full of the morning, Of love, and joy, and mirth; Of the bliss of the distant heaven, Of the kiss of the dear old earth. He did not send it spinning Through the endless round of years With a witless want of meaning, And He will dry our tears.

In all its shining circle There is not one soul I hate, From the King in his robes of purple, To the beggar at his gate; And ah ! for the light that glistens In the eyes of those I love; And oh! for the friends uncounted Whose golden worth I prove.

And the gentle woodland creatures, And the birds are mates of mine, And the tribes of the rolling ocean, And all the stars that shine. * * a * a My heart is full of the morning, My soul is full of the spring : I shall live and love for ever; And I cannot choose but sing! ARTHUR BENNETT.
We shall be glad to receive poetical contributions from our readers with a view to inserting that which appears to us to merit publication.

A CHARACTER SKETCH.

It would be an impertinence to attempt to act as sponsor for the new Editor of the Warrington "Examiner." Happily there is no need. His long experience has pro- vided a discipline both of intellect and charactei which falls to the lot of few journalists. Ability so modestly displayed, so unstintedly given was ure to be recognised sooner or later. Now Mr. Weston's hour has come. Certain crippling limitations now disappear. An atmosphere at once congenial, a wide range of topics, certain deep convictions and high ideals, which hitherto found but occasional expression, will henceforth have free scope. For Mr. Weston unites many and varied qualities in his own person. He has the didactic gift of a first- rate preacher veiled with consummate ease and skill; the insight of a seer; the zeal of a reformer ; and the practised grace of a ready writer. His knowledge is wide and accurate. He has a full grasp of facts and a capacious storehouse of sifted information. His mode of presenting his theme shows a personality strong and versatile. Now there is wit or humour, irony or invective, as the nature of the case requires. Behind it all and permeating it, is a spirit kindly, gracious and tolerant. He has scorn for the hypocrite, unstinted praise for the truth-speaker and writer, and , is able to appraise at his real worth the public man who gives himself because he must to the well-being of the civic state. No servant of the Commonwealth has a kinder critic or a more generous supporter. It would be rare to find profound scholar- ship in an Editor whose time for pursuing private studies and research is next to nothing; but all the same, Mr. Weston's intellectual aquirements have to be reckoned with. He loves our English tongue and its ' characteristic channels of expression in the ' Great Masters of thought and speech. He knows intimately that "for all the highest purposes of the poet, the philosopher, and the orator, it is inferior to Ihe tongue of Greece alone." He has himself tested its flexibility, and felt its magic and its persuasive witchery. He has used it as a vehicle for those moments when a man's best thoughts are called up from the hidden depths. He has made it forcible when other minds and consciences have had to be touched and roused. He has deftly and delicately sounded a note of tenderness and pathos when such has been needed. He has never debased this intellectual currency, but in his hands it has called forth no little admiration from those who know. _

„ All these things, however, are part of the man, and help you to know him. His friend- ship is a thing sui generis. It has been a source of satisfaction and enjoyment with the steady sweep of the years. It is strong and true because the man himself is strong and true. To know him at home is to learn something of the secret he possesses. He is a man who enjoys his work. Writing is his native air. He loves it. He revels in it. It is his life's task. Give him a subject. Tell him to write. Give him space, and if you have any mind at all he will provide it with something well worth its acceptance and (continued in the Next Column.)

div.head: COY DAMSEL.
div.p: THE COY DAMSEL.
MORE AMALGAMATION TALK A 7 STOCKTON HEATH.
A SPIRIT OF CAUTION.

The first business, after the ordinary routine business transacted by the newly-elected Stockton Heath Parish Council, at their meeting on Tuesday night, had refer- ence to the proposed Amalgamation of Stockton Heath and Warrington. Mr. James Whitley presided over an attendance including Messrs. J. H. Clarke; H. J. Westbrook, F. Pearson, John Hallows, C. W. Hallow, W. Mclntyre, J. McDerrnid, F. Rose, F. Warburton, C. Dukes and E. Bradshaw (clerk). Mr. Bottomley entered the room just as this discussion ended. ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES.

The Chairman said they were called upon to consider the advantages and disadvantages that would follow if Stockton Heath became incorporated with Warrington. The advantages were said to be cheaper gas, cheaper water—(" No ")—electricity supply to houses and shops and, if necessary, for street-lighting purposes, a halfpenny reduction of tram fires and, last but not least, preferential rating for ten or fifteen years. At present the Stockton Heath rates were es. 21 in the £ and the Warrington rates were Si... Mr. Westbrook called attention to the fact that the rate for the pat half-year was 3s. hi., but only 2s. 11d. for the next, so that the rates were not Gs. 2d. in the £.

The Chairman, proceeding, said that Wilderspool had a fifteen years' preferential rate emoted on joining Warrington sixteen years ago. Wilderspool now paid the Warrington rat's on the basis of Ss., or Is. UV. more than Stockton Heath. What advantages (lid Wilderspool enjoy over those of Stockton Heath? Besides, what guarantee had they that the rates in

div.head: wIARRINGTON FIFTEENYEARs HENCE
div.p: wIARRINGTON FIFTEENYEARs HENCE

would not be IOF. 6d. ia the ? he;;;.)-- Shortly Warrington would probably require £150,000 added to their large loans for elementary education purposes,and his expectation was that while in Stockton Heath the rates were not likely to rise above Gs., Warring- ton rates would go 4r. beyond that sum. (Hear, hear.) Those were matters calling for careful and serious consideration. Their passages were well r•ade and laid, sanitary matters were receiving close attention, and improvemeets were being rapidly made. He believed their parish matters generally were in advance of any other parish in the Rural Council district. Their ratable value was superior to all others within a very large radius ; and personally he could not tea any wisdom whatever in pressing forward to come to terms with Warrington for amalgamation. He believed they would in a very short time regret the step if they took it. BEWARE THE SUPPOSITIOUS CASE. MR. WESTBROOK'S ADVICE.

Mr. H. J. Westbrook. speaking as the proposer of the resolution at the Parish Meeting, said it seemed to him very undesirable—if they were to approach the question with open minds—that they should pledge themselves regarding, or even criticise, a supposi- tious case, before they had heard the case of Warring- ton. Personally he should carry out the mandate of the parish meeting and propose that the new councillors with power to add to their number any ratepa3,ers likely to be of wsistance,should go thoroughly into this matter of amalgamation in all its bearings and, in due course, submit the results of their deliberations to the parishioners. It had been left to them whether the whole Council should act, or whether they should appoint a sub-committee, but he thought all ought to be on the committee. It was not correct for anyone to say that the matter had been under consideration of that Council for ten )ears, and that they could not make up their minds. Such a statement could only be the result of lack of knowledge. This question and that of applying for urban powers had been dealt with, and had been the subject of formal reports within the period ramed. He moved that the Council, with outside aid as he had suggested, should consider and report upon the question of amalgamation in all its bearings. He would remind them that if the matter went forward thole would be a Local Govern- ment Board inquiry so they mu,t be very careful what they said now. They must be prepared to stand by what they said. Mr. John Hallows seconded.
Mr. Mc Intyre thought they should be csreful, in en-opting ratepayers to act with the Council, to see that the Council should he in a clear majority.

THE RESOLUTION was carried unanimously and the following five were elected as co-opted members for the purpose of the inquiry :—Mew:rs. Joseph Monks, J. H. Fletcher, J. R. Wood, J. W. Bouchier and Adam Bennett.

div.head: LICENSING SCHEME.
div.p: LICENSING SCHEME.
REMOVALS AND RE-BUILDING SANCTIONED.

The important licensing scheme, outlined at the annual licensing sessions, received the confirmation of the borough magistrates yesterday. Mr. Greaves Lord, barrister (instructed by Mr. A. Browne), on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., formally made the application for the provisional orders to be confirmed. On March 7th an application was granted for the removal of the full licence of the Royal Arms, Bank-street, to the Old House at Home. The alterations would mean the concentration of two licences, which at present exist, into one. In addition to that, it would enable the public authorities to acquire the Royal Arms withc.ut having t 9 pay com- pensation on the basis of licensed premises. In that way the Corporation would effect a great public improvement at a much smaller cost than would other- wise have been the case. The licensee had been dealt with generously. Plans for the Old House at Home alterations constituted considerable improve- ment to the present premises. They would be more adaptable and more convenient. With regard to the Bowling Green Inn, Liverpool-road, lie applied for the removal of that licence. At present the bowling green was on one side of the road and the licensed house on the other. They were intending to set up premises on the bowling green side of the road. The improvement would remove an awkward corner on an important road. Messrs. Greenall intended that the Railway Tavern should be referred for compensation and they undertook to accept .-:1,000 less than the sum agreed upon as proper compensation for that licence. They bad alro agreed to give up the out-door licence of Mr. Mayers, Powys-street, as from the time whets the alterations would be carried cut and the new house _

erected. They had made provision with regale to the licensee and %%mild not have the slightest difficulty in closing the other licensed houses the moment the alterations at the Dowling Green were carried out and the new preruiss opened. If the orders were granted, the Royal Arms would be closed from to-day. The magistrates confirmed the order.

div.head: LADY TYPIST'S FINE ACHIEVEMENT.
div.p: LADY TYPIST'S FINE ACHIEVEMENT.

The challenge issued by the well-known professional typist, Mr. R. G. Curtis (Royal Typewriter Co.), and accepted by Miss Doris Emmett, of Wood's Tutorial College, Warrington and Northwich. whose dexterity on. the Salter typewriter has been universally recognized as phenomenal, culminated in a most remarkable con- test held at the Business Exhibition, Glasgow. Miss Doris Emmett's wonderful performance showed her to be a " picked " competitor, and many congratulations were showered on her coach, Mr. F. Wilson Wood (the finest touch type-writing expert in the country), by the delighted onlookers and competition judges alike. Miss Doris Emmett was awarded the second trophy. A student in the Civil Service Section of the College, Miss Mary Makepeace, has been successful in securing first position and an appointment at Macclesfield Pgst Office, gaining 1,400 marks.

the ideal of any newspaper building on sure foundations. When I think of the service a newspaper like the " Examiner " must have rendered to live, and imagine the service it may perform as its horizon widens with ever- growing opportunity, I know its future must be assured. It is no mean task in life to reflect the striving effort, the hopes, the ambitions of a robust town, such as War- rington, with its 70,000 souls has become, and it is not a light responsibility. Nor should one forget the responsibility does not rest only upon the paper. The paper reflects the life about it. The " Examiner" may hold the mirror up to the native of Warrington, but the town should have some care for the reflection created by itself. That the paper will contrive to be worthy of the people, I know; with a due sense of responsibility I hope the people will be worthy of the paper. Always, the paper reflects the people and tke success of a journal, to my mind, is in exact proportion to the interest displayed by the town in its welfare. The " Examiner " will become a greater paper the more enthusi- astically its service is accepted. GEORGE EDGAR

div.head: ROYAL TOUR.
div.p: ROYAL TOUR.
THE KING'S TRIP THROUGH LANCASHIRE.
An Hour in Warrington.

The official programme orthe visit of the King and Queen to Lancashire towns, in July, was issued on Wednesday by the GAlnty Police. The number of miles .and the times of arrival and departure at the various towns, with times allowed for presentations and visits to works, are included in the notice, copies of which have been sent to the p.,lice authorities of each town. The total length of the tour which begins in Warringt in On, ugh Lancashire is 220 miles. The time-table for the first day is as follows : - Monday, July 7.—Train London to Watrington, leave Loudon 11.30 a.m.,arrive Warrinizton 3 o'clock. Presentations, 10 minutes ; works, 45 minutes ; carriage drive, 10 minutes. Depait 4.5, via Penketh (4.15), arrive Widnes 4.28. Leave here after presentations at 4.38, via litlyton for Knowsley, where they arrive at 5.10. The distance to be driven this day, 16 mites.

div.head: ROYAL TRAIN
div.p: THE ROYAL TRAIN

The London and North Western Royal Train in which their Majesties will travel to Warrington. represents the highest perfection yet attained in rail- way carriage building in England, and the guiding idea has been to offer the Royal travellers apartment., which shall, as far as possible, make them forget they are in a train—a delusion which the easy running on the splendid track of the L. & N. W. Railway materially assists. Another point has been to secure a type of decoration in the most perfect taste, all gauliness or exag-teration being carefully avoided. In the Royal train there is a coach specially thrsigued for the King and another for the Queen, with six_ earriqfzes for their suites, with of course, communica tion throughout.

div.head: BOWLER'S DISAPPEARANCE.
div.p: BOWLER'S DISAPPEARANCE.
Search for Well-known Warrington Man.

The police are making extensive inquiries concern- ing the disappearance of Stephen Henry Daintith, better known as Harry Daintith, Ivhe 1 Aged in Legh- street and has not been heard of since S.:lid on the morning of April 7th. Mr. Daintith is a member of a fawily vb hien is well-known and respecled in War- rington and Parigate, his father having at one time I e.m the licensee of the Stocks Inn, Padgate. The ‘v hole of Mr. Daintith's life has been spent in War- ran ton and neighbourhood and his mysterious dis- appearance is causing anxiety to a large circle of friends. _ _

Mr. Daintitb, who is 43 years of age, was employed as a gas-stove titter at the works of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd., Academy-street. A week last Monday he left his lodgings, put in an appearance at work, and went back to breakfast. After breakfast he left the house apparently to return to work, and a workman states that he was seen outside the works as the men were reassembling, but he did not go inside. From that moment not a trace of him can be found. He appeared to hemn good health and cheerful spirits and his relatives and friends are utterly at a loss to account for his disappearance. Air. Daintith is unmarried, and a man of some means. A search of his belongings shows that his money and securities were left intact. The following descripton is issued : Height rift. Oin. or 10in., broad-shouldered, blue eyes, hair and moustache turning grey, fresh complexion. He was wearing a grey cap, black jacket and vest with grey trousers, with a blue slop beneath the jacket, blue print collar and front without a tie, black stockings, and strong lace-up boots. Any informa- tion will be welcomed by the Chief Constable of Warrington, or Mr. Steel, Solicitor, Warrington, who has been consulted by the relatives. Information has been received to the effect that a man answering Mr. Daintah's description has been seen at Preston and the clue is being investigated.

div.head: Solway Prince's Interrupted Journey.
div.p: Solway Prince's Interrupted Journey.

The Solway Prince, which was sunk in the Ship Canal at Statham ou Saturday, March 22nd, through having been in collision with the Rossmore, and held up almost the whole of the traffic on the great water- way for four days, was finally refloated last Saturday and was towed to the Manchester docks for repairs. Before the vessel was raised, a patch was fixed on her starboard bow, covering a V-shaped hole about 9ft. by 10ft.

Mr. Frank Hickman offered for sale at the Blue Bell sale rooms, on Wednesday, two pairs of semi-detached leasehold dwelling-houses, 17 and 19 and 21 and 23, Lower Wash-lane, Latchford ; gross rental £B3 4s. ; ground rent £4 33. 4d. After gcod competition the property was sold for £SO2, another indication that the property market is improving. Mr. Arthur J. Willett was solictor for the vendors.

attention. He shines in his work. He has seen the public life of Warrington from many sides during a great number of years. He has been its principal focus and centre. What appears in a public print is nothing compared with what an editor has to keep out. What my friend does not know about Warrington during the last sixteen years is not worth knowing. Probably he has for- gotten more than many public men are evei• likely to know. He loves books with the ardour of an enthusiast, but he loves human kind more. Temperamentally religious, he yet never parades his beliefs. A gentleman by nature, he never has needed an artificial polish to fit him for the drawing room, the banqueting hall or the palace. He is fond of children and has long espoused their cause. We discussed Children's Courts and the need for them long before they came to be. He was among the first to advocate them. He believes in probity in public life and has lofty concep- tions of the morality of its officers and servants. Social work has always found in him a warm and sympathetic friend. The slum lords and their unholy spawn have never been condoned by him. He is a peace- ful man, but dangerous in a fight. He uses weapons which he has essayed to prove, and is a most certain victor. A genial companion, a faithful friend, capable, honourable and upright, he is the known supporter of all good work. His presence in the Editorial chair of the " Examiner " ought to give Warrington's progressive forces the best chance they have ever had. With unhampered freedom, generous confidence, loyalty and support, there is no reason why in his hands, and with his gifted guidance, it should not become one of the finest journals in the North-West of England. Such, at any rate, a y hopes for my friend.
