div.head: Some Reflections on Warrington Newspapers
div.p: Some Reflections on Warrington Newspapers
Past and Present.
By GEORGE EDGAR.

Assuredly, I felt a trifle old when the Editor of the "Warrington Examiner" asked me to write out a few thoughts about the paper, past and present, as a contribution to an issue likely to mark a more forward editorial policy. Making reminiscences has much the same effect on me as insuring my graceless life. I begin to see years as one sees telegraph poles from a railway carriage window. They seem to skip along too fast. At thirty-five I think a man may be counted young, even in this hurrying world. I look upon my greying hair and strive to think the colour, or lack of it, is prematured remember that at thirty-five one should not begin to be reminiscent And I have all sorts of whimsical thoughts when confronted with a request to trail my memories of byegone Warrington before its oldest inhabitants. I remember, with much regret and a little humour, that I knew a bright stripling of eighty-four or five, who was a man in Warrington before my parents were born. And then I catch my breath, for I recall that there are probably not more than four work- ing journalists in Warrington, who know, better than I do, what a Warrington news- paper office looked like twenty years ago. -

Editors and Ideals. Mr. John Sansome was editor of the "Guardian," having succeeded a fine figure of a man, a Mr. Brewtnall, who looked more like an editor than any man I have ever met, and I have known as many editors as most men. Mr. William Gill was editor of the "Observer." He went into the service of one of the Licensed Victuallers' societies, and was succeeded by Mr. Henry Isherwood, always one of the most genial newspaper men in the town. Just about that time, a Mr. Poison, or Powlson, who lived half-way between Warrington and Winwick, and had a stationary and printing shop at Market Gate, ran a moribund paper, then on its last legs. I believe he called it "The Warring- ton Advertiser." No mention of Warring- ton journalism, twenty years ago should omit Alderman Arthur Bennett, then a rising man. He Started the "Sunrise " about that time, and the little paper reflected his enthusiasm and visualised his ideals. I do not think the Warrington of his most ardent early hopes ever materialised, but do know that, through sheer hard work, he ensured by his public life the materialisation of some of his dreams into very solid advan- tages for the town. I was too young to understand what the " Sunrise " stood for in those days, but I recall, vividly, a man named Theodore London, picturesque in personality, young and very eager, a star amongst the " Sunrise " contributors, and, I should think, a man of singular force of character. I had not grown up when be died, but hazarding a guess, I imagine he was one of the most interesting younger men in the Warrington of his day. A Ghost Story.

And one realises the service a paper may give to a public. Slaves come to like the chains that bindthem ; prisoners to glory in the confinement of the pent housP. News- paper men, by the same process of tribulation, find an increasing joy in their twin task- masters—the paper and the public—and an increasing purpose. I see the papers I worked for, prior to the age of twenty, as a series of impish adventures. To-day, I see them as growing responsibilities. To serve must be
(Continued in Xczt Column.)

Mr. George Edgar. who is regarded as one of England's rising novelists, contributes, exclusively to the Examiner," a characteristic article on Warrington and its newspapers and newspaper men of 20 years ago. Mr. Edgar was born in Warrington, and, as one Of our most successful journalists, deals with his subject with an authority second to none.

frenzy in his rolling eye, followed me some minutes later. I was discovered. "Humph," he growled to Messrs Isherwood and Lawton, commenting on my appearance; "I suppose we'll have babies on the Press next." I was abominably hurt and affronted, but one is not hurt very long at a time, at fifteen. I suppose too, I was resilient. Anyhow, Speed, who had a separate life and individuality, distinct from his routine as a reporter, took kindly to me in time, as a colleague. We never bridged the gulf of years, but we became friends and he lent me a copy of his verses.

Mr. Ward was editor of the " Examiner " in those days. I believed he retired to follow the fascinations of poultry farming. Mr. Bond was business manager, then, or soon after. Outside of business, he was a keen amateur musician and used to indulge in chamber music at his house. Alfred Lake was I think, chief reporter—a man older than myself, of very distinguished appearance. His great friend was Grundy of the "Guardian." Lake left to run a paper planned by Mr. Shaw Green, the printer—a short-lived enterprise.

There came a time when I joined the War- rington "Examiner." I represented the paper in Runcorn, where a localised edition was published. I was very young in those days and not very discreet, but the "Examiner" was kind to my faults. Away from the office, representing the " Examiner " at Runcorn, was a pleasant task for a youth. I recall perhaps the most interesting thing I did there with great glee, to this day. I discovered a ghost story and told it in the "Examiner." The haunted house was in a little side street in the centre of Runcorn town. I made the ghost, a phantom little old lady, very spectacular and invested the house with an eerie flavour of a Christmas Number castle. The result somewhat surprised me. The "Examiner" was published , in Runcorn at five o'clock on Friday evening. By seven o'clock half the population of the town was about that little side street, hoot- ing and howling, and playfully engaged in smashing the windows of a harmless cottage. The landlord and owner of the property was I breathing dreadful threats as to what he would do to me and the "Examiner." I went home by all the side streets that night. He was in a more reasonable frame of mind I , the next morning. I compounded with him. 'As I had raised the ghost I offered to lay it. , I voluntered to stop in the house all one night and if I saw no ghost to say so in next week's paper. I remember we made up a nice little card party of about six. There was no ghost and I duly credited the house with an absence of spooks of any kind. The landlord was placated and I—well I retired on my vaguely won laurels. The " Examiner's" Future. Soon after that I left the " Examiner " and embarked in a rather restless life which has taken me to strange places and given me many strange tasks. I have found it moder- ately amusing. And mostly every month I see a copy of the " Examiner " and always I get the thrill a pressman must have at the sight of one of his first papers. "There are no folk, like you're am n folk," one saying goes and I might coin another. There are no papers to a pressman like the old papers. Yet the " Examiner " has not remained the same. I think it has developed a closer grip on its public of late years, and it is bigger, brighter and better printed. My friends tell me it is to do better in the future than it has ever done and that its horizon must continue to widen. lam sure that should be the desire of any living newspaper property, and so long as the desire is there,achievment must follow. I am afraid at the age of fifteen or sixteen. I was not of much use to the "Examiner," but the " Examiner " was of great service to me. Twenty years later, one is much chastened and has to take a sober view of things. At sixteen life was a joke and journalism the merriest jest of all. I had the sense of responsibility one might look for in a fox terrier pup or a young monkey. At thirty-five, I suppose I am at least a matur- ing pressman. One learns by experiences, bitter and sweet, what service to a news- paper really means. Duty of the Public.

div.head: MR. GEORGE EDGAR.
div.p: MR. GEORGE EDGAR.

A Joyous Task. I think to be asked to purvey reminis- ences is practically to admit the impeachment that one is falling into the place of the lean and slippered pantaloon. For this reason, I should have refused to fall in with the suggestion but for the fact that a good friend calls me. Again, another fact weighs heavily. Being born in Warrington is a memory apt to linger. I have never quite got over it. It seems a long time since I lived in the dear old town—too long since I was there. In the time, I have written quite a little dictionary of words for all sorts of papers and all sorts of people. But I find myself joyous in the task of writing a column for " Warrington folk onl:r." It is just like sitting down in some old chimney corner or by a familiar cottage fire and having a crack. Well remembered faces come and go in my mind as I think of the pleasure of it—and some come only to my mind, for they smile no longer in familiar streets. For this reason I am content to be reckoned in the sere and yellow and to come a puling amongst Warringtonians in the carpet slipper stage. The pleasure of chatting with old friends is not easily resisted. Still, in justice to the glorious gift of youth, I ought to insist on my age and to make it quite clear—l am not the oldest inhabitant. Boyhood's Landmarks.

What do I remember of the "Examiner ?" Easily, I recall twenty years of its life. I remember the " Examiner " as a paper coming weekly to my home—edited by Mr. John Walker. I recall the journal, as I saw it, when I grew to be a working man—aged thirteen. The "Examiner," the football issue of the "Echo "the Town Clock, Warrington Bridge, Fair Turner and the inside of St. Peter's Church (then in John-street) were the most familiar elements of my boy- hood. I did not first turn to journalism on the "Examiner." I recall my first effort as a being ultimately destined to live by the dribble of ink from a fountain pen. In those days, "The Warrington Observer "was in fine feather. The paper was edited ith a good flavouring of "ginger" by Mr. William Gill. What Mr. Gill did not say about Warrington worthies of his day was not worth talking about. I fancy he had a sneaking love for the journalistic tradi- tions of Messrs. Pott and Slurk. The paper offered a prize each week for the best funny story—so many shillings to be taken out in books. I won several of these prizes—red letter days for me. The first time I read my own name as prize-winner, in the "Observer," I was down with a juvemle cold. I wonder whether Dr. Geary remembers his visit to my home that day and the fact ,that he made a professional examination of a boy whose high temperature was probably due to the excitement of first seeing himself in print, at the age of ten. I think I had five shillings worth of books for that effort. Since, I have had more than five shillings for a story supposed to be "not unfunny," but I do not think I have ever drawn the warrior's guerdon with more pride than I displayed when I collected my parcel of books, which was as soon as Dr. Geary allowed me to get up. Baptism as a Pressman.

But the " Examiner " ! I had been in journalism a year when I began to know the " Examiner " and its men. The bitterest humiliation of my life came to me through the " Examiner." I was very youthful at fifteen and looked it, I suppose. In these days, the " Examiner " employed a reporter whose name was Speed—a good name for a reporter, I still think. He seemed old to me but I daresay he was not more than thirty or thirty-five. He was something of a poet and had published verses. He took his work seriously,held himself aloof,and had a whole some notion of the dignity of the Press. I turned up to represent a Liverpool daily paper in the Police Court. Even now I grow hot when I think of it. I climbed into the reporters' box, then very like a dog kennel with no roof on it. Mr. Speed, with a fine

div.head: Mho
div.p: Mho
I, DISTRICTtiEWS
LYMM.

A STEAM DISINFECTOR.—The Urban District Council having applied to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £5OO for the ptovision of a steam disinfector and a laundry at the Isolation Hospital. Mr. J. R. Hutchinson, M.D. will hold an inquiry in the Council Offices on Tuesday next at 11 a.m. THE NEW BRIDGE AT THE STATION.—The L. and N.-W. Railway Co.'s inspecting engineer visited the new footbridge at Lymm Station on Monday, and declared it ready for use. It was therefore thrown open to the public, but whether the said public will take advantage of the facility remains to be seen. LYMM AMATEURS AS FINALISTS.—The Lymm Amateur A.F.C. after a successful season defeated the Moss Side Baptist team last week at Chorlton-cum- Hardy in the semi-final for the Rhodes Cup by the com- fortable score of 3-0. This means that they will meet the Manchester Externers in the Final which is to be played on the ground of the Old Trafford St. John's Club, at Old Trafford, this afternoon. The Amateurs have played consistently well during the latter half of the season, not having been beaten in the past nine weeks. Great credit must be given to the defence players for this result. THE NEW HIGH SHERIFF.—On taking the chair at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Mr. J. W. Sidebottom intimated that Mr. Alfred Watkin would not be able to act as chairman of the Bench for twelve months, on account of his having been appointed High Sheriff of the County. On behalf of the public of Lyme), he congratulated Mr. Watkin on the honour conferred npon him. They all hoped that be would have a pleasant sear of office. He (the speaker) was quite sure Mr. Watkin would conduct the affairs of office with great ability and dignity, and reflect honour not only on himself but on the district in which he lived. OUGT•ITRINGTON CHURCH.—The annual exhibition and sale of work, which plays inch an important part in providing the funds for the working of the Sunday schools connected with the Oughtriugton Parish Church was held in the schools on Thursday and Friday. The room, which had been tastefully prepared for the occasion, contained the following stalls :—Farmers, ladies working party, pound, sweet and basket, and teachers' stalls, on which were a capital show of fancy and plain work, farm produce, groceries, sweets and other varieties of goods. There was also a well patronized tea room, cake and doll competitions, and a series of splendid entertainments. On the second night a jumble sale of new and second-hand articles formed part of the proceedings. The Rector and Mrs. Wethered were ably assisted by Mesdames Barnes, Bell, Brazendale, Brereton, Dale, Davies, Forrest, A. Homan, 'l'. Jones. Lord, Partridge, Rutter, F. Thomson, Travis, Whitlow, Wilkinson, Wood; Miss Peters, and Messrs. Crawley, F. Eaton, W. G. Limb and H. Profit. CONGREGATIONALIST JUBILEE.—Last week end the Lynim Congregationalists celebrated the Jubilee Anniversary of their church. On Saturday night they held a Church" At Home" and re-union of old mem- bers in the schoolroom which had been tastefully decorated in " drawing room" style by the ladies of the congregation. The senior deacon (Mr. J. Hardy Holt) presided and was supported by the Revs. T. W. Pinn M.A. (Stockport), and C. Earnest Watson (Rodboro), former pastors of the church ; Messrs. J. Astley (Chester), J. E. Bell (Stockport), E. Mumford (Manchester), former deacons; J. D. B. Smith, the Hon. Church Secretary ; and the Rev. H. W. B. Whiteway. Mr. J. H. Holt, in his opening remarks, gave a brief review of the history of the Church during his twenty years on the deaconate. —The Rev. T. W. Finn, M.A., pastor from 1872-1878, indulged in some very interesting reminisances of the state of the church Goring his stay at Lymm.—The Rev. C. E. Watson also spoke of the past history of the Church, and the pleasant and helpful memories of his pastorate (1899-1903.)--Mr. James Astley, who for many years was the choirmaster and• Church secretary, also addrsssed the gathering, as did Mr. E. Mumford. Both these gentlemen took an active part in the work of the Sunday School,—Mr. J. D. B. Smith read several letters of apology for absence from old friends of the Church. He expressed his regret at having to announce that the pastor, the Rev Arthur Penaliggon was prevented from attending by his illness. He also read a letter of cengratulation and good wishes from the members of the Broarlheath Congregational Church. Songs by Mrs. Wyatt,Miss Wright,Mr. J. H. Brazendale, Mr. J. Ellis; a -vocal duet by Miss and Mr. D. Holt, and pianoforte selections by Miss Wright, added to the enjoyment of the evening. Refreshments were also provided.—The Rev. C. E. Watson preached the anniversary sermons at both the morning and evening services on Sunday, his remarks on the latter occasion being based on the text "Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments." At the morning service the choir rendered the anthem "The Lord is my Shepherd, the bass solo being well rendered by Mr. D. Holt. In the afternoon a scholars' service was held in the church, at which Mr. Ernest Leather sang the solo "Passing along life's way," This he repeated, by request, at the even- ing's se:vice, when the choir also gave a good interpre- tation of "Hallelujah; King of kinks." Mr. A. Leather presided at the organ. On Monday evening a public tea meeting was provided in the schoolroom when the tables were presided over by Mesdames Brearley, Gotobed, Groves, Holt, A. Leather, P. N. Leather, Simpson, Willan' arid the Misses Boond, Forrest, M. Hesketh, E. Hesketh, and Rushton. The tea was followed by a lecture on " Shame, Frauds, and Forgeries," given by the Rev. C. E. Watson. The lecturer, in speaking about modern shams, made men- tion of the fact that even some ladies were shams, with their false teeth, hair, and complexion. Whilst exposing the deception that is practised on the public with regards to the true ingredients of jam' he said he had met a person whose occupation was that of providing seeds for the purpose of " making-up " straw- berry and raspberry jams. Frauds in religion and history were all touched upon. Speaking about forgeries, he said that one of the most frequent practices was the sale of so called " old ' oak furniture, and being a connoisseur he was able to tell his audience the methods of finding out any cases of deception. The lecture, while being a very humorous one, was also very instructive. In the absence of the pastor the chair was taken by Mr. J. D. B. Smith. He announced that the church was making a special effort to celebrate its Jubilee by raising a fund of £250 for the purpose of liquidating the present adverse balance and to complete the fund for the purchase of the chief rent. In order to do this, they hope to hold a sale of work next October. A carol, " All this night bright angels sing" was given by the scholars. A vote of thanks to the lecturer was proposed by Mr. J. H. Holt, seconded by Mr. J. Hewitt, and carried with acclama- tion. The attendances at all the Jubilee meetings have been excellent.

div.head: " ANCHOR " INN.
div.p: THE " ANCHOR " INN.
Licensee Summoned:
Case Dismissed.

At the Lymm Petty Sessions. on Wednesday, before M.. J. W. Sidebottom and other magistrates, Mary Ann Moston, licensee of the Anchor Inn, Lymrn, was summoned for supplying intoxicating liquor to a drunken person named James Heaney, a farm labourer, on March 24th, and also for permitting drunkenness on her licensed premises on the same date. Mr. Caldecutt ilinutsford) conducted the prosecution, and Mr. Hockin (Manchester) defended. Mr. Caldecutt stated that at 2 a.m. on the Tuesday in Easter week, P.C. Gould found the man Heaney in a helpless state of drunkenness in a lane about half a mile from the house. He was lying in the road and had been vomiting. There was also blood on his clothing. With the assistance of Sergeant Washington, Heaney was taken to the police station, and was con- victed the next morning. Mrs. Moston was in the court, and the evidence was read over to her. Heaney and another man named Henry went into the Anchor Inn and at 8 o'clock, and remained until 10.50. Henry would say that he had four pints of beer and Eleaney had three. Within 10 minutes of leaving the house, Heaney collapsed in the road. It was the duty of the licensee to take all reasonable precautions to prevent drunkenness. If the Bench were satisfied that the man was drunk and that there was a sale at this house. then the evidence was complete. P.C. Gould deposed to finding Heaney in the middle of the road, helplessly drunk. His lip was bleeding and there were marks on his face. Mrs. Moston stated that the man had been in her house drinking on the previous night. Mr. Hockiu : Were those marks consistent with either a blow or a fall ?—Yes, they were. _

Mr. Caldedutt : Was the man drunk ?—Yes. He was past talking. Sergeant Washington said his opinion was that the marks had been caused by a fall. The cut on the lip might have been caused by a blow. Henry had said something about Heaney having been thrashed by another Irishman. By Mr. Caldecutt : Heaney had never suggested that anyone had hit him. Michael Henry, Irish farm labourer, said he had nearly four pints and Heaney had two pints and a glass of beer. Heaney was quite fit to go home, as he was perfectly sober. He had had as much as he could deceutly carry. Mr. Hockin : A man ought; to be able to take his beer and carry it decently. It was wrong to carry it indecently. Witness: He was quite fit to go home and was perfectly sober. James Heaney (19), Irish farmer labourer, said he bad three pinta of ale in the Anchor. As he was going home a man came up to him and knocked him speech- less. He could not get up. He was sober and quite able to walk until he was knocked down by "a big tall man about six feet five inches. He had not seen the man before.
In reply to the Chairman, witness stated that he had not mentioned that fact before, because he was not asked about it.
Mr. Caldecutt : He was a big man you say ?—Yes. Mr.Caldecutt : He looked big that night. (Laughter).

Mr. Hockin submitted that no case had bean made out. There were cases where the police had made mis- takes and he submitted a mistake had been made in the present one. The man Heaney was suffering from the effects of a blow and not from drink. The evidence had shown that the man was sober and Heaney himself bad accounted for his injuries. It had been common talk in the village ever since. Mrs. Aloston repudiated both of the charges alleged against her. She had always conducted the house with every precaution and she had an excellent character. She generally closed the house ten minutes before the law compelled her to do so. Then again, the house had been referred for compensa- tion. If a conviction took place, the value to be awarded would be diminished He was not saying that to enlist the sympathies of the bench,but to illustrate that such being the case, the licensee would take special care to maintain the good character. Mary Ann Moston said the house had been in the family for 40 years and they had never had a conviction or a complaint made against them. _ Several witnesses were called and testified to the sobriety of the two Irishmen when they left the house. Luke James, Cherry Hall farm, said that soon after 11 o'clock on the 24th March be heard a.row in the lane and next morning he found a cap in the lane (presumably Heaney's, as he was arrested without any headgear. The Chairman (Mr. J. W. Sidebottorn) said there was not sufficient evidence to justify a conviction and the case would he dismissed.

div.head: URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
MR. S. DAVIES ELECTED CHAIRMAN. ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council was held in the Council Cbamber on Thursday evening, when the busineas included the appointment of chairman, vice-chairman and committees.—Mr. W. Mußard (clerk) was elected to the chair pro toil, and the following members were present :—Rev. G. B. Thurston, Messrs. 0. L. Watford, W. 0. Groves, J. H. Holt, S. Davies, G. Smith, f. H. Warburton, W. Gould, R. H. Gotobed, F. Lockyer, and T. F. W. Dixon, with Dr. Do Jong (medical officer). Mr. D. Mort (surveyor) and Mr. W. L. Donaldson (gas ruananer).

div.head: COST OF ELECTIONS.
div.p: COST OF ELECTIONS.
The Clerk reported that the cost of the recent Council elections, in which there were no contests, was £4 13s. 6d.

THE NEW CHAIRNIAN. Mr. Warburton proposed that Mr. Groves be re--elected Cuairman for the ensuing year, as a large amount of business had to be transacted in view of the purchase of the materworks Sze. Mr. Groves had been the right man in the right place and had the whole scheme at his finger ends, having had to come down to the offices frequently. After a brier silence Mr. Holt seconded the proposi- tion. Considering Mr. Groves had taken on such a large amount of work during the past year, it was only right that he should see matters through, and it was their duty to back him up. r, Mr. Gotobed moved an amendmPnt that Mr. S.

avies be elected Chairman. He did so with no dis- respect to Mr. Groves. Last year they had a heavy year before them and the Council considered it their duty to appoint Mr. Groves, who was one of the oldest members of the Council to enable them to have the benefit of his long experience. The appointment was made on the understanding that it was only for twelve months. He came to the meeting feeling sure that Mr. Groves could not expect to be appointed for a second year. , They were all deeply indebted to Mr. Groves for the valuable services he had rendered during the year. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Davies had been a member of the council for a considerable time and had rendered good service as chairman of the Roads Committee for several years. He was a frequent attender at the Council meetings and he thatignt they would be doing the right thing in appointing him as chairman. The office of chairman and the honour which was attached to it, should go round, and when they bad suitable gentlemen on the Council, personal feeling should be waived and honour should be bestowed on those to whom honour was due. (Hear, hear). Mr. Gould seconded. He did so with no disrespect to Mr. Groves, but, as they all knew, he had had his fill of honours. Mr. Davies hed been a member of the Council for many years and it was time they recognised his services to the district, Mr. Holt said it was decided last year that Mr Groves's appointment should be for 12 months. The Council was in a peculiar position last year. Mr. Gotobed had expressed the opinion that the office of chairman ought to go roun4, but his (the speakers') chief reason for supporting Mr. Groves was the fact that he had such an intimate knowledge of the important work before them. He did not think it was Ake to change horses whilst crossing a stream, Mr. Groves, replying to Mr. Gotobed. said he did not come to that meeting expecting to be made chairman. He was not expecting to be elected. Mr. Gotobed: I did not wish to convey that impres- sion at all. Mr. Groves: That was how you put it.

Five voted for the amendment and two for the pro- position and eventually Mr Davies as unanimously appointed chairman. Mr. Davies took the chair and:thanked the council for the great honour they had conferred upon him, He hoped that the good feeling which had existed in the past would be continued. '1 he work before the Council was fairly heavy, as two or three important questions had to be settled. He hoped that if at any time he did not conduct the business of the chair to the satisfaction of the members, that they would hear with him. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: VICE-CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THE VICE-CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Gould proposed the election of Mr. Gotobed as vice-chairman. He was a capable man and worthy of the honour. He bad worked hard for the benefit of the district, without feta or favour. Sometimes he said things which might not have been popular but at the same time he had the full respect of the Council. (Hear, hear). Mr. Holt seconded and the proposition was carried unanimously. Mr. Gotobed then took the vice-chair. He said be would have very little to do, as their new chairmen was a very regular attender. He thanked the Council for the honour they had conferred upon him.

div.head: RATE.
div.p: THE RATE.
The Clerk informed the Council that the rate collected during the year amounted to L'2,765 and the amount irrecoverable from empty property was £249 14s. 4d. CHAIRMEN OF COMMITTEES

The following Chairmen of committees were appointed : Sanitary and Sewage Farm.—Rev. G. B. Thurston. Housing and Town Planning.—Mr. O. G. Smith. Gas —Mr. T. H. Warburton. Fire Engine and Building.—Mr. J. H. Bolt, vice- chairman, Mr. T. I. W. Dixon.
Finance.—Mr. G. Welford. General Purposes Committee.—All the members o the Council.
Mr. Groves wee appointed to represent the Counci on the Statham School.

div.head: RATES.
div.p: THE RATES.

The Council sat in Committee to levy the general district rate which was fixed at 2s. Bd. in the £, an increase of 2d. on the previous rate. The advance is necessitated by the cost of the sewerage seheme.

div.head: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY. Before Mr. J. W. Sidebottom (in the chair), Messrs.T. J. _
Ridgway, S. W. Gould, S. Davies, A. W. Callender d W. G. Gioves.

A STRAY Doc.—Barry Simpson.- West Lorne Farm, High Legb, was summoned for being in possession of a stray dog and failing to notify to the police, particulars of sarne.—The defendant said he had no idea of keeping the dog and was saving it for an owner.—The case was dismissed on payment of costs. MISCELLANEOU.S.—For having ridden bicycles without lights. William Brett,Bent Corner,Warburton; and 'thus. Terrill. 326, Ordsall-lane, Salford, were fined 2s. ild. and Wm.Hilton,Lock-lane,Partington ss. Catherine Cs wood, widow, Brook-road, Lymin, was fined 2s. 6d. for allow- ing her dog to be at large at night time.—Percy Perry, Newfield House, Lyeim, wAs fined 7s. 6d. for allowing his dog to be at large without a collar or muzzle.— George Walter Smith, Bear's Paw Farm, High Legh, was mulcted in a fine of ss. for being in charge of a horse and sprinking machine and riding without reins to guide it. OLD GhNTLEMAN ASSAULTED —Joseph Whitfield, Whitfield-street, Cadishead, was summoned for assault- ing his father-in-law, Thomas Griffiths (78), Loch-lane, Partington,on March 15th.—Griffiths said that Whitfield threatened to throw him out of a boat into the canal. He also struck him on the ear. He was afraid of the man.—Defendant apologised to the, complainant and said he would pay the costs of the case.—He was bound over for 12 months in the sum of £lO and ordered to pay the costs.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, April 19, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, April 19, 1913.

Mr. Bottomley : Free of charge? Mr. Clarke: To anyone who cannot afford to pay. The charges have always been met by their insurance companies ; we have never received a single penny from persons who occupied the premises where the fires occurred. I think that Mr. Bottomley will find when we meet as a Parochial Committee that we shall be in a better position to deal with the matter than a Parish Council.
Mr. Prank Warburton: We might make some arrange- ment with the Wilderspool Brigade. Mr. Bottomiey : That is not the resolution, Mr. Chairman.
On the motion of Mr. McDermid, seconded by Mr. Rose, an amendment that the matter be left with the Parochial Commitee was carried by seven votes to two
MR. BOTTOINILEY'S RESENTMENT. WHOSE WAS THE CIRCULAR?

Mr. Bottomley said he very strongly resented the action of one or two members of that Council in denouncing him as an " undesirable !" The Chairman : I think that is a matter we ought not to go into to-night. We don't want to throw any discord or discontent among the members. We want to carry out our duties as honest men and as Christians for the benefit of the parish amicably and comfortably together. Let bygones be bygones, and let us enter into cone gooebusiness. Mr. Bottomley (wainaly) : Is what I have com- plained of, Mr. Chairman, a Christian spirit ? Why should be denounced as an undesirable by members of the Council, and then you ask me to work amicably together with them?
The Chairman: You should ask those who know some- thing about the matter. I know nothing about it. Mr Bottomley : I mentic.n the fact. The Chairman: Is this the right place in which to mention it ?

Air Bottoinley : I say so distinctly. It has been done in connection with two or three members of the Parish Council, who have denounced me as an undesirable. The Chairman : And other councillors have taken other courses which have not been desirable.

Mr bottomley : I am resenting the action from my point of view, and I ask you to mention anything that have done to show that I am an undesirable. 1 sly it is a dastardly trick, a most ungentlemanly action, and unworthy of any person to sign such a etatement. Mr. McDermid : I don'r know to whom Mr Bottomley refers, but his language is rather strong Unless he is prepared- The Chairman : It is out of place altogether. The rneeting is now closed. _

Mr. gottorriley : It is abominable, and it clearly points out the bringing up of any person who has msde such a statement. It is a dirty, despicable trick. The word undesirable is an abominable word to use, and those who have used it ought to be ashamed of them- selves.

Mr. Pearson : It is very unfortunate,Mr. Bottomley. Mr. Bottomley : It is unfortunate, and there are those outside who have resented what has been done and admit that the circular did no good. What right have two or three to use the names of others? If I were one of the others, I could make them smart for it. Mr. McDermid Was it a member of the Council?
_ Air. Bottomley : I have a strong opinion. ?Mr. McDermid : lam sorry there should have been such a word uEed, but he should go to the person who used it.
Mr. Yeaxson : I likewise had nothing to do with the flatter.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

PARISH COUNCIL—The first meeting of the newly- elected Parish Council was held on Tuesday night, Mr. James Whitles in the chair.—Discussions on the ques- tion of amalgamation with Warrington and fire appli- ances for the village appear in to-day's " Examiner " under other headings.—On the motion of Mr. Pearson, seconded by Mr. Westbropk, Mr. James Whitley waa appointed chairman for the ensuing year.—Messrs. Pearson, Westbrook and Hallows welcomed the new members. Messrs. Dukes and Bottomiles.—Mr. Whitley was appointed a manager for the Church Schools.— Messrs. Clarke, Pearson, Dukes, Mclntyre, C. Hallows, F. Warburton and F. Rose were appointed a committee to join the representative of Lower Walton and Latch- ford Without in the election of four Council school managers of which two should be nominated by Stockton Heath. It was decidfd that these two should be Messrs. Pearson and McDermid.—The Clerk (Mr. Edwin Bradshaw) asked for a precept on the overseers for £34. and stated that the election had cost £l7 19s. 10d.—The precept was agreed to, on the motion of Mr. Westbrook.

div.head: MR. BOTTOMLEYS' LOSS.
div.p: MR. BOTTOMLEYS' LOSS.
As New Member of the Council Advocates Action.
REED FOR PROPER FIRE EQUIPMENT.

At the first meeting of the newly-elected Stockton Heath Parish Council, held on Tuesday night, Mr Whitley presiding, the principal subject discussed, not- withstanding the introduction of the question of amalgamation, was that of providing efficient fire extinguishing facilities, either directly Cr indirectly by arrangement with outside bodies or authorities. Mr. Bottomley, who has been placed on the Council since that disastrous night that in a few minutes rendered him homeless, originated the discussion, which increased in heat as it progressed. Mr. Bottomley asked the apparently harmless questlen—Was the Parish Council or the Parochial Committee responsible for the consideration? _
The Chairman replied that the Parochial Committee had the matter in hand. . _ _ .

- Mr. Bottomley failed to see why the matter was left ti•erl, and thought it was their duty as a Parish Council to gri into the question by means of a sub-committee. The Chairman : There is a sub-committee appointed to consider the fire appliances, and then submit a report to the Parish Council from the Parochial Committee. Mr. Bottotnley : The Parochial Committee is some- thing altogether diatinct from this Council and fire appliances are a Parish Council matter entirely. I think it would be better to have a committee of our own to consider the vestion. You are very far from

being equipped es you'ought to be for such a district as this. Proceeding, Mr. Bottomley said that if a fire occurred in the district their present appliances would be utterley useless, and the matter ought to be dealt with at once. Being interested in the matter, he had gone into it particularly. As ratepayers they were told they bad to do a certain thing, but, they found out that it was all bunkum. Instead of the actual thing being where it was stated to be, it was locked up in a stable in a backyard. The alterations since made were a farce and were not what they ought to be for a district like Stockton Heath.
Mr. McDormid said the Parish Council had no power to deal with the fire apnliances—only power delegated to thorn from the Rural District Council as a Parochial Committee.

Mr. Dukes said that if they as a Parish Council could deal with the matter, and Mr. Bottomley was prepared to move a resolution, he was prepared to second it. The Clerk: We could go into it. Mr. Pearson : We have always dealt with the fire appliances through the Parochial Committee. Mr. Bottomley knew perfectly well that the Parish Council had absolute power to deal with the question of fire appliances and if they did not feel inclined to go to the expense of providing them themselves, they had power to deal with a neighbouring borough. He asked the Parish Council to keep their powers to them- selves. If a proper equipment was provided the rate- payers would have to pay for it, and they had a right to have something for that payment. He proposed that a small committee be appointed to consider the matter. Mr. Dukes attributed their failure in the past to their amateurish iashion of going about these things. If they attempted to fully equip themselves without relegating the function to some neighbouring borough, it appeared to him that they would have to have someone paid to see to things being efficiently carried out. The fire brigade in the past had been the laughing-stock in the village. He did not blame the men who volunteered to take on the job, because they followed their ordinary employment and did not in the main realize the respon- sibility of their position, with the result that it had been commonly remarked that had a serious fire broken out clarityg the week-end the men would not have been there. If they dealt with the subject they must not burk the responsibility for paying someone who could be held responsible. He seconded Mr. Bottomley's motion.

The Chairman said that members of the best regulated brigades might sometimes be absent. Their men were in better font) than they had been for some time. Be could quite understand Mr Bottomley feeling strongly on the point in the circumstances, and every member of the Council bad expressed his great sympathy with him. Mr Bottomley : That is all right, but did you ever know such a thing? The Chairman: What has occurred might never occur again. Mr Bottomley: When the Parish Council knew the notice was misleading and untrue, it ought to have been taken down immediately. The Chairman : You are right. Mr Bottomley: And I ask for a committee to be appointed to go thoroughly into the matter. Mr. McDermid, as a member of the responsible com- mittee, took his share of whatever odium might attach to what had occurred, but if they wanted better provision in the future than they had had in the past, they had only to say so. They had been told that the brigade was . farce. It seemed to him that there were a great number of people in the village who, in the absence of cinematographic picture palaces and other amusements, thought the fire brigade was a fit subject for ridicule. The fire brigade might not be what it should be, but with few exceptions it had been found to be fairly ample for the purposes required of it. They all regretted what had occurred, but it was all very well to be wise after the event. In this case there was an unfortunate mishap, and they all regretted it. Mr Bottomley said he had made full inquiries into the matter and had found that the fire equipment at Stockton Heath was not sufficient for the purpose. Mr McDermid : It is primitive, undoubtedly, but we cannot afford to go to the expense of an elaborate fire equipment and keep a permanent staff here. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Bottomley: lam not asking you to do anything of the kind. There are other things you can do. Mr Dukes said some things were better equipped and if they as a Council were not prepared to act efficiently and separately the sooner they made arrangements with someone who could do so the better.

The Chairman: Every member of the Parish Council is willing to advance and, if possible, obtain better appliances or communicate with other authorities to engage their cervices, when required. Although I take upon myself, with others, a portion of the blame, I don't like that word farce used in connection with the fire brigade, and I hope it won't be used again. Mr. Clarke sympathised with Mr. Bottomley in the loss he had sustained. No-one had a greater desire than he (Mr. Clarke) that the tire brigade should be efficient. He bad no objection to the proposal which had been made, although he thought it was superfluous for the reason that in a fortnight from that day there would be a meeting of the Parochial Committee which had its sub-committee for dealing with the question of fire appliances. Ile believed that the matter would be dealt with in a better manner if left with the Parochial Com- mittee.

It should be remembered that they had \an efficient fire brigade within five minutes' call from that place. He referred to the Wilderspool Fire Brigade, the members of which had proved themselves to be efficient, and had been publicly thanked _ for their service's.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.
PARISH COUNCIL MEETING.

The first auarterly meeting of the new Council was held !n the Council Schools on Wednesday evening. Prior to the election of the new chairman,l%lr.A. Lister. Kaye presided. Tbere were also present :—Messrs. F. M. Appleton, E. Allen, J. Bradford, A. Earwaker, W. Lomas, It. %V. Wilde, NV. Winstanley, W. A. Wooaing and Charles H. Hoult (clerk).

div.head: ELECTION OF CIIAIRMAII.
div.p: ELECTION OF CIIAIRMAII.
Mr. Bradford moved, awl Mr. Lomas seconded that Mr. A. Lister-Kayo be re-elecced chairman for the ensuing year.
This was carried unanimously. Mr. I:a} e thanked the new Council for the confilence they had reposed in him, and said that be would du all iu his power to facilitate the business of the Council.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS.
Mr. Wooding proposed and Mr. Appleton seconded that Mr. A. Lister-Kaye and Mr. F. Fox (the retiring overseers) be re-elected. This alao was carried unanimously. SCHOOL MANAGER. - - _ _
On the proposition of the Chairman seconded by Mr. Bradford, Air. Wooding was untnimously elected to serve as the Council's representative ou the church school management.

COUNCIL MEETINGS. It was decided to continue the Council meetings once a quarter as herwofore, the only alteration being the da). In future the council will meet on the first Thurs- day in June, September, December and March at 7.30 p.m. Should any special business arise, the Chairmn will have power to call a special meeting.

div.head: SPECIAL RATE REMUNERATION.
div.p: SPECIAL RATE REMUNERATION.
For the collection of the special lighting and sewerage rate, the Clerk was granted a sum of £5 for the yedr.
ELECTION EXPENSES.
The Clerk read a statement of the recent election expenses, which amounted to £l2 10e. 6d. The Courted unanimously decided that the overseers be authorised to sign a cheque for payment of same.

div.head: IMPASSAELE FOOTPATH
div.p: IMPASSAELE FOOTPATH

Mr. Woodine drew the attention of the Council to the bid state of a footpath which :eads from linutsford-road to Chester-road. He stated that quite a brook of water was constantly running down a portion of the footpath. The cause was stated to be the block- ing of the drain on Mr. Connors land behind Victoria- road.
The Clerk was instructed to write and ask Mr. Connor to put the drain in order.
THE SEWERAGE SCHEME.

Mr. Wilde asked if there was any new development to report in connection with the sewerage scheme. Mr. Kayo: As district councillor I can only state that we might try to induce the authorities to refrain from taking the scheme into those parts of the parish where it is not really needed. As far as the whole scheme is concerned, 1 am afraid we are too late in the day to prevent its ultimate completion.

div.head: TAR SPRAYING.
div.p: TAR SPRAYING.

Mr. Wooding moved and Mr. Winstanley seconded that the Clerk be instructed to write the County Surveyor asking him to recommend the tar spraying of Knutsford-road from the Swing Bridge to Cliffe-lane Bridge. The Chairman: I don't think you will be able to get it done. It was only done last year, and lam afraid they will not do it two years in succession. The resolution, however, was put and carried.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

VISIT OF THE BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL—The Lord Bishop of Liverpool visited the parish of Orford on Tuesday. lie arrived about 2.30 and proceeded to the schools, where he was received by the headmaster, Mr. J. Cann and conducted over the premises. He next visited Orford Hall Training College, where he was received by the Principal, Canon Morley Stevenson. After a tour of inspection, he delivered a short address to the students, and afterwards proceeded to the parsonage. lie next went to the site of the proposed new vicarage, and met and discussed the plans with the architect, Mr. A. Warburton. At seven o'clock the Bishop met the Church xvorkers,to the number of about sixty, at tea in the school, and afterwards addressed a few words of praise on their past efforts and advice for the future. At eight o'clock all walked to the church where a good congregation had assembled to hear the Bishop's remarks on all he had seen and heard during his tour of the parish. A short service was conducted by the Vicar (the Rev. G. Vale Owen). In the course of his address, the Bishop explained that he was trying to visit every parish in his diocese. He paid a glowing tribute to the Vicar, and asked the congregation to support him in the hard work which he had set himself. He hoped to sea the endowment increased, so that the vicar could have a larger stipend, £2OO a year was not much for a clergyman now, and a clergyman was entitled to a living wage. He would do all in his power to secure an addition. He made reference to the churchyard, and said it reflected great credit on that small band of voluntary workers who kept it in such splendid order. He also referred to the good work which the day school teachers were doing. He noticed while in the school, a tablet to the memory of one of their number who had given up his life, for his country, in South Africa. They had also immor- talized his name by awarding a prize called "Fred Wood's memorial prize " to the scholar bearing the best record. The Bishop was surprised to find that some of the scholars had never been absent or late, for five, six and even seven years. This was a credit to the parents and if it were kept up. would ensure success in after life. It gave him great pleasure to see the way in which they had all worked to clear off the church debt, and also in raising the sum of .£1,400 towards the vicarage fund. He hoped they would be able to com- mence building about next March and that he would have the privilege of taking part in the opening cere-

monv. Another thing which was needed was an organ. Unfortunately there was no diocesan society to assist in the buying of an instrument, as there was in the Case of a vioartge. Still he thought if they were to write to Mr Carnegie,be might help them to raise sufficient to buy one. Work like this could only he accomplished by earnest prayer. He was pleased to see in a copy of the " Parish Magazine," which the Vicar had sent him, special prayers to be used on behalf of these big efforts. In the words of St. Paul, they should be all working and giving together. The Bishop then asked the congre- gation to kneel and join with him in an intercession to God on behalf of the vicar, and all workers who were connected with the Church. After the service the Bishop went to the door of the Church and shook hands with the congregation as they left the Church. APPOINTMENT Or PEoPLE'S WARDEN.—At a special meeting, held in the vestry of Orford Church, on Mon- day evening. Mr. J. Povey was appointed people's warden, in place of Mr. C. Woods who has resigned. Mr. H. Williams was elected a sidesmen.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
PARISH COUNCIL.

. - - Dr. Murray presided at a meeting of the Parish Coun- cil held on Tueslay evening in the Council Schools, Stocks-lane. There were present, Miss Tiosley, Messrs. William Davies, James Ditclifiald, Richard lioutledge, J. G, Withinshaw, James Woodward and Mr. E. Foster (clerk).

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
Mr. Routledge proposed the re-election of Dr. Murray as chairman.
Mr. Withinshaw seconded and the proposition was carried.
The Clerk saidlt was in 1900 that Dr. Murray was first elected chairman of the parish council and he had held the office since then. (Hear, hear.)
VICE-CHAIRMAN,
. _ Mr. Davies proposed, and Mr. Woodward seconded, the re-election of Mr. Withinshaw.
This was agreed to. OTHER ELECTIONS.
The three retiring overseers were re-appointed, viz. : Messrs. Dr. Marry. James Ditchfleld and J. G. Withinshaw.
Dr. Murray was re-elected a representative on the Lancashire _Education Sub-committee,.Earlestown.
The Chairman stated that the Parish Council were empowered to elect two school managers. The two retiring members were Messrs. Robert Aldcroft and John Midwood.

• Mr. Routledge considered that the school managers should furnish the Council with a report quarterly or Lalf yearly. They were elected by the Council and it was unfair not to have a report from them. The Chairman : Do you suggest that the clerk write to the managers to request an annual report? Mr. Routledge : Yes. This was carried unanimously. Mr. Davies proposed the re-election of Mr. Robert Aidcroft and th 3 election of Mr. Frank Ward in the place of Mr. Midwood. Mr. Withinshaw proposed an amendment that Messrs Robe! t Aldcroft and J An Midwood be re.-elected. Mr. Woc.dward moved that Mr. Midwood be not elected, because he was dead against children attend- ing the Council school at the age of four years. The question was voted upon with the following reault : --Mr. Aldcroft, 5; Mr. John Midwood, 4; Mr. Frank Ward, 2.

div.head: RECREATION GROUND.
div.p: RECREATION GROUND.

Mr. Woodward proposed that the following resolution be sent to the District Council :—" That the recreation ground is not a tip bnt a recreation ground and that they may be requested to remove the heavy clinkers and stones." This was carried. Mr. Woodward also proposed that the south side of the recreation ground be fenced with iron fencing. After discussion it was resolved to leave the matter in the hands of a sub-committees for further report. VALUE FOR MONEY.
Mr. Woodward proposed that the Clerk enquire how much return they were having from the Warrington Union for the is. 2d. in the £ rate, and to see if they could not have the rate reduced.

The Council agreed to this course. Mr. Woodwara proposed that the Parish Council ask the County Council to purchase a watering cart for Penketh. Mr. VVithinsbaw proposed an amendment that the Parish Council of Penketh strongly represent to the County Council that they were dissatisfied with the way in which the roads were now kept, and the Clerk was instructed to write.to the County Council to ask them to give the matter their special attention. Mr. Woodward then withdrew his proposition.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

• PRESENTATION To VIE MISSES WE:TM-LT.—On SatUr- day afttrnoon the Misses Wright, of Castle Park. Frodshatn, were presented with a handsome illuminated album and purses of gold from the Overton Sunday school teachers, past and present, in appreciation of their work in connection with the school. The Vicar (Rev. M. W. Myres) made .the presentation in a felicitous speech. The album is an interesting record of events connected with the parish of Frodsnam for many years. It is bound in morocco leather, with suitable inscription, and inside it are to be seen the photos of the last three Vicars of Frodsham—the Rev. W. C. Cotton, the Rev. Canon H. B. Blogg and the present Vicar.

THE LATE MR. JOSEPH STOKES.—The funeral of the late Mr Joseph Stokes, of Froasham and Rocksavage, a well-known farmer and a former member of the Cheshire County Council, took place at Runcorn Cemetery on Monday. The Rev Myles W Myres (vicar of Frodsham) officiated. The chief mourners were Messrs Joseph Stokes (son), H Jeaceck and W Massey (sons-in-law), W Stokes (nephew), J Biker, T Baker, Brocklehurst, W Norcott, T Wright, Ringrose, JNorton, J Austin, and W Shaw, sea. Tee Runcorn Board of Guardians, of which body the deceased had been a member for thirty years. was represented by Messrs J Spruce (chairman), C E Linaker, see, T Baxter, W M Morris, W Mclntyre, W Harrison, J W Temperley, A Greenway, G A Hayes, J A Jones, G F Ashton (clerk), and the officials. Alderman A R Norman and Mr James Pritchard represented the County Council.

div.head: WALTON.
div.p: WALTON.

PARISH COUNCIL—REDUCTION OF RATES.—The annual meeting of the Walton Inferior Parish Council was held on Tuesday evening, when the newly elected members signed the declaration of office.—Mr. Weir, the retiring chairman did not seek re-election and he nominated Mr. William Allanson for this position for the ensuing year, the Council unanimously approving. Messrs. AlJanson and Dodd were re-appointed overseers and with Messrs. Ward and Pemberton were elected burleymen with the oversight of Morley Common which is under the charge of the Parish Council.—A long discussion took place with reference to the use made of Morley Common by persons depositing house refuse, &c. on the land, also by others placing obstructions across the public road. The Clerk was instructed to write to the persons concerned to have the obstructions removed so that the public could have full enjoyment of the use of the Common. The overseers' audited accounts were placed before the meeting and the assistant overseers announced that the overseers would be able to meet the cills from the Union by levying a poor rate of 25., and a special expenses rate of 3d. in the which would mean a reduction of 4d. in the £ for the half-year. This reduction could be made without in any way depleting the balance at the bank, standing to the credit of the township. A heirty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Weir for his services as chairman during the past year.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

THE LATE MR. LEWIS BIRCIIALL.—The funeral took place in Crott Churchyard on Saturday afternoon of Mr. L. Birchall, who died at his residence, Oak Tree Farm, on the 10th inst., in his 51st year. He had lived at Oak Tree Farm from the time he was about three years old, and was highly respected. He took a great interest in the affairs of the parish, and had been a member of the Parish Council and a school manager. Mr. Birchall, who was a widower, had survived his wife by 22 years. Floral tributes were sent from " Philip and all at Kenyon,"" Lewis and Eliza," Mr. and Mrs. Fazakerley and family," From all at Arbury," " From all at Home Farm at Ashton, "Antic and Frank," all Mr. and Mrs. E. W. Sankey and family.

div.head: Ifixamin.er, Saturday, April 19, 1913.
div.p: The Ifixamin.er, Saturday, April 19, 1913.
WARRINGTON SHOP-KEEPERS OF SIXTY YEARS AGO
THE LATE MR. F. MONIcS'S RECOLLECTIONS OF
OLD BRIDGE STREET.

The mention of old Bridge-street will touch a responsive chord in many Warrington hearts, for despite the inconvenience of narrowness (and lithesome boys used to boast that at its lower end it could be leaped in a hop-jump from kerb to kerb) it had the flavour of an old street in an old town.

Bridge-street, as some of us knew it,was a street that had grown as distinct from a street that had been made, and its odd courts and delightful irregularities were things we parted with in no small regret of mind. j Since the West side, save for the Old Academy, has entirely gore, it may give , pleasure to our readers to place on record the names of its occupants sixty years ago, mentioning therewith their callings and some features of the premises in which they plied them. For the spanning of this long period we are indebted to the memory of the late Frederick Monks. Our readers may remember that the columns of the " Examiner " contained a reference to one of the last conversations of that fine old Warringtanian,and to the loving interest with which he recalled the scenes am.l experiences of his youth. Though to many the recollection will be only a list of names and callings, there are still with us many for whom the recital will have real and living interest. Of former occupants of the east side of Bridge-street we were able some time ago to give a complete list by the kindness (and fine j
A shop devoted to umbrellas and kept by a Mr. Pearson came next and at the corner of what is now Rylands-street the familiar name of Podm ore adorned the sign,

_ The roadway, expanded in modern times and named Ryland's-street in memory of the Mayoralty of Peter Rylands, was then a pass- age leading into Black Boy Yard and here stood another old Inn "The Black Boy," kept by Betty Phillips, a sister of the famous chairmaker across the way, and succeeded in the proprietorship by Mrs. Woods an ancestor of the present writer. The brew house of the "Black Boy" was a familiar Bridge-street object for the old houses brewed their own beer and regaled the nostrils of the passer by with the soothing odours of malt and grain. The large sign of the "Black Boy," contain- ing the picture of a not very alluring negro, faced the entrance of the yard,and the square was lined by at least a dozen stables. Over one of these, in premises approached by a stone stair, Mr. William Lingley (we hesitate to write the name in the more accurate form of" Bill Lingley ") gave professional advice in the capacity of veterinary surgeon. A confectioner's shop kept by Miss Lurtin gave variety and attractiveness to the scene and next door lower down was Sherlock's tea shop (afterwards the business place of Mr. Peter Leigh). Peter Longshaw, saddler, plied his trade in the shop adjoining, and next in order was
Photograph by Birtles.

div.head: OLb -BitIDGE-STREET. AS SEEN FROM BRIDGE FOOT.
div.p: OLb -BitIDGE-STREET. AS SEEN FROM BRIDGE FOOT.

memory) of Mr. Joseph Clare. In this present recital we follow the account of Mr. Frederick Monks. At Market Gate corne r stood the establish- ment of Mr. Houghton, devoted, for two generations at least, to the sale of ironware. Next stood the" George Inn," an ancient Warrington hostelry re-named in homage to one of the Royal George's who honoured it as a resting place when upon a journey. As known to most of us the " George " was approached from Sankey-street, but in earlier days its had its frontage upon Bridge-street. Its proprietor sixty years ago was named Henshall, a picturesque figure who added to the quaint flavour of the hotel by the wear- ing of knee-breeches, buckled shoes, and stockings that drew the eye of the beholder irresistibly downwards. The linen shop of Miss Reid with its old- fashioned circular window was next to the "George," and lingered long enough to fasten itself upon the memory of most Warringtonians. Adjoining was the shop of Mr. George Blackhurst, a name associated then and up to a comparatively recent day with watch and clock making. Modern taste would find some incongruity in the suggestion of the clogger plying .his trade next door to the jeweller, but clogging had better status half a century ago, and Robert Woods, who made and fitted clogs so near to Market Gate held up his head as a "citizen of credit and renown." Next to Robert Woods was the draper's shop of Miss Hatton, and a step lower lived Joseph Leftwich, shoemaker, who after- wards gave place to Mr. Collinson. Tinsley's wine and spirit store was next in order. The sign adjoining showed the familiar name of Carter, one of the very few business names that linger with us yet from that period. The sign had, however, only just been removed from the opposite side of the street for Mr. James Carter began business in a quaint and modest shop that stood upon the site of the shop now occupied by Mr. Grimes A passage here, led to the " Green Dragon," and on the opposite side Messrs. Cunningham and Owen carried on a drapery business. Their neighbour was Mr. Davies, who kept a seed shop, and who was succeeded there by Mr. Green. A narrow roadway anciently known as Patten's Lane ran at this point to Eagle and Child yard, upon the right side of which was the fine old brickwork of the old home of the Patten s. The "Eagle and Child" Inn stood aside from Bridge-street, filling one side of a small square, and was one of the coaching Inns of which the street had once so many. A flour warehouse with a prominent hoist adjoined, kept by Mr. Hodgson and the next establishment was that of Mr. Stirrup well known as a cabinet maker. Earthenware was sold next door by Blundells ("Blundells mug shop " was the popular designation), and next door Mrs. Chrimes met the needs of her fellow towns- women by providing baskets, and the modest and indispensable dolly-tub. Clearly there was no invincible prejudice against dolly-tubs in Old Warrington for Mrs. Chrimes, as wife of Mr. Joseph Chrimes, was called to combine the duties of tub and basket expert with those of Mayoress and did both, we believe, with credit. Another draper's store which stood next in order was kept by Mr. Worrall.

James Monks, gunsmith. A passage to his workshop (afterwards used in the same business, we believe,by Mr. Daintith) divided the shop from that of Miss Evans, milliner, whose shop was afterwards occupied by Mr. Hesketh.
Mellor's "Black Pudding Shop" adorned de corner. Then came Sutton, "the hardware man," who made dolly tubs and butter pats, and then Furnival the stationer.

A yard divided the shops, in which Mr. Chandley for more than one generation con- ducted the business of painter and decorator. Adjoining the yard was the " Feathers Inn ", and next door Mr. Leyland conducted the now almost extinct trade of tallow chandler.

Friars Green was then, as middle-aged Warringtonians know, a narrow thorough - fare. One of its old buildings still stands occupied by Mr Coates and bearing the label "Bank House." Long before it became a Bank this was the spacious residence of Thomas Watts, tallow chandler, soap boiler and Quaker.

At the corner of Friars Green,on the south side, wls a baby linen shop, kept by Miss Laverack. The old shop with small-paned windows facing both on Bridge-street and Friars Green was sacred to body linen until its demolition some twenty-seven years ago. _ _
A clock maker named Bethell held the shop two doors from Friars Green and Mr. Charnley another tallow chandler and candle seller kept him company on the lower side.

Mr. Edward Twiss sold shoes next door to the candle shop, and his premises adjoined the "White Bear," then kept by Mr. Wilson. Next came a name that may still be read in Bridge-street, Ralph Johnson, Cabinet Maker. His place of business adjoined the Roe Buck yard, another coaching centre of the old time, yet famous more for conven- tidies than for coaching, and the early meet- ing place of the Baptists and Roman Catholics.

On the lower side of Roebuck yard was a tinsmith's shop reached by stone steps and kept by Kinder and next came a carting con- tractor named Samuel Woods. The name of Martin Corless adorned the projecting window of the next shop, his business being that of corset maker. Mr. Leigh, a painter and plumber shared with Miss Lees some premises in front of the Old Academy which effectually hid the building. With the demolition of these the Academy came back to view, the only portion left of the west side of old Bridge-street and the portion of which we have most reason to be proud.
A. M.

div.head: LITTLE CHAPTER OF NEGRO PROVERBS.
div.p: A LITTLE CHAPTER OF NEGRO PROVERBS.

I have been reading a very interesting book called "The Land of Mud" written by Mr. Alfred Hardy. The Land of Mud is British Guiana, and Mr. Hardy has been a missionary there. In one of the chapters he gives a selection of Negro proverbs and some of them are so good and amusing that I am going to copy them out for you with some brief explanations. Here is one of the funniest.

When we in England want to express the impossible we say "That will happen when pigs begin to fly." The negro says "Dat will happen when mosquito pull chigger out of sand-fly foot wid a crowbar." To see the force of this we have to know that a mosquito is only the size of a large gnat and that the sand-fly is not much bigger than a grain of sand. The chigger is a tiny insect that gets under the toe-nails and in the skin and causes itching, and which they remove with a fine neeule.

The idea of a mosquito removing chiggers with a crowbar from under a sand-fly's toe- nail is too funny for anything. When we say "Put yourself in his place" the negros of Guiana have a picturesque proverb. " Rockstone at river bottom does not know what rockstone on the road feels." To see the point of tbis we have to remember the tropical heat. The stone which lies under the cool water undisturbed and serene has the negro ideal of comfort. But the loose stone on the road is under the dust and glare and is kicked about and run over a hundred times a day. No, the river stone doesn't understand the road stone.

The habit we all have of pointing to other failings and forgetting our own is put in a very happy proverb "Finger nebber say, look here, him always say, look yonder," that is to say the index finger does not point inwards but always outwards. And here is a fine little proverb for young folks who forget to be grateful. " When fowl drink him lift his head and say; tank God! tank God! But when man drink, him say nutten (nothing)." The next time you watch the fowls drinking just listen and you will hear them say," Thank God." Then there is a picturesque little saying on the subject of keeping out of danger and bad company. They say "Cockroach ebber so drunk, him no walk in de fowl yard." This means that the cockroach knows his enemies.

On the subject of inquisitiveness and its drawbacks they say "Flea say, him rader hab man wid two yies fi catch him, dan for blind man fi hold him," which is by inter- pretation, "The flea say he would rather have a man with two eyes to catch him than for a blind man to hold him." The man with two eyes will be curious to see him and he may jump away; the blind man will hold him fast.

I have room just for another very good proverb. We haven't anything quite like it in our language but we ought to have. It is a proverb that reminds us that there is a good deal to be learned from other people's experiences. They say "If mud fish come from ribber bottom and tell you alligator hab teet beliebe him." In other words, don't go down to the river bottom and let the alligator try his teeth on you. Dont want to try everything for yourself. Wise folks will take the evidence of the mud fish on the subject of what an alligator's teeth are like. Perhaps it wont weary you if I give you a few more of those little gems of wisdom next week. The book from which they were taken is published at 2s. 6d. by C. H.. Kelly. It is written for "the young of all ages" and has not a dull page in it.
IF NOBODY SHIRKED,

I know not whence I came, I know not whither I go ; But the fact stands clear that I am here In this world of pleasure and woe. And out of the mist and murk Another truth shines plain— It is my power each day and hcur To add to its joy or its pain. I know. that the earth Warts, it is none of my business why; I cannot find out what it's all about, I would Int waste time to try. My life is a brief, brief thing, I am here for a little space, And while I stay I would like, if I may, To bi ighten and better the place. The trouble I think, with UB all Is he lack of a high cot,ceit. If each man thought he was sent to this spot To make it a bit more sweet, How soon we could gladden the world, How easily riE,ht all wrong, If nobody shirked, and each one worked To help his fellows along !

Cease wondering why you came— Stop looking for faults and flaws ; Rise up to-day in your pride and say, " I am part of the First Great Cause ! However full the world, There is room for an earnest man, It had need of me, or I would not be— I am here to strengthen the plan. " —ELLA WHEELER WII.COX.

TRIALS OF A SCHOOLMASTER. Here is a little poem from a new book called " Fatuous Fables." With emphasis a trifle strong, I said it was completely wrong. Again he puts it ; then I storm And made him stand upon the form. Then he commits the self same sin A third time—and I keep him in. To get it right he still declines; I give him several hundred lines. Ile makes the same mistake again; Then comes my last resource—the cane.
I've looked the matter up to-night And find the little beast was right!

div.p: THOMAS KNEW.

"Here," said the teacher, pointing with her cane to the blackboard. "we have an example of a compound word—' Bird-cage.'" She paused dramatically, while her pupils bent forward in their seats to read the bold, white letters in profound silence. "In compound words," she resumed,." a hyphen is employed to show relation between the two terms that form it. Ahem! For instance—Thomas," she broke off suddenly, "you're not attending." Yes, I was," murmured Thomas. "Well, if you were," retorted the teacher, pointing again to the blackboard, • perhaps you'll tell the class why the hyphen is placed between bird and cage ? " For a thrilling second Thomas racked his brain for light.
"I know-1 Its for the bird to perch on."

ion was the celebrated Joshua Brooks, the 'anions Lancashire_ cleric who gfires in Mrs. . _ _

Linnaeus Banks' "Manchester Mail." It is told a this gentleman that when, at the favourite seasons for weddings, Lancashire lads and lasses presented themselves in large numbers at the old Parish Church (now the Cathedral) to be married, he used to seize and marry them. off in pairs, regardless of whether "ilka laddie had his lassie," and answer their protests by telling them to sort themselves out when it was all over.

Then there is the history of the wedding on the wild coast of Cornwall, which was inter- rupted by the guns of a ship which was driving an tho rocks. The ceremony was almost over; but off went the parson, off went the bride and bridegroom, and all the wedding guests, to ;lean their accustomed harvest from the edge 3f the angry sea. Mention of this incident suggests another story of a seaside wedding. It was in the days of great Elizabeth, on the 3oast of Devon, and a fair maiden was just ibout to be married to a wooer who had not won her heart. But her own lover was far away, taken, some thought, by the Spaniards, or lead in a foreign land; and so she had yielded :o the pressure of her wooer and her own kin. Ind then a strange thing happened. She was m her way to the church when a cannon-ball which seemed to come from the sea, although lo vessel was in sight, alighted a little before .nnd rolled slowly to her feet. "My lover lives," silo saw, "tnis Is sent to tell me sot'. and forthwith turned back from the church, steadfastly • refusing to allow the marriage to be solemnised. And alive indeed he was, and able to come home and marry her before the year was out!

div.head: (COPYRIGHT.]
div.p: (COPYRIGHT.]

There seems to have been from earliest days a singular attraction for poets and novelists in dramas of the wedding day. Some unexpected and perhaps unwelcome guest; some interpos- ition of mischance to stay the progress of long-planned and contemplated nuptials,—the intrusion of the dark presence of death himself into a setting provided for with hope and gaiety, —these things have a peculiarly tragic and dramatic: effect by reason of their contrasting gloom as compared with the brightness of the wethling-day. Very often, too, desperate reme- dies have been called for on the part or devoted lovers, screwing up their courage at the last moment to thwart the wishes of stony-hearted parents. - Everyone's sympathy is, of course, bestowed upon the young Lochinvar of Scott's ballad, who had, it is said, a foundation of fact. But there is really a good deal to be said on the her side. One can imagine, for instance, the position created at a modern wedding by a twentieth- century LochinVar or .Jock o' Hazledean, whiz- zing his bride off in a motor from the :Nlammon- altar of a loveless marriage. The reception, become suddenly unnecessary,—the return of wedding presents to such as did not wish them transferred with their good wishes to the new bridegroom,—the prospective " in77aws " to be pacified! Assuredly, from some points of view the bride-snatcher is an extremely incon- siderate person.

GINENTRA AND THE MISTLETOE BOUGH. No less difficult must be the contretemps brought about by the disappearanoe, on the eve of marriage, of •ither bride or bridegroom: and there are a good number of such cases, both tragic and humorous, on record. First of all, there is the famous tale of the beautiful Ginevra : a tale which is used in a sightly altered form in the old song of "The Mistletoe Bough." Ginevra, so the story goes, a beautiful Italian maiden, was betrothed to a youth whom she loved, and who was equal to her in degree. Not a cloud seemed to threaten to mar. their nuptials, fortune smiled her sweetest. - -

Then, or. the very day of her marriage, Ginevra vanished—vanished as if she had been spirited.- utterly away; and no amount of tears and cries, of agonised calling and despairing search, availed to bring her back to her waiting lover, _

The years passed on, and most of those who had mourned for Ginevra lay dead; when by chance opening a large coffer in the great de- serted rooms of the palace which had been Ginevra' o home, some one discovered the skeleton of a girl. It was that of Ginevra, wlio in playful hiding on the eve of her wedding, had immured herself through the falling of the lid, and consequent snapping of the lock.

div.head: HAUNTED OAK.
div.p: THE HAUNTED OAK.

A somewhat -similar legend is that told about the "Haunted Oak" of Wales. The marriage of one Howel with a young and beautiful bride had been duly prepared for. The bride waited for him; the minister stood ready to perform the ceremony; the wedding-guests were bidden from far and near; yet Rowel never came, The bride, according to some versions of the story, lost her reason, and became a raving maniac; and about this time the neig,hbourhocd was also disturbed by mysterious supernatural noises which were even said to proceed from a gnarled and light- ning-blasted oak. The terrible shrieks and cries which the ghost uttered had, of course, the effect of keeping the superstitious inhabitants away from the Haunted Oak, as it soon came to be called. It was not until many years after that the reason was disclosed for Rowel's disappear- ance and the mystery of the Haunted Oak. Another lightning stroke completed the ruin of the ancient trunk. It was riven in twain from top to bottom, and there stood revealed a ter- rible sight to those who looked upon it after the storm. The skeleton of a man was firmly wedged into the cavity! The remnants of clothing and personal property which still hung to the bones disclosed the fact that here was none other than the unfortunate Howe!, who having for some reason climbed the tree had slipped down into the hollow trunk ; and having then become in- extricably wedged bv his elbows, so that he could not move in either direction, had there died a lingering and miserable death; his cries for help only making him the more hopelessly alone in his terrible prison. DICKENS' TRITE STORY.

The story of Miss Havisham, as told by Dickens in " Great Expectations," is substan- tially a true one; and the shut-up rooms where no sunlight was ever allowed to enter, the wedding-gown worn for many years till it was as withered as its once comely owner, the decaying wedding feast never removed from the tables where it had been spread with such joyffil an- ticipation, all really did exist. There is a lighter side, however, to this matter of the disappearing bridegroom. It. may sometimes be accounted for by a form of stage- fright; and there are histories current of prominent political personages who have had to be literally dragged from the coal-hole to the altar. Both bride and bridegroom being pre. sent, however, the lack of the lesser accessories may be easily got over, and when the Duke of Hamilton secretly married his bride (one of the beautiful Misses Gunning), no ring being forthcoming, the deed was done with one taken from a bed-curtain The annals of Gretna Green no doubt might furnish a good many incidents, humorousi and otherwise, of successful elopements, as well as narrow escapes of silly schoolgirls from the clutches of unscrupulous fortune-hunters. The wonder is that there are no grim tales of re. venge to stain their pages, as there certainly would have been had the people of these islands been gifted with a more emotional disposition.

div.head: TrALTER OR ALTAR?
div.p: TrALTER OR ALTAR?

There used to be in existence a curious idea that by being married a man condemned to death could save his neck, and there is an old ballad concerning a Chichester tradesman who was -Ictually, saved by the consent of a courageous girl to marry him at the very foot of the gallows. On another occasion a girl wrote to King George 1., begging for a reprieve for a condemned man whom she was willing to marry; and in New York. a little later in the century, a. prisoner actually was saved by. such a dramatic wedding.

The dramatic marriages of fiction are very numerous. ranging from the grim interrupted nuptials of Lucy Aslton, to the escapade of Mr. Jingle and Miss Wardle in "Pickwick." Dickens, indeed, seems to be rather fond of such situations. for an interrupted marriage is one a the main incidents of "Nicholas Nickleby."
