div.head: CHESHIRE EDUCATION ESTIMATES.
div.p: CHESHIRE EDUCATION ESTIMATES.
The Demand for Government Relief.

The Cheshire Education estimates were presented to the committee at a meeting at Crewe on M wday by Mr. R. T. Richardson, the chairman of the Finance Committee. The estimated expenditure on elementary education is £247,533, compared with £241,412 in the previous year. The increase is on account of teachers' salaries, handicraft centres, loans and National Incur. ance payments. The income from Government grants do is expected to reach £120,268, compared with £127,222. The amount to be fonnd from the rates is £0.7,270, against £114,190 last year. A tenpenny rate will produce £113,200. There was an estimated credit balance at the commencement of the year of £9,297, and Mr. Richardson hoped that no increase of rate would be necegBsr3. (Hear, hear.) The rate was Iod. last year and lid the year before. The higher educa- tion estimates showed an expenditure of £86992. The income grants were expected to produce £54,865, leaving £32,127 to be provided out of the rates. A rate of 2d would produce £28,068. As the credit balance at the commencement of the year was £5,059, Mr Richardson hoped that they would maintain the rate at 2d. He added that the "whisky money," which before amouwed to 214,70 a, was now £13,077, and they had also sustained a loss of £3,873 through Wallasey becoming a county borough. The Chairman, Dr. Hodgson, raid they had built secondary ecbools and accomplished much good work in the promotion of higher education out of the 2d rate. It would not have been possible to have done nearly so much had it not been for the sum of .£20,000 which was some years ago by the casting vote of (lie chairman placed as county reserve fund to meet exceptional expenditure. - _
A question was asked as to what was proposed to ba done about any scarcity of teachers.

THE SCARCITY OF TEACHERS. The Chairman said that tbo subject was receiving con- sideration. The policy of the Board of Education was to raise the qualifications end status of teachers as much as possible. They were strongly against any lowering of the standard of attainment. The poor had as much right to good teachers as the rich, and what was wanted was more money for good teachers. If under the new regulations the county had to find more money for teachers, buildings, and so forth the Board of Education must help them. Professor Gonner and that this year the Committee would have to consider the salaries of cert'ficeted teachers, and he hoped that they would not have to consider them at the expense of the County. (Hear, hear.) A serious position had arisen with regard to the teachers, and that was one of the difficulties of the future.

div.head: GOVERNMENT AID REQUIRED.
div.p: GOVERNMENT AID REQUIRED.

The Chairman referred to the resolution passed by the Education Committee of the County Councils Association urging the Government to provide adequate relief from a burden which invited daily increasing opposition by ratepayers to all proposals for further advancement and progress in educational work. The meeting adopted the resolution, and the Director of Education was instructed to send a statement of the case of Cheshire to Che Cheshire representatives in the House of Commons.

whole thing wasn't nomberisicalrrd aay you were on the track of that girl at last- "l " Raid Witham. aimnlv. "I've seen her. She's a country vicar's daughter, and she lives at Lang Ghyll." "Oh!" said his companion, " you're I'm a fourth-rate imaginative painter, but J never dreamt that a comparatively sensible man was capable of falling in love with a pic- ture. Any way, the folks she belongs to would in all probability never let her speak to you, unless you had friends they knew whc would vouch for your character and genealogy." "Well," said Witham, drily, "I have tackled one or two rather difficult contracts before."
"You haven't shewn me, that portrait," said .his companion.

Witham handed it him somewhat reluc- tantly. "I wouldn't show it to you now .only that you will probably see the original very shortly." "It's pretty," said the artist, who studied the picture carefully. "Still, that doesn't quite express it. There's a little more than prettinecs there—something ycru could call serene and wholesome. In fact, I almost think I could make rather a striking study out of it."

Witham frowned at him. "It's quite cer- tain that you won't. Do you suppose for a moment I'd let you experiment• in your wretched niggling style with—that?", "After all," laughed his companion, "I'll probably come with you to Lang Ghyll. It seems to me you want a keeper." They. set out on the morrow, and were, at least, rewarded by a glorious tramp across the fells; but that was all, for during the first seven days Witham had not a glimpse of Miss Radcliffe, though he attended two, Sunday and one week evening services in the little, ivy-covered church. Then fortune favoured him, for he came upon her endeavouring to open a gate in a somewhat miry lane. She started a little at the sight of him, and Witham, wrenching the rickety gate back, stood bareheaded until she passed through. "Thank you," she said, and then, perhaps remembering that this was the last thing she had said to him, she smiled. "It is rather a coincidence that you helped me the last. time I was in difficulties."
" Yes," said Witham, "it rather looks like that."

The girl glanced at him sharply, but there was nothing in his quiet face to (thew what he meant, and he walked forward with her a pace or two. "Miss Radcliffe," he said, and she won- dered how he had learnt her name, "I asked you a question that didn't go quite far enough the other day. Will you tell me if you ever knew a yo-ung man who lived in this country and went to South Africa a few years ago. He looked a little over twenty, and was rather lightly built. He had blue eyes and a curious white mark on his fore- head."

Agatha Radcliffe started visibly. "You said his name was Cargill." "Well," said Witham, reflectively, "per- haps I did. Still, that doesn't matter. if you knew him the scar should fix it." "I do," said Agatha Radcliffe, gazing at him with a curious intentness. "I was with him when the scar was made—ever so long ago. He was Major Braithwaite's son. Still, we heard that he was dead."
"He is," said Witham, simply. "I buried him."

Agatha Radcliffe drew her breath in. "Ah!" she said, "then you must be the man Major Braithwaite has longed to meet. He lives up yonder on the hill." "I wonder if you would tell him that I am staying at the inn, and have a watch and one or two little things that I should like to give him?" -

The girl said that she would do so, and went on her way lost in wonder, while Witham wandered down to the river. She had thought about this stranger, whose voice and manner for no apparent reason had stirred her curi- ously, more than once since she had last seen him, and now it seemed circumstances were to force him on ber acquaintance. She, how- ever, did what he had asked, and next day Witham went up to the housc on the hill. There he told the story quietly to a grey-haired gentleman, and a little faded lady whose eyes grew hazy as she listened. There was silence for a minute when he 'concluded, and then the Major coughed once or twice. "I am heavily indebted to you," he said. "As of course you guess, we quarrelled—per- haps I was too hard on him, and he had a spice of my own temper. I have regretted it ever since; he was my only son. We heard nothing for over two years, except that he had i landed n Durban, and then I made inquiries. My agents traced him to Johannesburg, and reported that he had died in the hands of a mining engineer, who had been kind to him." _
He sighed as he went on., "The thing has left its mark on me—but wd needn't speak of that. Can Ido anything to shew how I recog- nise my debt to you. You are staying here long?" _ . _
"-I don't know," said Witham. "Perhaps a month, though I may be longer." "Then t iymo e t l u awilleatsatk?,, take up your quarters with u 6fr

Witham said it was out of the question, but eventually compromised by promising to come to dinner occasionally, and when he went back to his inn that evening the artist asked a question: "What have you done about that Mexican affair?" _ _ _
"Said I wouldn't go," Witham answered. " Weuen't the terms tempting? ".
"Yes," said -Withanr; "they certainly were. Still, you see, I shall probably stay here for a month Cr two."

_ He went up to the house on the hillside again a few evenings later, an 4 was duly pre- sented to Miss Radcliffe by Major Braith- waite. It also happened that he walked home with her in the cool stillness of the creeping dusk while a full moon sailed slowly above a big black fell. It was Reggie Braithwaite who had died in South Africa she talked about.

"It was all a horrible .pity, but perhaps one could hardly blame the Major," she said. "Poor Reggie was dreadfully extravagant, but that was not their only quarrel, as I sup- pose the Major told you." "He hinted at another reason—somebody the lad wanted to marry." Witham broke off for a moment. "It couldn't have been you." Miss Radcliffe smiled. "I wonder why you feel sure of that?"
"It's perfectly simple. You could never have looked with any favour on a lad like that —and if you had the Major would have made no difficulties."

His companion flushed a trifle, but slre did not resent the speech. "I really, was fond of Reggie in one way, but I think the Major was right in objecting to the girl," she said, quietly. "It is very curious that ,you should be the man who was kind to him.'

"Very curious," said Witham, with a twinkle in his eyes. "Don't I look capable of doing that kind of thing?" "Oh," said his companion, "that was not what I. meant. I meant it was curious you should, come fishing here of all places." "And that you should be the one to set me on the track of the people- I was looking for?" said Witham. "Will, it seems only honest to tell you that you are not altogether a stranger tome."

He sropped and stood still with the moon- light on his face while he took a little leather case out of his pocket, and again Agatha Radcliffe was almost startled by a feeliag that, although she had only seen him three times, she knew him well. His voice and his quiet, forceful manner sent a little thrill, which, though she had never experienced it before, seemed, familiar, through her. She felt that, alAurd as it seemed, it was something that she had been half-consciously expecting. "There," lie said, as he opened the ease, "you will recognise that picture. I found it among Braithwaite's things, and 1 couldn't give it up. After all, I think you can never quite realise what you have been to me." Agatha stood very still watching him with signs of tension hi her eyes, and he smiled at her as he went on.

div.head: Long Ostrich Feathers to be the
div.p: Long Ostrich Feathers to be the
Feature in Hats.

The size and adornment of women's hats continue to attract the attention of the masculine legislation, and police authorities. In Berlin the police not only require the points of protru3ing hatpins to be pro- tected but also prohibit the wearing of ornaments, feathered or otherwise, which project beyond the circumference of the hat, and are stiffeLed with wire or other means. In Texas in Miseries, there is a Bill before the Legislature to make it unlawful for any worran to rear at church, theatre or public gathering, headgear exceeding certain narrow limits. In this country we have the Plumage Bill which has been introduced in the House of Commons, and is said to command the support of 250 members of Parliament. The Bill seeks to prohibit the sale in the United Kingdom of the plumage or skins of wild birds and it may possibly give some concrete effect to the long continued agitation against "murderous millinery." To balance up Ihings a little tha " mere man" is himself taking to sporting feathen and brush plumes in his now fancy for Alpine and Trilby headgear. MODISII MILLINERY.

Some milliners use ribbon on nearly all their hats, others make s3arcely any use of it. For the moment the trimming seems to consist of an upright tall feather mount standing erect from the centre of the hat. In some instances the feather is little thicker than wire. The popular Tam 0' Sbanter hat is quite fascinating when made of tulle, for in this material it is so very much lighter than in velvet. Very modish is a black tulle tam with dull gold roses. Since this charm- ing materill has been so very much improved it is by no means so expensive as formerly when it was so liable to be spoilei by moisture and easily crusher,. Long ostrich feathers are this season to be the feature of hats for smart wear and the demand for them was never greeter. Certainly perfection has been reached in the treatment of these beautiful and graceful decora- tions. They are dyed in every lovely and fashionable shade and the shot and shaded effects are nothing short of marv.lleus. TUNICS.

Paniers have disappeared, but tl eTr infironce remain,: in the draperies that are a feature of this season's frocks, for their outline is followed in many instances. Tunics are more popular than ever, and very ornamental. Beads are very largely used for the decoration of these accessories in fringes and other ways, and often supply the whole design as well as the finiah. On reception and evening dresses also, beads worked by hand in beautiful designs are a marked feature. For a number of years beads disappeared from the world of dre,s, but have come into their own again, and will be wed this year even more than lest. Their manufacture is assuming the proportion of an important industry, and the beautiful shades in which they are made admit of the carrying out of very lovely colour schemes. THE VOGUE FOR BROCADE.

Brocades are carrying every thing before them this spring and are seen not only in the filmiest of materials but in wool epougss and other cloths never before associated with this fabric. Very modish is a plain black satin skirt, with which is worn a coat of wool brocade. A seamless skirt is among the novelties and with this is supplied a coitee or bolero of brocade. For afternoon coats and wraps again it is in the more expensive makes and is almost universally used. Long floviing coats for smart wear are also built of chiffon and other transparent materials, and although expensive may he made to snit two purposes since they can be worn in the afternoon as well as in the evening. Amens afternoon coats are those of tlret-quarter length, which partake of several styles since one garment may be Russian in theca of the neck and yet have the low s3t Chinese sleeve. There is certainly notLis g masculine in the charming and essentially femenine afternoon and evening coats designed for the year, however, much this may be said of other garments. SHOP ESPIONAGE.

It i 3 always advisable to retain ones receipts for goods purchased at large departmental stores. With the freedom allowed the public on entering large estsblishments, shop-pilfering has become a fine art,and so also has the system of espionage adopted by the proprietors to check it. Qoods are everywhere temptingly displayed inviting customers to examine them, but it is not. always pleasant to feel that e 3 el a'ie watching you and that just possibly a mistake might be made. It is somethirg lite the fear with which thp woman with muff or bag in hand approached a draper's stop front when the suffragist winiow-smashing campiign was at its height. It is very rare that shop detectives, many of them being women and young girls, make a mistake but it does happen somet.mes and it behoves the shopping public to be a little careful.

div.head: [ALL 11;G/ITS RESIItIED.;
div.p: [ALL 11;G/ITS RESIItIED.;
HIS LADY'S PICTURE.
BY HAROLD BINDLOSS
Author of "A Wide Dominion," "The King- -dom of Courage," "'The \ Mistress of Bona. venture," "His Adversary's Daughter," Ste.

It was a spring evening when Witham, who was tired of fishing, lay amidst the boulders of a "little frothing river in the North Coun- try. It broke out from the shadowy depths of a big larch wood, and pale stars of cowslips were scattered amidst the springing grass across the stream. High up on a rugged hillside straggling firs cut black and rigid against the sunset, and there was no stir among the lacelike birches that hemmed the lower meadows in. Spe for th,3 Sound of running water all was viiry still. The quietness affected Witham curiously. It was a thing he was unaccustomed to, for he was fresh from the riotous life of a South African mining town, and the jarring crash of the, stamp-heads that beat the gold quartz to powder had rung in his ears continuously. There were two sides to his character, which is not a very unusual thing, though few of his friends ever suspected that there was a vein of fantastic imagination in him. He might have developed into a second-rate poet had it been given rein; but, as it happened, fate had made of him a first-class mining engineer. He took out a letter from his pocket, and glanced at it for the third or fourth time. It was frbm his employers in London, and ran: "If you are prepared to forego a part of the leave you are entitled to we would like to send you out with the new crushing plant to Mexico. The terms "—and they mentioned them—" would, we think, be satisfactory. Failing that, you would have to wait until the machinery for the Spanish mines is ready. We await your decision." Witham wrinkled his forehead, for it was a tempting offer, and there was only one palpably absurd reason why he did not wish to go. Still, it was one which had some weight with him, and which had, indeed, brought him fishing into the dales of West- morland. He next took out a little leather case made_ for him by a Russian in Johannes- burg, and drew out from it a photograph. It portrayed a girl's face of a comely English type, which for all its freshness and dainti- ness had a certain gracious composure and hint of strength in it; and a curious look crept into Witham's eyes as he remembered how he had obtained it.

He had found a young Englishman lying very sick rind almost penniless in a hovel of the mining town, and had taken him to his own quarters. The lad did not recover, and Witham, who buried him and found the photograph in his possession, only discovered that he had come from somewhere in West- morland. He kept the photograph, and, while at first he did not exactly know why he did co, hung it up in his room; but it seemed to bring the scent of the firwoods and the freshness of the North Country dales into that lurid, sun-scorched town. Then by de- grees it gained a strange and 'almost inex- plicable influence over him. The exiles on the gold reefs live somewhat riotously, and he had all the strong man's lust of excitement; but he felt he would like to meet that girl with nothing to regret, and, though this seemed preposterous, that he would surely Yneet her,some day. That was one reason why, though he had been born in the shadow of the fells, he was then wandering through the dales between Eden and Lune.

- It had grown a little darker when a girl in a long white dress came brushing through the cowslips in the shadowy meadow, and, as it happened, stopped close beside him. There we stepping-stonee across the stream just there; but it was running, a little higher than usual, and two or three of them were under water. She glanced at them dubiously, and nt first Witham did not see her face, though her white-robed figure, which had a certain elusive grace in it, cut sharply against the green of the springing grass. Then he started as.ahe turned towards him, for he would have known-her anywhere.

"You wish to get ocross?" he said. The girl looked at him gravely, and ssaw a young man, with a bronzed face and clear grey eyes, whose manner was deferential. "Yes," she said. "It is a long way to the, bridge. Still, the uncovered stones are rather far from one another."
Witham, who was usually prompt in action, waded knee-deep into the stream end held out hie hand. "Perhaps I might be of some assistance."

The girl laid her hand in his with an ab- sence of hesitation that at the time somewhat puzzled her, and stepped lightly from stone to stone until they were half-way across the river. Then they came to a gap the stream frothed through which she could not step across, and Witham, who glanced at it a mo- ment, turned to her quietly. "I won't let you fall," he said. "Rest your hand on my shoulder—now." The thing was done spontaneously without time for reflection. She felt a firm grasp upon her waist, and she was across, balancing her- self upon a froth-lapped stone with a faint colour in her face. Witham, however;- was perfectly grave, for which she was thankfu), and when she stood upon the further bank he went back for his rod. He seemed to take it for granted that she would wait, and, as it happened, though she had not the faintest notion why,- she did. "You are going up to the high road?" he asked.

The girl said she was, and Witham walked quietly beside her into the wood, which, though she was generally quick to resent pre- sumption, did not seem an unusual thing to her. "I am afraid you got rather wet," she said. Witham laughed. "I'm used to it. You see, I have now been a month in this country.".

His companion liked his laugh. "Weil," she said, "it does rain rather often here. You are a stranger to the North?" "I was born in it, but I live in South Africa, and elsewhere. I wonder if I might ask if you know any people called Cargill in this part of the country?" The girl said she did not, at which Witham was not astonished, for there are a good many men in Johannesburg with borrowed names:,_

"It really doesni. matter," he said. "I met a man of that name who I fancied had friends in this neighbourhood out yonder." "It is possible,' said his companion. "You see, I am only staying here." Witham said nothing further. He was, after all, not a brilliant conversationalist, and it was sufficient for him to be walking with her through the scented shadow of the larches in the dusk of the spring evening. A late thrush was singing riotously; the hyacinths filled the wood with a dim blue sheen; and it seemed to him that there was glamour in the dew-chilled air. Then as they reached the high road he took off his cap. "Thank you again," said his companion, and he was left alone.

She walked away rather quickly witli a faint warmth in her cheeks, for she once more felt the grasp of the unknown man's hand on her fingers and on her waist. She also wondered why she had neither shrank from nor re- sented it. In the meanwhile Witham strolled into a little, grey-stone village, where he pur- chased several things be did not want from the local postmistress before he asked a few apparently casual questions. The wrinkled dame/looked at him curiously with shrewd old eyes, but she gave him the desired information. It's Miss Radcliffe," she said, "the vicar's daughter from Lang Ghyll. She's been staying here with her cousin, but she's going home to-morrow." - -

_ Then he proceeded to his inn, where an artist comrade of his youthful days who had come North with him was waiting. - "Any sport?" asked the latter. "Indifferent," said Witham. "Two or three quarter-pounders. In fact, I'm going on to Lang Ghyll to-morrow. I believe there's tolerable fishing there." "Fingerlings, said the artist. "I was sketching there last year. Any way, my draw- ing isn't finished. I'll go next wee"." "I'm going to-morrow. You can cc me when you like." _

:10w and lhi kltthe thfl7Frinflfat tno big for me. I think it would have crushed Ine once or twice if I had not had the courage your eyes to fall back upon. Then—and think it must be said—the tide of life runs fast and fierce in the Gold Reef City, and Mei,. mast off n.ll serunles in the race for wealth. ,h,nk you laid a restraining band on me. seemed t 6 stand for all that is clean an, wholesome and English. Once, too, when lay very sick under the hot iron roofing used to talk to you. You brought the souna of the North Country rivers int 6 that lurid,. town, and when I looked at your picture A could smell the hyacinths and hear the Bng' lish thrushes sing." He broke off for a moment with a little laugh. I believe my friends consider me a severely practical man, but I felt like that, and I made up my mind that one day I would find the original of the photograph.' Agatha heard him with a faint trace of heightened colour, but though her heart beat a good deal faster than usual she was very composed. " Ah," she said, "you really expected to do that? " "Yes," said Witham simply, "I should have done it if I had tramped through every valley between Eden and Lune. I wanted to thank the girl I used to look to for encourage- ment for what she had been to me." Agatha looked him steadily in the eyes. "She only exists in your fancy with the qualities you have endued . her with. You made the robes and halo. The image you have decked with them is of clay." Witham . made a little forceful gesture- " Then how could it have produced the effect it certainly did on me?" She turned away from him somewhat sud- denly, and they went on again until they stopped at the gate of the little grey -Vicarage i which nestled n a _fold of the lulls.

"In one way I have no right to this pie' bare. Still, I should be sorry to part with it," he said. "Then," said Agatha, softly, "you mai keep it." She brushed past him next moment, and, as it happened, afterwards sat by an open win-, dow until rather late that night, looking down into the misty valley and thinking about this stranger. There was no doubt whatever that she was, interested in Him, though that was hardly going far enough, and once more she was troubled by the vague suggestion of something familiar; something she had almost expected, in his face and manner. Then she flushed crimson as it was borne in upon her that this was the man she had been waiting for. Now he had come, and she had, without clearly understanding it at first, recognised him. Witham did not, however, see very much of her for some time after that, though he fre- quently went up to the house on the hill and listened patiently to the grey-haired Major's animadversions upon the military authorities, who it seemed had long cherished a grudge against him. H. e also contrived to accompaq Mrs. Braithwaite to tho Vicarage now tine then, but it was seldom he saw Agatha there, or elsewhere alone. In fact, six weeks had slipped away .when the rural postman brought him a letter from London one evening, and after wrinkling his brows while he read it be walked resolutely to the Vicarage. There was no one in but Agatha, and, so the evening was hot and still, she came out and sat witn him beneath the clipped yews 1.0 the garden. The light was slowly dying out, behind the great black fells, and the sound et the river came up out of the misty valley. For a while they talked of indifferent things, and then Witham turned to his coin- panion with something in .his manner that warned her that she had a decision to make._

"I am," he said, "to be sent to Spain a' week to-day." He saw her little start, and it sent a thrill of exultation through , him, but when she spoke her voice was as quiet as usual. "Will you be very long away?" she asked. "Six months at least, said Witham. " is too long for, one to remain in uncertainty. would not like to wait until I came back here again." "Then you mean to come back again?" "Of course, if I had to walk across Franc?: and England With sharp thorns in my shoes. Agatha laughed softly, but she looked hita in the eyes. "Oh," she said, "I wonder if you reallf would? Still, in one way, it could not b:!' stranger than that you should have come at all. "That," said Witham, "was not strange the least. I came to find you, and I woulu -have done it if I had searched every valley the country. What is more, now I have foun" you I cannot let you go. You see, it 'NA' clearly arranged somehow that you should be. long to me." "And you are not disappointed? After all, perhaps, it is easy to weave misleading fancies round a picture." "The picture, said Witham, "is a colour. less, lifeless thing compared with the original. Still, that is not the question. You have bee° happy here. One can see it in your face. Dare you leave this sheltered valley and corao out and face the noisy world with me? want you."

Agatha looked across the misty hollow, where the sound of the river emphasised_ th,e deep quietness, and the sleek cattle stood among the dew-touched grass, to the ridge fells that cut in a great black rampart agawat the sky. Then she smiled as she turned to her companion. " Ah," she said, "I have wanted to go oIA there beyond those hills often, and see whabt the wider life has to offer me, but I could n°" go alone. Still, I seemed to know that soul° day someone would come to take me—sonve; one that I could trust myself to. Then "—ar she flashed a swift glance at him while till colour burnt in her cheeks—" you came—an I knew it was you." "And you will be ready to leave the hills with me when I come back from Spain?" Yes," said Agatha, simply. "If you can take me not as the girl your fancy created ouv of the pict4ie, but as faulty flesh and blood' I shall be ready to go anywhere with you."'
[THE END.]

The League table is as follows For. Arst. Per-

Dewsbury got some consolation for their Cup-tie debacle in the unexpected defeat of Hun:let at home by Batley. This result gave I tewsbury the fourth place, and ousted Hunslet. The Cup-holders will thus have the privilege of tackling Huddersfield at Fartown to-day. it would pay some of the Warrington men to witness this encounter, with a view to the great con- test of Saturday next. How to humble Huddersfield is a problem which \Varrington have none too much time to solve !

Warrington quite fulfilled expectations on Wednes- day at Swinton. by losing! It could hardly be thought they would give a repetition of Saturday's form when there was nothing at stake, and as a matter of fact they played like a tired team. Toe forwards had left all their energy at home, but in the rear. Jolley played at:other brilliant game, and Nicholas was quite the cleverest half on the field. The chief concern of the Warrington men was to avoid injury, and in this they were successful. Cheaters got a crack on the ankle just before the close, but it was nothing serious.

For to-day's match at Hull, the xvirepullers will play practically the same side, and under all the circumstances they will be lucky to avoid a heavy beating. Hull are rather proud of the capture of W. Batten, and seemed inclined to run up a tall score wherever possible.
The last match of Warrington's programme is the home match with Barrow, wnich has beeu re-arranged for the Monday following the Cup final.
THE FINAL. OFFICIALS IN THE WARRINGTON AND HUDDERSFIELD MATCH.

For the final tie in the Northern Union Cup com- petition, to be played at Headinglay next Saturday, the officials were, at a meeting cn Tuesday, appointed as follows : Referee, Mr A W May (St. Helens). Touch judges, Messrs W 0 Smart (Hunslet) and M`Gowiin (Broughton Rangers). The Cap and medals will be presented after the match by the Earl of Derby, president of the Nor,hern Union.

div.head: BOWLING NOTES.
div.p: BOWLING NOTES.
Local trundlers are becoming more and more enthusiastic each week, and a spell of really decent weather would no doubt tempt more sportsmen out on the greens.

Five matches in the first round of the " Finlayson " Cup Competition, in connection with the Works Bowling Association, will be played to-day if the Clerk of the Weather will only act as the participants in this competition desire him to do.

All the games arranged for April 26th have been postponed until May 17tb, as the valions secretaries find a difficulty in raising a team when so many players will be journeying to Leeds to witness the N( ithern Union Cup final.

The draw is as follows :—To-day (Saturday), 2 o'clock prompt: Croflelds Shipping v Greenings White Cross Wire Drawers v St Helens Cable No 2 Houghtons v Rylands No 1 Grappennall Tannery v Ropery No 1 Penketh Tannery v Firth Co Ltd Referee, Mr. J. Willett. May 3rd,2 o'clock prompt.

R A Naylors Ltd v P Stubbs Led Crosfields No 3 v Fletchers No 2 P and K Fitters %nd Turners v St Helens Cable No 1 White Cross Engineers v Rylands No 2 Fletchers Moulders No 2 v Mersey White Lead Referee, Mr J Rand lea. May 10th, 2 o'clock prompt. Whitecross Netting v P & K Wheel Shop Fletchers Moulders No 1 v Hanson and Edwards Monks Hall & Co Rivet v Richmonds Grappenhall Arnal Soo Carpenters and Joiners v Fletchers No 1 Referee, Mr E Lunt. May 17th, 2 o'clock prompt. The following games postponed from April 26th will be played : Tnewlis Griffiths and Edelstens v Longford No 2 Crosti9lds No 2 v Union Tanneries Orford Beam Shed v Cheshire Lines • Robinsons Glass Works v Rylands Wet Shop Ropery No 2 v Howley Tannery Referee .Jr F Dean.

The following have reeived Byes: County Asylum, Armitage and Rigby, Longford No 1, Castle Rubber, Crosfields No 1, Crosflold Joiners, Warrington Tanning Co, Richmonds Academy-street, Robertson% Fennell- %treet Tannery, Corporation Gas Works, Warrington Printers, Lockers.
The Horse and Jockey Green is in fine condition and it is hoped that a large numbr of spectators will attend this afternoon as the games promise to be highly interesting.

The Peter Peacock Challenge Cup Competition in c,nnection with the Warrington Liberal Association, will be commenced on May 4:h. Considerable interv4t is being taken by the members of the various ward teams and the propects of another succe,sful season are very rosy.

Each rrember will be handicapped individually both for the comp-tition and the annual main. This system, although involving considerably more work, is con- sidered the most satisfactory handicapping arrange- ment that could be made.
The officials of the Association, including Mr. E. A. Sanders, the energetic secretary, are doing their utmost to wake the competition one of the best in the town.
We have been allowed to publish the appended con- ditions of the competition for the benefit of the vat ions teams who, however, will be ciicularised specially.

Teams to consist of eight men and two reserves as far as practicable. A Captain shall be chosen by the Cup Com- mittee. and shall be responsible for the team throughout the season. A player to entitle itimself to a prize, must play in at least three matches.

A Captain must therefore, distinctly under staid, that whilst he has full power to manipulate his team to the best advantage, a reserve must be given every chance to play in three matches, and so qualify for the prize. Games 13 up. Each player will be handicapped as in a main and the aggregate will be the handicap for each team.

Matches to be played on Saturdays, but in the months of June and July, by mutual arrange- ment, evening matches may be played. Entrance fee is. must be paid to the Captains before the matches commence.

A Ward having more than 8 entries, the first drawn out of the hat shall comprise one team, the second 8 another team, and so on ; and if a number not sufficient to comprise a full team, be left in the hat, then these shsll form a reserve to be called upon to fill vacancies in their Wald teams.

Opponent teams shall be placed in the hat, and members shall play one another as drawn out of the hat, and the captains shall be on the green at least 10 minutes before the commencement of the matches, to take part in the draw. Players will be notified when they have to appear in their first match. All other notifica- tions will appear each week in the" Examiner." At the close of the Cup Competition a bowling main will b 3 arranged for members who have paid the Is. and t Ikea part in the matches. Mr. Campbell, the proprietor of the Bowling Green Inn, has kindly placed the green at &Ilk Quay at the disposal of the Committee for another season and reports it to be splendid condition.

The first round championship in connection with the Warrington and District Bowliug Association will commence on Saturday next unless it is found that the N.U. Cup final places difficulties in the way :

The draw is as follows : Wbitecross v. Junior Conservatives. Liberal Club v. Senior Conservatives. Ring an (-I Quecn v. Fecrnhead. Rylands' Recreation v. Bull's Head. Penketh Tannery v. Crosfield's No. 2. Cemetery v. Crostields' No.]. To be played on tho greens of the first-named clubs.

We were sorry to note that in the fcurth round of the Easter handicap in connection with the British Crown Green Association, played over the green of the Chapel House, Hotel, Heaton Chapel, last Baurday, W. Bridge, the Warrington Central player,was beaten by W, Walker, Conapstall.
The local player was handicapped at five, and his Opponent at 4. The scores sere 21-11 in favour of the Compstall man.
Bridge has received a bye in the third round and had played a good game all along.
NORTHERN UNION.
MEETING AT HUDDERSFIELD.

A meeting of the committee of the Northern Union League was held at Huddersfield on Tuesoay night, Mr. J. B. Book° (Wakefield Trinity) presiding. The following players were placed on the registers of the clubs first named :—Barrow, A Cr Burgoyne (Haverigg) ; Batley, W Wedgewood (Gomersall) mud A Ogilvie (Otley Rugby Union Club) ; Bramley, John Speed (Hull St. Vincent's) and W Fieldhouse (Leeds Rifles thigh), Union Club) ; Broughton Rangers, J W Horrigan (Weaste); Dewsbury, James O'Neill (Leeds) and W Cartwright (Wigan Athletic); Halifax, C Earushaw (local) ; Hull, W Batten (Hunslet) end Ralph Roper (Hull and Barnsley); Hunslet, F Wild (Burley Lawn), P Carr (Dewsbury Moor), and W Wood- burn (Warrington) Keiglaley, 1' Sharp (Keighley Z ngari); Leeds, Daniel D Lewis (Cross Keys); Runcore, John Hughes(local);Swinton,Thomas Wharton (Millom) and James Hinds (Roose); Wakefield Trinity, A C Cockroft (Knottingley Albion) and J Parkin (North Featherstone); Pemberton, John Dean (Wigan). Hunslet ware fined as for a late start at Hull liingston Rovers.

div.head: LEA G UF. SEMI-FINALS.
div.p: LEA G UF. SEMI-FINALS.

Officials for the League semi-finals were appointed as follow :—fiuddersfield v Dew6bury : Referee, Mr A Smith (Halifax) ; touch judges, Messrs C Peel (Brad- ford) and A Slater (Keightey). oo igen v Hull Kingstuu Rovers : Referee : Mr Whiteley (Waaefieid) ; touch judges, Messrs J It Lawton (Oldham) tiud 11 Lowe (Bruughtou). REFEREE .S VINDICATED.

Mr Longbottom, tny referee in ttae match Bradford v Hunslet, appeared before the committee at the request of the Bradford clan to explain various decisions' by him whilst officiating in the above match. After hear- ing Mr Longbottom's statement and his replies to vai ions questions, the committee accepted his explana- tion, and ordered the Bradford cobetoetinpga.y Mr. Longhottom's expenses iu attending t.e rn COM PENSATIuN Fort s WINTON. The Swinton club attended in support of their claim for compensation from the Oldham clue for the post- ponement of their League fixture from March 15tn to March 29th. After hearing the evidence the committee decided that the Swinton club were entitled to com- pensation, and awarded theta the sum of REG sTitAT lON CONFIRMED. Representatives of the Hull Kingston Rovers club appeaied before the committee to submit the grounds of their objection to the registration of IN BAtteu frwin Hunslet to the Hull club. Having heard the statements of Hull, Hunslet, and Hull Kingston Rovers clubs' representatives, the committee decided that, in the absence of a breach of any League rule, they had no option but to confirm the registration.

div.head: WARRINGTON AT SWINTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON AT SWINTON.
A Tame Display.

Swinton entertained the Cup finalists on Wednesday 1 evening at Chorley-road. In the first half the home side had the wind and sun at their backs, but the visitors were the more polished side, and for a consider- able period.they were in the home quarters, but failed to penetrate a good defence. Close on the interval Swinton secured a foothold close to the Warrington line, and Moores crossed, Ryder adding the goal points. Thelbome team early on attacked on resuming, and Anderson, gathering from the pack, dashed over near the corner flag, Ryder failing at goal. Shortly after- wards Warrington opened their account, Nicholas kick- ing a penalty goal. Subsequently the home side had the best of matters, and Gartrell scored again,Anderson missing the goal. Result ;—Swinton, 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points), Warrington, 1 goal (2 points). Teams : Swinton—Frudsham, back ; Ryder, .1. D. Martin, Morris and Stephenson, three-quarter backs; Anderson and F. Wharton, half backs ; Bailey, Blears, Riley, Gartrell, Smith and Price, forwards. Warrington—Joliey, back ; Bradshaw, Renwick, Tranter and Brookes, three-quarter backs ; Nicholas and Jordan, half backs ; G. Thomas, It. Thomas, Skelhorn, Fearnley, Cox and Cheaters, forwards. Referee, J. F. May, St. Helens.
MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. FIRST DIVISION. RYLANDS' RECREATION v. FLIXTON.

Rylands' gained a hollow victory at Flixton on Saturday. The home team were without five of their 'egular players, who were engaged in the Broughton rorkshops Competition. Rylaiids', who were short of •allop, won the toss. Flixton kicked off, and the Wiremen," who were in one of their liveliest moods, ion began to mike things hum. Bramhall, fielding a Acal. kicked and followed up, and the Flixton players misflelding it, Bramhall took the ball on the run and scored under the posts, Morris failiug at goal. A few minutes after Horrocks scored, followed by Carter. Leah, Griffiths, and F. Horrocks, half-time arriving with the score 32 points to nil. div.head: Examiner, Saturday, April 19, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, April 19, 1913.
CUP FINALISTS AGAIN!
Warrington Confound the Critics and
make a New Record.
THE DRUBBING OF DEWSBURY.
By " Ovalist."

There seems to be nothing more certain than the success of Warrington in cup-ties if the Manchester critics will only fotecast their downfall. Warrington were to have lost at Salford, but they declined to oblige ; on Saturday they should clearly have played second fiddle to Dewsbury, the Cup-holders, instead of which they smashed the fiddle and upset both Dewsbury and the prophets. Incidentally they qualified for their fifth final, which is a record for the Northern Union. _ _

It was a grand day for the job. Rain and snow had fallen for the previous 24 hours, but Saturday opened bright and clear and the conditions by raid-day were positively summer-like. Consequently the four special trains which the Warrington Club had organised for the journey to Oldham were well- patronised. Crowds besieged both Central and Arplay Stations, and somewhere about 4,000 people followed the team—a fine testimony to the truth uf the saying that nothing succeeds like success. Oldham was reached in smart time, hut with the ground-6 mile and a half from Glodwick-road Station the eager thousands from Warrington had to scurry a bit to see the kick- off. Once at Watersheddings, and the ground was found to belie its name. Snow mantled the hill-sides in all directions, but the famous headquarters of the Oldham Club leoked their best from a footballer's point of view. Under the bright sun and light breeze the turf had made a suprising recovery from the previous day's soaking, and was in absolutely persfect order for a fast game. The stands were rapidly filled by the eager throng, which included a thousand or more from Dewsbury. Warrington favours were ever ywhere,and ear-splitting rattles added to the chorus of acclamation as the teams appeared promptly to time, Dewsbury in bright blue jerseys and Warrington in the familiar primrose and blue. Both sides were fully represented and turned out as follows :

Dewsbury. Jackett, full hack; Rhodes, Ware, E. Ward, Sharpies, full back; Price, :Milner, half backs; N'Neill, Gatnett, Hamill, Abbishaw, Evans and Stringer, lore ards. Warrinoon.—Jolley, lull back; Bradshaw.lienwick, Tranter, Brookes, three-quarters ; Daintith, Nicholas, half backs; G Thomas, Cheaters, Skelhorne, Fearnley, R Thomas and Cox, forwards. Referee: G. F. Dickinson, Halifax. WARRIN3TON START WELL.

There was not a great deal of advantage in winning I the toss, but Warrington had this early success to I their credit and took up a position with their backs to the sun. Paddy O'Neill, the ex-Leigh forward, set the ball in motion for Dewsbury, and within 60 secs. the crowd was rocking with excitement. The War- rington forwards went away from the first neck with a tremendous burst and swept the Dewsbury men away like chaff. Well in the Yorkshire half Skelhorne picked up smartly and swung out a beautiful pass to Renwick. The Warrington rkipder took the ball on the run and when faced by Jackett be passed to Bradshaw. The latter had only to take the ball to score, but the pass was a bit high; Bradshaw was over- eager, and missed the ball amid a chorus of groans hich startled late-corners on the ground. It was a fine attacking movement badly finished, and might have spelt disaster to some League teams. But Warrington were only made the more eager. They fair'y peppered tie Dewsbury line, and the cheering was incessant as Brooks first forced ever for Rhodes to clear. and Jolley took 6 quick drcp at goal which was very near the mark. Dewsbury seemed to be bustled out of their wits and within five minutes Warrington got the substantial lead of five points. Renwick made a de-perate attempt to rush the Dee sbury cantles, and when challenged put his toe to the bal. Cox and Fesrnley were off like a flash and a sec nd's hesitation by Jacket: proved fatal. Cox secured and passing promptly to Fearnley the latter romped over the line near the pots amid a pe.fect salvo of cheering, which was renewed when Renwick kicked the goal. Up to this point the Dewsbury men had been overwhelmed but they rallied finely. The burly forwards began to heel out, and some smart passes were sent along ay Milner and Price. But the three-ouarters foand Warrington's third lino impassable and it was only by judicious cross-punting for the wings that the Warrington half was at last invaded. Sharpies made a strong run on the left, but was finely grassed by Bradshaw. The Blues kept it up, however, and Warrington were forced to defend. Jolley was called upon for the first time and punted beauti- fully, but the Tykes were persistent and a desperate rush saw Renwick collared near the line. Skelhorne and Cheaters came to the rescue and worked the ball away, Stringer marking in good position and hitting the upright with a fine shot at goal. The rebound of the ball might have put Warrington in a tangle but for the coolness of Tranter, who picked up and cleared beyond half way with a powerful left foot lunge. Dewsbury were still aggressive and the backs tried to exploit the passing game but with poor success. The centres were quite unable to break through and the wings never got much beyond the quarter-hue. Warriugton's defence was great, and the coolness of the four inside men resulted in a gradual clearance of the invasion. Daintith led the way back to centreaind set the three-quarters on the move. Dewsbury obstructed and were promptly penalised, Renwick kicking a magnificent goal from a position fully forty yards out and giving Warrington a seven points lead. The game continued at a very fast pace, and some great tackling was seen. Rhodes and Stringer made a brilliant effort on the Dewsbury right with a fine passing run, and the wing man was only stopped five yards from the line by Brooks. A desperate melee ensued near the flag, but Nicholas got hold and cleared with a Si onderful over-head punt from the goal line. A penalty against the Blues enabled Warrington to transf T play to tlio other er d and a remarkable change came over the scene. The Warrington forwards raced down to Jackett, who attempted to pass to a colleague. Skelhorne got one I hand to the ball and broke through, but was uratde I to bold the leather or he must have gone in under the posts. Warrington were now attacking brilliantly and Nicholas tricked his way past Milner, only to be laid out by Hammill and carried to the touch-line for repairs. Brooks took up the vacant position and Cheaters went to the wing. Warrington tried hard to get the threequarters moving, but a poor pass from Tranter to Renwick enabled Dewsbury to save the situation, and just before the interval Nicholas returned. Warrington kept the upper hand till the whistle blew with the score: Warrington 2 goals, 1 try (7 points) ; Dewsbury nil.

ball over the bar and raised Warrington's total to 12 points. Dewsbury made a spasmodic bur:A and Jolley was injured in the rush, Daintith having to fall back to the rear for a few minutes. The Blues had a big chance here, but some shocking pissing on the leit wing ruined the opportuliity. Warrington seemed content to play " keeps," and at a critical moment Ward followed up a punt, secured the ball on the bounce and dropped over the line near the Warring- ton posts. Stringer added a goal. There were still six minutes left for play, and Warrington showed their great reserve of strength by at once driving Dewebtry to the other end. Jolley made a glea.t run and punt which caught Jackett napping. The Warrington forwards were up in a trice, and Cox fielding beautifully on the run, passed to Chesters for the burly forward to gallop unopposed round the posts. Nicholas added another go4l, and sealed the fate of the cup-holders in pronounded style. Warrington held the advantage to the end, which came with the score reading : Warrington, 4 goals, 3 tries (17 points) ; Dewsbury, 1 goal, 1 try (5 points).

div.head: THRILLING SECOND HALF.
div.p: A THRILLING SECOND HALF.

Warrington again opened strongly, the forwards displaying brilliant footwork which harrassed Jacket t's charge. Dewsbury were all at sea in attempting to cope with Warrington's varieS moves and twice got penalised in good position, but neither Renwick nor Thomas could find the mark when they tried for goal. There was no holding Warrington at this period, and from a cross-kick by Skelhorne, Chesters cantered behind the posts, only to b.• ruled (if-side. Rhodes at last dribbled away and Dewsbury attacked. Time after time Jolley replied with beautiful punting and the Warrington citadel appeared invulnerable. Dewsbury had one big chance, however. A punt in the air gave thelforwarcls a chance and they descended upon Jolley like an avalanche. For a second the Warribgton custodian disappeared among the blue jerseys and what a roar there was when he emerged with the ball and his heel well down for a mark! The youngster was the essence of pluck and nerve and at this stage of the game became the idol of the crowd. Dewsbury had another shot at goal but Ware was yards wide, while a combined move by Milner, Ward, and Sharpies only ended in the last named being swept into touch at the Warrineton quarter. The Warrington players never lost their grip of the game, and the forwards seemed to become fresher and faster as time went on. Skelhorne again came into the picture with a brilliant solo effort which only ended inches from the line as be was tackled from behind. A great struggle ensued under the posts. Nicholas being foiled as he tried to bore his way through. Dewsbury could not get possession and from another pack the ball came out on the Warrington side. Fearnley was on the fringe of the pack. and snapping up the ball he dived over the line in the twinkling of an eye with his second try of the game. I'l he position was easy, and Nicholas calmly put the

div.head: GATE. The crowd was estimated at 15,000, and the receipts totalled ..4:25 ; of which Warrington take one-third.
div.p: THE GATE. The crowd was estimated at 15,000, and the receipts totalled ..4:25 ; of which Warrington take one-third.
COMMENTS BY THE CRITICS,
Most of the daily papers pay generous testimony to the merit of Warrington's victory. " Centre" of the " Daily News " writes : WONDERFUL FORWARDS.

The super-excellence of the Warrington forwards in the loose provided the greatest feature of an always interesting but not over urilliant contest. The Dews- bury men certainly had an even share in securing possession, but this encounter proved an exception to the rule that the securing of possession in the scrummage is nine-tenths of the battle. There was no holding the Lancashire forwards. They wheeled many of the scrums in tine style, and came away time and time again with the bail at their toes. They were simply irresistible, and the scoring goes to prove it, for each of their three tries are credited to the forwards rhey assisted their backs wonderfully well, and tackled low and surely. The Warrington scrummagers undoubtedly paved. the way of success. . _ _

The recta -prominent player on the field was undoubtedly Skelhorne the Warrington wing forward. He played a really magnificent game in the loose, and was ably supported by Chesters and Fearnley, the 53rumai5ge work and a great share of that done in the open being performed by the Thomases and Cox.

div.head: PACK OF WORRIERS.
div.p: A PACK OF WORRIERS.

Above everything, the Lancastrians had to thank their forwards for the victory. They were a pack of worriers. Giving away lumps of weight, they, never• theless. stuck gamely to their work in the fight, got a realonable amount of possession, and were infinitely superior in the loose. Breaking up quickly, they were always right on the top of the ball, and their pace and dash from start to finish were tremendous. Their tackling, too, was of the type designatei as grim, while some of their rushes proved that dribbling is still not a lost art in Northern Union football.—" Daily Mail.'

div.head: SPARKLING DISPLAY.
div.p: A SPARKLING DISPLAY.

The spectators were treated to a sparkling display of football which was full of interest and brought out many of the finer points of the gain°. The Warrington players were in splendid condition, especially the forvcards, and much of Warrington's success was entirely due to the excellent way in which their forwards fell back to support the defence. Than was nothing to equal it on the Dewsbury side, whose backs were often left unsupported, and during the game they gave away fully ten points.—" Manchester Guardian."
"THE FORWARDS WERE THE BOYS."
" W.L.5.." in the "Athletic News "writes :

It was like old times to see Warrington winning a great cup-fight as they did on Saturday at Water- sheddings. . . . In succession to the old brigade who in the last decennium won the Cup there have arisen in succession to Isherwood, Fish and Dickenson a comparatively young side of capable players,and these keen men fairly outplayed and outstayed the bigger and weightier opposition from Crown Plaits. On the day, and on the match, Warrington played the winning game ; they can now proceed to the final test at Headingly with some degree of confidence. They will not be beaten for lack of fitness or want of trying. Huddersfield will have a more difficult task than they had at Thrum Hall.

A regards the individual players,l liked young Jolley. He collected the ball confidently and well, and either with lusty lunge or else by swerving runs and passing he made good. He seemed to me to a rattling good little back. But when all was said and done, the forwards were the boys for me. They were splendid, and probably of the lot Sselnorne, who played himself to a standstill at one stage,was the best. He is really a fine player."

A REVELATION. The play of the Warrington men, and especially cf their forwards, was a revelaticn to those onlookers at Oldham who had previously seen little of their play during the season. Dewsbury were practically a beaten side from the first minute. Though strong, fast, and determined, Warrington certainly cannot be classed as a clever and accomplished team. They are a good cup- fighters—that, and nothing more. They are such a side that it is probable they will bustle even the lludderileld backs, and are not likely to be in the least inferior to the Fartown forwards ; hut so far as the honours of the final are concerned, the opinion may at once be given that a few chances will be quite sufficient for Huddersfield to carry off the cup. It is due to the Warrington forwards to say that though their play was tremendously earnest and keen,tbere was nothing in any way reprehensible about it.—" Yorkshire Post."

div.p: LATCHFORD _RECREATION V STOCKTON HEATH.

At Victoria Park on Saturday. The Latchford forwarOs soon settled down to work, and following a capital centre by Cnerratt, Woodhead opened their score in the first five minutes. Still keeging up the pressure Rigby quickly added a second point fer them. Midfield play followed for some time. From a good run by Antrobus and Blease, Lockhart shot past, whilst a few minutes later Harrison cleared well from Holmes. , The Rees again took up the running and before the interval -arrived Cherratt increused their tttal to three. Half-time :—Latchford Recreation, three goals; Stockton Heath, nil. In the second half the game was of a very even nature. With only 10 minutes to go, Hawthorne added a fourth point for the Recreation with a wonderful drive, whilst Lockhart scored for Stockton Heath, the game ending :—Latchford Recreation, four goals ; Stockton Heath, one goal. ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CENTRE).

The close season up to the present has been a failure, as far as local rods are concerned. The eels undoub- tedly want warmer weather to get them on the run, especially those which frequent the canals. Several catches have been taken from the Dee and the Gowy, but nothing in comparison with previous close seasons, and anglers may rest assured that as long as the cold snaps continue, there will be no groat bags taken. Trout also have been conapicious by their absence and there is not yet a decent specimen marked up on the board. The heaviest does not reach Suz. Pike are also in their favorite .aunts still, and those anglers who have had a few days pikiug hare failed miserably in their attempt to net the " Specials " placed on the list for them.

Those who visited the Dee and the Gowy on Sunday had almost a blank day. After the fresh during the latter part of last week, it could only be expected that the Gowy would not be favourable to offer good sport..
Unless there is a great change in the weather, the only thing to look forward to is the rambling match. A.S.

div.p: The Warrington P.S.A. Society,

A musioal service in connection with this s ciety was held on Sunday in the Park Picture Palen. There was a large attendance, presided over. by the Rev. N. Cooper. After the opening hymn, Mr. Nelson (pre,ident) read the 33rd Psalm. The Sylvan Quartette Party rendered "There is a Green Hill." Mr. Millington followed with a piccolo solo with orchestral accompaniment. —The Chairman, before calling upon *Madam Sara Silcock to sing "Nearer my God to Thee" commented upon the fact that that was the anniversary of the loss of the Titanic. Messrs. Sephton and Dutton then gave the duet" Watchman what of the night." The chairman, in the couise of an address, said he believed that there was good in all music, of whatever kind. He pro- ceeded to draw some very useful lessons from the subject of the duet "Watchman what of the night." He said that humanity had ever been looking for the dawn —a glorious dawn—and although there was much that was dark and dismal, a great deal had already been done to improve the lot of man. Still as much remained to be done, particularly for the power classes. He asked all to strive after nobler ideals. Mr. S. Ankland followed with the concertina solo. "The Volunteer Organist" The Sylvan quartette party next gave" God is a Spirit." Madam Bessie Ecke'aey effectively rendered "Ye that are Weary." Another auet "Love Divine " was contributed by Madam Silcock and Mr. Sephton The orchestra, in charge of Mr. Turner, gave their gplection in fine style. The accompanists were Miss Butterworth and Mr. Trow. The thanks of the Society were expressed by Mr. W. Clegg to all who had sustained the programme, and to Mr. Starkey, who had arranged it, and to whom great credit was due.
RIR. HARVEY U. ADAMS, non, secretary of the Commemoration Committee.

common saying about an impersonation of an ordinary well-graced actor is "How did he do it ?" It should rather be, I think, "What impression does he give? What does he make you feel ?" ITHE STUDY OF SHYLOCK.

If there were no preconceived notion in my mind of the character of Shylock as Shakespeare has limned him for us.l think the effect of Mr. Charles Law's acting of the part would have been to create in me an idea of incongruity in the Jew's proceedings. and the forming of a somewhat low estimate of the character intellectually, apart from moral considerations, savouring more of the modern type than of the Oriental Jew of a period when much of the Eastern dignity of the race was in full preservation. Eastern dignity is not a thing of pomp. It consists of natural calmness, a tranquil force, speech without effort, attitudes in which there is neither apparent study nor accidental awkwardness. In this respect, it appeared to me that Mr. Law failed to realise the calm dignity of • the old Hebrew, who links himself on to the Father of his race and shows in all his proceedings a proper regard for the sacred character of the nation to which he belongs. Undoubtedly there were fine passages in which Mr. Law showed to advantage, but there was a lack of cohesion in the tones employed by him, and on many occasions he lapsed into a light utterance of phrases which reminded one rather of the suave professional manner than the serious and measured tones of the Shylock we have imagined to ourselves. Mr. Law has a tendency to degenerate in attempting the simulation of passion into violence and rant and in Shylock he displayed an agility in skipping about the stage which we thought was quite out of accord with the age and character of the Jew. Mr. Law's actirg in the Court scene, especially at the close, was exceptionally, good, though he did not succeed in evoking the feeling of sympathy and commiseration in his overthrow which we should have liked.

Mr. W.P. Ashton was elaborated to the verge' of boredom. We no longer wonder that thie chaLcter is frequently omitted from the acting version of the play.

ARTISTRY OF THE LADIES. I now come to the most agreeable part of my duty—the mention of the ladies in the play—and am delighted that I am able to speak of them enthusiastically. First of cow se, a tribute must be paid to Miss Gladya Adams' most exquisite performance of Poi tia- The winsomeness, buoyancy and coquettish ness of her impersonation of all that 1,5 brightest in womanhood, the skill of her, - performance, its variety, its gesture and pantomime, even its pretty fidgettings were all as full of good art as of charming nature. Notwithstanding a somewhat rapid deliver 9 of her words, Miss Adams was exceedingb: clear in her enunciation, and it appears to tfr, impossible to have found a better exponetw of Portia than she was. Next in order conies Nerissa, played bY, Mrs. Garton Stone, and though she did 11.0 t quite succeed in in vesting it with the requisite Shakespearian cast of humour, she was never- theless very charming, if with a modern manner. The Jessica of the play was impersonated by Mrs. Charles Law on Wednesday evening, by whom it was very intelligently repre- sented. A "most sweet Jew" as Launcelot describes her. Jessica on Thursday evening was played by Miss Milly Truslove, with equal success. There were many minor parts, and numbers of ladies and gentlemen who i ' appeared n the various scenes, all of whom looked (and deported themselves) well, and, lent a most finished and well-appointea appearance to the scene. - " MACBETH."

This great tragedy of Shakespeare's was produced last (Friday) night, and will agalo be played to-night (Saturday). A repetition of the great success of two years back has been recorded, both in attend- ance and in the presentation of the plaY, under the able direction of Mr. Charles Law, who also plays the principal part, Macbeth. Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., repeats his assumP- tion of Macduff ; Mr. H. M. Ashton that of Banquo ; Mr. W. H. Brown, Rosse ; Mr. it Hallard, the Porter; Mr. Harvey Adams, the Ist Witch, and Mrs. H. E. Griffiths. tne 3rd Witch, the 2nd Witch being now played by Mr. John Lowe. One of the most attrac- tive features in the reproduction of this plal is the opportunity afforded of witnessing the unique performance, viewed from the amateur standpoint, of Mrs. Robert Garnett, as Lady Macbeth. Not only for the benefit of the Infirmary (a deserving object enough) but for the intellectual benefit of the individual, we would strongly recommend all who have not seen it to avail themselves of the opportunity to-night. The piece is magnificently produced and the acting throughout is of a very high order There are very many of the subsidiary Parts in other hands than those of the previous productions. Should there be occasion for special corn- ment on any new feature in the acting,' maSr take an opportunity briPfly to call attention to it in a subsequent issue. I trust that the performances may yield a. handsome surplus for the benefit of the Infirmary.
ALFRED PERRIS.

div.head: SPIRIT OF COMEDY.
div.p: THE SPIRIT OF COMEDY.

Of the other male parts, Mr. Harvey 0. Adams as Gratiano and Mr. H. M. Ashton as Launcelot Gobbo, must be singled out as having approached most nearly in fidelity to truth to the spirit of Shakespearian comedy —though in Mr. Adams' acting there was a slight tendency to draw upon his reserve of tragic power in certain passages which caused us to lose touch with the character. Mr. Ashton most certainly succeeded in identifying himself with the character of Launcelot very effectually. The Old Gobbo of Mr. A. Chester had not the necessary unction and did not, therefore, furnish an adequate foil for Launcelot in specifying his wishes to Bassanio.

The Bassani° of Mr. John Lowe was very good, though his delivery of the lines was a little heavy and laboured at times, and his movements on the stage are apt to be a little impetuous. Mr. W. H. Brown as Antonio distinguished himself greatly,his fine appear- ance and physique being most noticeable, and he has learned to move upon the stage with much greater ease. His lines also were spoken clearly and with expression."Atainted wether of the flock " was certainly not interpreted as indicating advanced years in Antonio's case, for he was represented as one in the bloom of manhood.

The Lorenzo of Mr. Leslie L. Langford was very nicely played, the beautiful lines in the last scene being spoken very effectively, though a little too ponderously dealt with, a light and delicate utterance being so much more in harmony with the spirit of the scene. Salanio and Salarino, by Mr. T. B. Lawton and Mr. A. C. Hodgson, were not quite the characters we always judged them to be in the opening scene with Antonio. Their mirth and laughter over the delivery of their lines—somewhat forced and not following naturally their -words—gave them the aspect of mere gadflies rather than respected and esteemed friends of Antonio's and Bassanio's. But I may err in blaming them for this interpretation. The Prince of Morocco by

SHAKESPEARE WEEK. AMATEURS IN "THE MERCHANT OF VENICE " AND " MACBETH," - SUCCESSFUL COMMEMORATION. The Shakespearian Commemoration per- formances, which are now becoming an institution in Warrington, were begun at the Royal Court Theatre on Wednesday night with the presentation of" The Merchant of Venice." There was a well-filled house, and an audience evidently disposed to accept with favour the efforts of the amateur actors and actresses who had applied themselves so assiduously to the acquirement, and had succeeded in attaining to a degree of efficiency which is not commonly found in such representations. ' It may be said at once that the all-round presentation of this ever fresh and absorbing play—the comedy portion perhaps most con- spicuously—was very creditable to all con- cerned, but especially so to the director and producer, Mr. Charles Law. The mounting of the piece was most effective—in perfect taste,nothing garish and —with the exception of the Court scene, which appeared to lack something of the impressiveness with which we have always associated it—everything was appropriate, and the fair moonlight scene of the last act was not unworthy even of Shakespeare's moonlit poetry. With regard to the acting. I think it is ' to the advantage of those interested that a healthy criticism should be applied. The
